en: The Brahmajāla Sūtra: The Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Spoken by Vairocana Buddha, Number Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
*Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra*, Fascicle One, composed by the monk Shengzhuang of Chongyi Temple. In order to explain this sūtra, it shall be analyzed through five gates:

(1) the title and the occasion for the arising of the teaching; (2) the discernment of the sūtra’s essential doctrine and substance; (3) the determination of the scope of the teaching; (4) the identification of the capacities of the beings to whom the teaching is addressed; and (5) the evaluation [of the teaching].

In the first section of this commentary, "Explaining the Title," we first address the relationship between the teaching and the title, followed by an analysis of how the scripture derives its name; this is the initial part.

Now, as for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is profound and still, its principle transcending the realm of form and appearance. The path of awakening is remote and mysterious, its traces hidden beyond the reach of names and words.

Yet, when the capacity of the practitioner is ready, the response is certain, like water or a mirror reflecting whatever comes before them. When conditions diminish, this penetration is unimpeded, resembling an empty valley.
The echoing resonance of this cliff is not merely the manifestation of the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) responding to beings through boundless transformations;

it reveals the wondrous scriptures of the Three Vehicles and expounds the true meaning for the Eight Classes of Beings. Thus, the Great Dharma is established as the primary teaching, causing the sun of wisdom to shine brightly upon the dark alleys, while the Great Way is illuminated, launching the compassionate vessel across the sea of desire.
Its wondrous functions are inconceivable, and its divine efficacy is unfathomable.
Now, this sutra is the secret treasury of all Buddhas and the fundamental cause of Bodhisattvas;

by opening up the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and cultivating the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the fruit becomes ever more pure. It arrays the three bodies (*trikāya*) and fully illuminates with the ten thousand virtues.
As for what is called the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, this is the general title of this single section, so named because it was preached upon observing the net of the Brahma King.
Therefore, it is called the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* because it is eternal (*nitya*) and its prior dharma remains unchanged from beginning to end; thus it is designated as "eternal.

Because it involves abandoning the heterodox and returning to the orthodox, it is termed "dharma" (*dharma*). Regarding the statement that it was spoken by Vairocana Buddha, this refers to the title of the speaker.
"Vairocana" is translated here as "Pure and Full" (*viśuddha-pūrṇa*); because he is eternally free from the two obstacles and his two fruits are perfectly complete, he is named "Pure."

The "Chapter on the Ground of Mind" (*Cittabhūmi-parivarta*) is a specific title within this section. Because these forty stages serve as the basis for practitioners of contemplation and can encompass the mind of contemplative practice, they are called the "Ground of Mind.
As for "Bodhisattva," this is translated here as "one who awakens sentient beings" (*bodhisattva*).

Because they seek supreme enlightenment above and rescue the multitude of living beings below, they are termed "awakening sentient beings" based on their objective sphere of focus; this is a possessive compound (*sādhana* or *matup* suffix).
The second section explains how various sūtras receive their names. Generally speaking, there are seven ways in which sūtras are named:
first, by way of the person; second, by way of the dharma; third, by way of a metaphor; fourth, by way of both person and dharma;
fifth, by way of both person and metaphor; sixth, by way of both dharma and metaphor; and seventh, by way of person, dharma, and metaphor. [The first category] is naming by way of the person.
Furthermore, there are four ways in which a name is established: first, a sutra receives its name from the person who speaks it, such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*;
second, a sutra receives its name from the person who asks the questions, such as the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*;

third, a sutra receives its name from the person for whom it is intended, such as the *Tiwei jing* (*Upāli-sūtra*); and fourth, a sutra receives its name from the person who is the subject of its exposition, such as...
The *Sūtra of Prince Sudāna* and other such works are called "sūtras named after persons.
Those named after the Dharma derive their titles from the phenomena they expound, such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Those named after metaphors include the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*.
Those named after both persons and the Dharma include the *Śrīmaddevī-bhaṭṭārikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Those sūtras that derive their names from persons and metaphors include this *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (spoken by the Buddha Rocana), which derives its name from both a person and a metaphor;

those that derive their names from dharmas and metaphors include the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (the Lotus Sūtra); and those that derive their names from persons, dharmas, and metaphors include the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
As for the present sūtra, it is named after a person and a metaphor, according to the *ṣaṣṭhī-vigraha* (genitive compound) among the six types of grammatical analysis.
The Master Śīla explains that some say a sutra is named after its subject matter, such as the *Śuṣkavṛkṣa-sūtra*.
However, since the *Śuṣkavṛkṣa-sūtra* is named after both its doctrine (*dharma*) and its metaphor (*upamā*), this [principle] does not apply here.

Second, regarding the determination of the essence (*śarīra*) of the sutra: first the doctrine (*siddhānta*), then the essence. Within the doctrine, there are two parts; first, a general discussion of all [sutras].

The Pope later separately elucidated this scripture’s "pervasive penetration of the schools" (*zongtong bianzhujiaozong*), which states that the teachings proclaimed throughout the Tathāgata’s single lifetime consist of no more than three types:
first, the school that conceals emptiness and reveals existence; second, the school that conceals existence and teaches emptiness;
and third, the school that remains far removed from both extremes. Regarding what is called the school that conceals emptiness and reveals existence: it refers to...

The various Hīnayāna sūtras, such as those on the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths, which implicitly teach the school that propounds emptiness—including the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and the teachings on signlessness—this is called the Wheel of Signlessness (*animitta-dharmacakra*). As stated in the second fascicle of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*:
"In the past, during the second period, the Bhagavān taught solely for those who had set out in the cultivation of the Mahāyāna, based upon..."
All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa; thus,
although the turning of the wheel of Dharma through the mode of secret intention was most marvelous and exceedingly rare,
the wheel of Dharma turned at that time was still surpassable, possessed of room for further interpretation, and of provisional meaning, being far removed from [the ultimate].
The school of the two extremes refers to the definitive Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
This is precisely what is called the Wheel of Dharma that is Fully Manifested (*vibhaktika-dharmacakra*). As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana*:

"O Bhagavat, at this present third period, for the sake of those who have set out in all vehicles, you have universally taught—in reliance upon all phenomena—that they are all without intrinsic nature, without arising, without cessation, and primordially quiescent."
The turning of the Wheel of Dharma that reveals the nature of tranquility, self-nature nirvāṇa, and lack of intrinsic nature is the foremost marvel and most rare occurrence;
this Wheel of Dharma turned by the Bhagavān at present is unsurpassed, admits of no further addition, is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and is not a basis for disputes.
This was proclaimed by the great Bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and Asaṅga.

By composing works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, he thoroughly elucidated the true doctrine, departing from the attachments to existence and non-existence and realizing the Middle Way, as stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*:
"False conceptualization exists; herein both [existence and non-existence] are entirely absent. Herein there is only emptiness, and that [emptiness] also exists therein.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty, because of existence, non-existence, and the existence thereof."

This accords with the Middle Way and specifically reveals that the primary tenet expounded by this sutra is the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi-dharmamukha*), which constitutes its central doctrine.

The Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground shall be explained in detail according to the text. Next, to clarify the essence: regarding the essence of the teaching that expresses [this truth], there are briefly four gates.
First, the gate of subsuming the delusive and returning to the True: all phenomena have True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their essence, as stated in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
The Sūtras state that all phenomena (*dharma*) are suchness (*tathatā*). If one relies on this perspective, the true teaching of the Tathāgata has suchness as its essence.
Second is the perspective of subsuming the branches back into the root: all phenomena have consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their essence. As the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
"All objects of cognition are manifested solely by consciousness. If one relies on this perspective, the true teaching of the Tathāgata...
The teaching states that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the essence [of mind], because external phenomena apart from consciousness cannot be apprehended. Now, there are two kinds of consciousness:
namely, the consciousness of the speaker and the consciousness of the listener. It is not yet known which consciousness constitutes the essence of the holy teaching.
To explain: in the West (India), there are three interpretations. First, Nāgasena—translated here as Longjun (Dragon Army)—who is also called Fuguo (Fruit of the Buddha).
Because there is no quality of sound, the sixth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
'As the World-Honored One has said, from the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I entered parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken in the interval.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 425, also states:"
Since my attainment of enlightenment, I have not uttered a single word. Furthermore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Whoever sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Because such scriptural injunctions and proofs are numerous, we know that in the stage of the Tathāgata, there are no qualities of form or sound. If one relies on this...
It is taught that the consciousness of the listener alone constitutes the essence of the teaching; as the *Nirākāra-viniścaya-śāstra* states:
"The collection of appearances manifesting upon the consciousness of the listener constitutes the essence of the sūtra. Second, the master Sthiramati says:

"By the power of the Tathāgata’s compassion and original vows, the aspects of word and meaning manifest upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata. According to this explanation, it is the speaker alone who [manifests the teaching].

Consciousness is taken as the essence of the sūtra because all aspects of the perceived and the perceiver (*nimittabhāga* and *darśanabhāga*) within the defiled consciousness of all sentient beings are of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpitasvabhāva*), and therefore are not the essence of the sūtra.

Third, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla states that it is precisely the consciousness of the speaker that constitutes the essence of the sūtra, because the Tathāgata’s teaching flows forth from the pure *dharmadhātu*. This includes...
1. Regarding the body of the Sūtra as the consciousness of the hearer: because it is able to produce understanding, this is the "subsuming the provisional for the real" perspective.
2. Regarding the body of the Tathāgata’s holy teaching as sound: because apart from sound, the sets of names, phrases, and syllables have no separate essence.
3. Regarding the fixed essence of the categories of phenomena (*dharmasaṃkhyā*): the various schools differ; the Sarvāstivādins maintain that the essence of the Buddha’s teaching is sound.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 126, states: "What is the Buddha’s teaching (*buddha-vacana*)?
It refers to the Buddha’s speech, utterances, discourses, vocal sounds, paths of speech, verbal karma, and verbal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*); this is called the Buddha’s teaching. Question:

For what reason is the Buddha’s teaching exclusively verbal intimation and not non-intimation (*avijñapti*)? Answer: Because it produces correct understanding in others, it is called the Buddha’s teaching.

He is currently producing understanding solely through manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) and not through non-manifest action (*avijñapti*). Question: What constitutes the essence of such Buddhist teachings? Answer:
Those who speak thus maintain that verbal action (*vāg-karman*) constitutes the essence, because what is intended by the Buddha’s mind is heard by others; this is explained in detail as is customary.

Regarding the Sautrāntika school’s own position, there are three interpretations: first, it is said that the essence of Buddhist teaching is the sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*), which is called "name" (*nāman*).

First, it is said that because sound and its separation have no distinct entities, they are one; furthermore, since the sacred teachings state that [sound] is apprehended solely by the mental consciousness, its intrinsic nature consists of the conventional sound of the continuity included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Second, it is said that both conventional and real sounds constitute its nature;

according to the Mahāyāna, its intrinsic nature consists of the bodies of phonemes, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), as well as the meanings they express, with "sound" being the substance within that essence.

The bodies of phonemes (*śabda-kāya*), names (*nāma-kāya*), and phrases (*vyañjana-kāya*) are called the "expressors" (*abhidhāna*); all phenomena (*dharma*) as they correspondingly apply are called the "expressed" (*abhidheya*).

Thus, these meanings of the expressors and the expressed constitute the essence of the *sūtra*, because both the words and the meaning can generate correct understanding, and because discourse cannot be established apart from that which is expressed.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81, and so forth: [text continues].
What constitutes its essence? Briefly stated, the essence of a sūtra is twofold: first, the letter (vyañjana), and second, the meaning (artha).
The letter is the support, and the meaning is that which is supported. These two together are collectively termed the "entirety of the objects of all that is to be known" (sarvajñeya-viṣaya).
What is meant by "letter"? There are six kinds: first, the body of names (nāma-kāya); second, the body of phrases (pada-kāya); third, the body of phonemes (vyañjana-kāya); fourth, ... [and so forth].
Regarding the five [types of] speech and the six aspects of the mode of activity (*ākāra*), the commentary explains: these six kinds are all capable of manifesting meaning;
therefore, they are called "phrases" (*vyañjana*), because they are phrases in the sense that they can manifest meaning.

Furthermore, it is said that "name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*) refer to conventional designations (*adhivacana*) commonly known; these, in brief, are of twelve types: first, nominal names (*prajñaptināman*); second, substantial names (*dravyanāman*).
1. The name based on the object; 2. The name based on the three [aspects]; 3. The name based on association with the same class; 4. The name based on association with a different class;
5. The name based on following a quality; 6. The name based on metaphorical designation; 7. The name based on what is commonly understood; 8. The name based on what is not commonly understood;
9. The manifest name; 10. The non-manifest name; 11. The abbreviated name; 12. The extensive name.

"Provisional designation" refers to the provisional establishment of names such as "self," "sentient being," and "life-principle" with respect to the internal, and the provisional establishment of names such as "vase" and "garment" with respect to the external.

"Designation of a real entity" refers to the provisional establishment of names such as "eye" and so forth within the referential objects of the various characteristics of the eye and so forth, and of form and so forth.
"Designation corresponding to a similar category" refers to [the designation of] sentient beings, form, sensation, and the primary elements.
Names that designate different categories (*nāma-viśeṣa-saṃprayukta*) refer to names such as "Buddhadatta," "Guṇamitra," "blue," or "yellow.

Names that follow from qualities (*guṇānuvidhāyin*) refer to such as "form" (*rūpa*) because it undergoes transformation (*vipariṇāma*), "feeling" (*vedanā*) because it experiences (*anubhavati*), and "sun" (*sūrya*) because it emits light (*prabhāsvara*).
Names that are conventional designations (*prajñapti-nāma*) refer to calling greed "wealth" (*dhana*), or other such instances where [the name] does not depend on [any other factor].
A name whose referent is commonly understood is one where the name and its designated object are identical;

that is, it is a name for which the conventional designation is universally recognized. A name that is the opposite of this is one whose referent is not commonly understood. An explicit name is one whose meaning is easily understood.
A non-explicit name is one whose meaning is difficult to understand, such as the *Dhāraṇī-mantras* and so forth. An abbreviated name is one consisting of a single syllable.
"Extensive names" refers to those consisting of many syllables. "Phrases" refers to the completion of names and words.
Furthermore, there are six types: first, incomplete phrases; second, complete phrases; third, resultant phrases; fourth, causal phrases;
fifth, indicative phrases; and sixth, explanatory phrases. An incomplete phrase refers to one in which the wording is not exhaustive.
One should know that if the meaning is not ultimately complete, it is only through the second line that it becomes fully perfected.
As it is said: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good; thoroughly restrain your own mind—this is the sacred teaching of all Buddhas.
If one were to say only "commit no evil," the phrasing would not be complete; if one were to say only "those who commit evil," the meaning would not be [fully realized].
Ultimately, it is only by not performing further [actions] that one attains fulfillment; this refers to the "fulfilled phrase" (*pariniṣpanna-pada*) and the "established phrase" (*siddha-pada*).

Regarding the established phrase: it means that a preceding phrase is only established by means of a subsequent phrase. For example, when it is said, "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent;

they have the nature of arising and ceasing; what arises must perish; therefore, their stillness is bliss," herein, in order to establish the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, the subsequent statement is made.

Regarding the statement that there are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing: the former is the "probandum" (the thing to be established), which is the "sentence of the probandum"; the latter is the "probans" (the means of establishment), which is the "sentence of the probans.

The "indicative sentence" (*uddeśa-pada*) is, for example, the statement "the nature of goodness. The "explanatory sentence" (*nirdeśa-pada*) refers to the phrase "properly proceeding toward a true person" (*samyak-satpuruṣa-gati*).
The "body of words" (*vyañjana-kāya*) refers to the forty-four letters, whether ultimate or non-ultimate, which serve as the basis for names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*). Within this context:
Desire is the head of names; a name is the head of phrases. A phrase must have a name, and a name must have syllables (*vyañjana*).
If there were only a single syllable, it would not constitute a phrase. Furthermore, if there were a syllable not subsumed under a name, it would be a mere syllable without a name.
Question: For what reason are the three types of bodies—name and so forth—established? Answer: It is for the purpose of causing the reception of various designations (*adhivacana*).
Question: What is the meaning of the term "name" (*nāman*)? Answer: It is called "name" because it causes various things to be mutually understood;
it is called "name" because it causes the mind to form various mental images;
and it is called "name" because it is that which is summoned by speech. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is so named because it possesses these three meanings.
Regarding "name" (*nāman*), it refers to that which corresponds exactly to what has been done; for this purpose, the term "suchness" (*tathatā*) is established.

Just as when seeking [something], one should follow the composition of verses so that they accord with the meaning, it should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, the term "summoning" (*ākāra*) carries the sense of "conjoining. Moreover, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Because it gathers all names and ultimately clarifies meanings that are not directly perceived, it is called a 'phrase' (*pada*); it follows the manifestation of names."
Because it consists of phrases, it is called "text. One should know that speech is briefly comprised of eight factors: first, excellence; second, beauty; and so forth.
Due to the correspondence of those words, phrases, and sentences, up to the factor of constant application and the provisions for the path, one is able to preach the True Dharma.
Regarding "speech of excellence": because it takes the palace of Nirvāṇa as its primary goal, it is excellent. Regarding "speech of beauty": its sound...
It is pure and beautiful because it is like the voice of the kalaviṅka bird; it is clear because its terminology, phrases, and syllables are all skillful;
it is easy to understand because it is explained with clever discernment; it is pleasant to hear because it draws out the meaning of the Dharma;
it is independent because it does not rely on the hope that others will believe it; and it is non-contradictory because it is spoken with moderation.
Therefore, "boundless speech" refers to its vast skillfulness, and so forth, as extensively explained.

Regarding the "characteristics of practice," this refers to the correspondence with the aggregates (*skandha*), the correspondence with the elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, up to such correspondences in speech.

Regarding "inquiry according to capacity," this refers to the arising of discourse based on questions posed according to the listener's capacity. The explanation states that these six types are all termed [speech].

The composition [of this treatise] is for the purpose of being able to reveal the meaning that is to be explained. Furthermore, what constitutes that "meaning"? It should be known that, briefly, there are ten kinds:

first, the meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*); second, the meaning of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); third, the meaning of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth; fourth, the meaning of the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*);
fifth, the meaning of faults (*ādīnava*); sixth, the meaning of benefits (*anuśaṃsa*); seventh, the meaning of the objects to be countered (*vipakṣa*). Eighth...

The meaning of "that which can treat" (the therapeutic); ninth, the concise meaning; tenth, the extensive meaning. Regarding the meaning of the "stages" (*bhūmi*), there are briefly five stages: first, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*);
second, the stage of application (*prayoga-bhūmi*); third, the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*); fourth, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*); and fifth, the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).

Regarding the meaning of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), one should know that there are five kinds of characteristics: first, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); second, the... [general characteristic]... [and so forth].

The three common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) are: first, the conventionally established characteristic (prajñapti-lakṣaṇa); second, the causal characteristic (hetu-lakṣaṇa); and third, the resultant characteristic (phala-lakṣaṇa).

Regarding the meaning of "attention" (*manasikāra*) and so forth, it refers to the seven types of attention. Regarding the bases (*āśraya*) for the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and so forth, there are briefly three kinds:

first, the basis of entities (*vastv-āśraya*); second, the basis of time (*kāla-āśraya*); and third, the basis of persons (*pudgala-āśraya*). Furthermore, the basis of entities has three [subdivisions].
There are three kinds of bases for activity: first, the basis of fundamental matters; second, the basis of matters concerning the attainment of skillful means;
and third, the basis of matters concerning compassion for others. These are explained at length in that [text]. Regarding the bases of time, there are briefly three kinds of verbal objects:
first, verbal objects of the past; second, verbal objects of the future; and third, verbal objects of the present.

Regarding the basis for persons (*pudgala*): as for the meaning of the defects of entities such as the great faculties, in brief, it refers to generating revulsion toward that which is to be reviled, whether it be a phenomenon (*dharma*) or a person (*pudgala*).
As for the meaning of the excellence of phenomena or persons, in brief, it refers to generating praise toward that which is to be praised, whether it be a phenomenon or a person.
Regarding the meaning of what is to be remedied by the *pudgala*, in brief, it refers to all defiled activities.
Regarding the meaning of what can remedy this, in brief, it refers to all purified activities. The concise meaning is the teaching on the corresponding association of phenomena of the same class;
the extensive meaning is the teaching on the corresponding association of phenomena of different classes. The explanation is as stated above.

The six phonemes (*vyañjana*) and ten meanings (*artha*) that have been explained as being able to generate correct understanding are all designated as "substance" (*tattva*). This is the actual meaning;
however, in other places, it is said that names (*nāman*) and so forth constitute the substance, or that sound (*ghoṣa*) does, or that sound, phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) do.
These various explanations are not mutually contradictory, as each is based on a particular sense.
Third, regarding the classification of the categories of the teaching (*śāsana*), there are again three types: first, the twelvefold division of the teaching;
second, the inclusion of the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*); and third, the inclusion of the twelvefold division of the teaching within the two baskets.

As for the inclusion of the twelvefold division of the teaching according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*, this present sutra is comprised within the *geya*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, and *vaipulya* divisions of the twelvefold teaching—specifically, it is said to belong to the four [latter] divisions.
The Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages of Mind (*daśa-citta-bhūmi*) belongs to the Vaipulya section;

it correctly reveals the characteristics of the precepts and employs causal analysis and parables to clarify its meaning, thus belonging to the Avadāna section as explained below. The statement, "For example, like the sun and moon," refers to the verses of the subsequent sutra and is termed *geya* (recited verse).
If one discusses its general inclusion within the *sūtra* genre, it is also subsumed under the Sūtra Piṭaka among the Three Piṭakas.
This is included within the *Vinaya-piṭaka* (the Treasury of Discipline) among the two treasuries, specifically subsumed under the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Fourth, clarifying the types of practitioners for whom the teaching is intended:

generally speaking, there are five such types for whom the teaching is intended—namely, those with fixed natures in the three vehicles, those with indeterminate natures, and fifth, those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa. This sutra is intended only for...
Because [the audience consists of] Bodhisattvas and those of indeterminate nature, this sutra is taught for them and not for the other three [vehicles].
At that time, Śākyamuni himself provides the fifth section, which is the formal analysis and correct interpretation of the text; this current chapter is largely divided into three parts:
first, the introductory section (nidāna), also called the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, the words of Śākyamuni Buddha...
In this world, the section following "Next, the clear exposition" is also called the "Section on What is Taught in the Holy Teaching.
Third, at the end of the second fascicle, from "As suchness, all... onwards, is the section clarifying the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation), also called the "Section on Following the Teaching in Practice.
The distinct meanings of these three sections are as explained in the usual commentaries on the sutras. From "The Buddha Śākyamuni said... onwards, the second part clarifies the holy teaching.
The division of the text as explained has two parts: first, the detailed exposition; second, the summary at the end of the section on Śākyamuni Buddha’s preaching of the *Upapadma* [Lotus].
Within the detailed exposition, there are further two divisions: first, the clarification of the meaning of the "mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*);
second, the explanation of the practices to be cultivated. The "mind-ground" is precisely that which is relied upon—the locus of reliance for the mind.
The term "mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*) is explained as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound, meaning that the mind is the ground;

alternatively, it is explained as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound, meaning that the mind itself is the ground, because the mind is the ground. Furthermore, at this time, Śākyamuni descends from the initial lotus.
Regarding the second explanation, the practice cultivated is the "supporter" (*āśraya*), because the practice cultivated is that which issues forth based upon the aforementioned mind-ground.
In this context, "ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to all the conditioned and unconditioned virtues present within the forty mental states;
because it serves as the superior support for the practices cultivated therein, enabling them to increase, it is called a "ground.
Regarding the precepts cultivated, they are regulated by relying upon this ground. Therefore, herein we first explain the ground that serves as the basis, and subsequently clarify [the precepts].

Regarding the "Practices Previously Cultivated," there are two parts: first, the formal explanation of the meaning of the *cittabhūmi* (stages of the mind), and second, the encouragement to uphold and propagate [the teaching] at the beginning of the second fascicle.
Within the first part, the formal explanation, the text is divided into four sections: first, the question; second, the brief answer; third, the repeated request;
and fourth, the Tathāgata’s detailed exposition. These four sections are as explained above in the preceding fascicle.

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up from among the dharma-gates of ineffable teachings as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers—that portion of the Ground of the Mind (Cittabhūmi) which is like the tip of a hair—and said:

"This has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, shall be taught by the Buddhas of the future, and is now being taught by the Buddhas of the present. It is that which the Bodhisattvas of the three periods have studied, will study, and are now studying; it is that which I have [already] taught a hundred times."
Having practiced this mind-ground for kalpas, I am named Vairocana. You Buddhas, turn what I have spoken over to all sentient beings to open the path of the mind-ground.

At that time, upon the lion throne of radiant celestial light in the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury World, Vairocana Buddha emitted a light, and that light announced to the Buddhas upon the thousand petals: "Hold this Dharma of my mind-ground."

Having departed from the Chapter on the Gate, he again manifested as thousands of billions of Śākyamunis and taught the Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Supreme Ground of the Mind to all sentient beings in succession.
"You should receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice it with single-minded devotion."
Volume Two. The Sūtra says: At that time, Vairocana... [The second section on] Exhorting to Uphold and Propagate has two parts:

first, clarifying Vairocana Buddha’s exhortation to uphold and propagate; next, from "At that time, the Buddhas upon the thousand petals" onwards, clarifying Śākyamuni Buddha’s reception and propagation.
Within the former, there are four sections: first, concluding the preceding discourse.
The second part shows that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past were able to preach without falsehood;

the third part, beginning with "Furthermore, after I had completed a hundred kalpas," reveals that his practice was fulfilled and he attained the fruit; the fourth part, beginning with "You Buddhas, turn what I have preached," clarifies the exhortation to uphold and propagate the teaching, as can be understood from the text itself.
At that time, the thousand Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses—the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis—arose from their majestic lion thrones in the Lotus Treasury World.
Each took his leave and, emitting inconceivable light from every part of his body, transformed that light into immeasurable Buddhas.
Simultaneously, they offered immeasurable flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white to Vairocana Buddha, receiving and upholding [this teaching].
The "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" having been concluded, each [of them] vanished from this Lotus Treasury World.

Having vanished, they entered the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature-Space (*tattva-ākāśa-puṣpa-prabhā-samādhi*) and returned to their original world, beneath the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa.
Emerging from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature-Space, they then sat upon the thousand-rayed vajra-throne.
On the royal throne and in the Hall of Sublime Light, the ten oceans of worlds were taught.
At that time, the Buddha upon the thousand-petaled lotus descended himself to clarify the second point: Śākyamuni Buddha’s upholding, turning, and teaching [of the Dharma].
Within this, there are nine sections; the first clarifies the Buddhas’ taking their leave, as stated in the sutra: "At that time, from the thousand-petaled lotus... until each took his leave."
First, because of the retreat; second, because of emitting light, as the sutra states that light is emitted from the entire body, which was previously inconceivable;
third, because of making offerings, as the sutra states that the light transforms into immeasurable [offerings] and even makes offerings to Vairocana Buddha;
fourth, because of receiving and upholding, as the sutra states that one receives and upholds the aforementioned "Chapter on the Mind-Ground Dharma"; fifth, because of illumination.
Regarding "passing away from here," it is as stated in the sutra: because they each pass away from this Lotus Treasury World. Sixth, "entering samādhi" is as stated in the sutra:

having passed away, they enter the *tathatā-ākāśa-svabhāva* (the space-like nature of reality) samādhi. As for what is called the *tathatā-ākāśa-svabhāva-puṣpa-prabhāsa* (Flower-Light of the Space-like Nature of Reality) samādhi:
it means that the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, which is *tathatā*, is termed "nature" (*svabhāva*). It means...
Because this dharma is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it is *tathatā* (suchness); it is called "space" because among all phenomena it is without substantial obstruction.
Because one contemplates this, it is called the "Space Samādhi. This name is established based on its object; it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (dependent determinative).
For example, as with the "Emptiness Samādhi," the light emitted by this samādhi is like the radiance of a flower, and is thus called a "flower."
The *Prabhāsa-samādhi* (Light Samādhi) is interpreted according to the *bahuvrīhi* compound;

as it is said, "do not plant [the tree]," the seventh [point] concerns returning to one's original world, as the sutra states, "returning to one's original world" and so forth. Regarding Jambudvīpa, this refers specifically to Southern Jambudvīpa.
The first fascicle of the *Qǐshìjiè jīng* (*Sūtra on the Arising of the World*) states: "In Southern Jambudvīpa, its land is seventy yojanas in length and breadth."
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* agrees with this sūtra. Moreover, the *Lokadhātu-vibhaṅga* states:
"In this Jambudvīpa, there is a great tree named Jambu; its trunk is seven yojanas in length and breadth, its leaves cover fifty yojanas, and it is one hundred yojanas high.
The commentary explains: "The land is named Jambudvīpa after the tree; because this tree exists there, it is called 'Jambu'."
Regarding the eighth point, "The Floating Island possesses wealth": this refers to emerging from samādhi, as the sūtra states that he emerges from the *tattva-svabhāva-gaganakusuma-prabhāsa-samādhi*.
As for the term "samādhi," in the Sanskrit language it is called *samādhi*, which is translated here as "equipoise" (*samāhita*).
It is termed "equipoise" because one is far removed from dullness and agitation; it is termed "holding" (*dhāraṇa*) because the mind does not scatter. Ninth, the explanation.
Since the Dharma, like the sutra, is established only after [the Buddha] has sat down and so forth, within the discourse on the Dharma there is further a twofold division:
first, the explanation of the Dharma by the thousand Buddhas; second, from "the remaining hundreds of billions" onwards, the explanation of the Dharma by the hundreds of billions of Buddhas.
This refers to the teaching of the tenth Dharma-gate by the first of these thousand Buddhas, which is itself divided into ten parts; this is the first clarification.
The ten world-oceans refer to the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which, being without limits or boundaries, is difficult to measure; it is metaphorically likened to an ocean.
"Seated upon the King of Thousand Rays" refers to sitting upon a lotus flower with a thousand stalks of radiant light.
The "Hall of Sublime Light" is the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka*) described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where the Buddha resides in the kingdom of Magadha at the site of tranquility.
In the Hall of Universal Radiance at the Site of Enlightenment, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva spoke on the ten oceans of world-systems.

Regarding the "oceans of world-systems," this refers to the exposition of the ocean of causes and conditions for the arising of world-systems, up to the ocean of the expedient means for their destruction,
as described in the third fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, rising from his seat, he went to the palace of Śakra and preached the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, rising from his seat, he went to the palace of Śakra and preached the Ten Abodes. This is the second section below, clarifying the preaching of the Ten Grounds.
According to the *Avataṃsaka*, when the Buddha was in the Palace of Sublime Victory (*Vaijayanta*) in the realm of Śakra, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati [preached it].
Regarding the explanation of the meaning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), as stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"O Sons of the Buddha, what are the ten stages of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas taught by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present? What are these eleven [stages]?

First is named the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*); second is named the Stage of Preparing the Ground (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*); third is named the Stage of Cultivation (*caryā-vihāra*); fourth..."
The first is named the Stage of Birth in Nobility; the fifth is named the Stage of Endowment with Skillful Means; the sixth is named the Stage of Rectitude of Mind;

the seventh is named the Stage of Non-retrogression; the eighth is named the Stage of Youthful Truth; the ninth is named the Stage of the Dharma Prince; and the tenth is named the Stage of Consecration. These are explained in detail as therein set forth.
Furthermore, he proceeded to the Suyāma Heaven to expound the Ten Practices.
Regarding the second instance of proceeding to the Suyāma Heaven to expound the Ten Practices, this is the third section clarifying the exposition of the Ten Practices.
"Suyāma" refers to the third heaven, Suyāma; in Sanskrit it is called *Yāma*, which means "time" (*kāla*). It is so named because [the gods there] follow the divisions of time.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 21, states:
"The Yāma Heaven refers to that celestial realm where, at various times and for the most part, they exclaim, 'How joyful!

Furthermore, according to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, when the Buddha was in the Yāma Heaven, the Bodhisattva Maṇiratnavyūhaguṇakānanapraveśasuvinīta entered the *Suviniścita-samādhi* and expounded the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). Moreover, as that same sūtra, fascicle 12, says:"
Bodhisattvas have ten practices. What are these ten? First, the practice of joy; second, the practice of benefiting others;

third, the practice of being free from anger and resentment; fourth, the inexhaustible practice; fifth, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion; sixth, the practice of excellent manifestation;
seventh, the practice of non-attachment; eighth, the practice of skillful means; ninth, the practice of wholesome dharmas; tenth, the practice of reality. These constitute the ten practices.
He spoke as before.
Then, rising from his seat, he went to the fourth heaven and there preached the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
Rising again from his seat, he proceeded to preach the Ten Dedications; regarding the mention of "four heavens," this refers to the fourth heaven, Tuṣita.

If one relies on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, when the Buddha was in the palace of Tuṣita Heaven, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja entered the Samādhi of Clear Wisdom (*prajñā-vidyā*) and taught the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) to those in Tuṣita Heaven.

"Tuṣita" is correctly rendered in Sanskrit as *Dṛṣṭānta* (or *Tuṣitā*), which means "Contented. As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*: "The fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven; this refers to that celestial realm."
Regarding the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) that take great joy in one’s own rebirth as their object, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, chapter sixteen, states:
"The Bodhisattva has ten dedications. What are the ten? First, the dedication to protect all sentient beings;
second, the indestructible dedication; third, the dedication equal to all Buddhas; fourth, the dedication to reach..."
1. Dedication in all places; 2. Dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; 3.
Dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality; 4. Dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings;
5. Dedication according to reality; 6. Dedication of liberation without bondage or attachment; 7. Dedication to the non-duality of the dharma-realm.
The detailed explanation of the dedication of merit is as described therein.
Furthermore, rising from his seat, he proceeded to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and taught the ten meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
The Sūtra says: "Rising again from his seat, he went to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and taught the ten kinds of concentration. This concludes the fifth section.
Regarding the "Ten Dhyānas of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven": the new translation of the *Śāstra* states that the "Heaven of Delighting in Transformations" refers to the pleasure of desire.
As the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The five [kinds of] pleasures of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven mean that in that place, one transforms objects of desire and experiences pleasure therein.
Regarding the "Ten Dhyānas," this refers to the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) cultivated in the ten stages (*bhūmi*). (Consult the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*). "Dhyāna" is the new translation.
The sūtras and śāstras name this *dhyāna* (meditative concentration); because one relies on this tranquility to closely examine the object of focus, it is called *dhyāna*.
Furthermore, rising from his seat, he proceeded to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) and there expounded the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).

The Sūtra says: "Again, rising from his seat, he went to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) to expound the Ten Stages. This section, the sixth from below, clarifies the exposition of the Ten Stages.
Regarding this "Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations," it refers to the sixth heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin. As the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"That heaven is so called because its inhabitants exercise mastery over the objects of desire emanated by others and experience pleasure therein. As for the "Ten Stages," the first is... [text fragment ends].

1. The Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*): Because one first attains the nature of a noble being (*āryatva*), fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), and is able to benefit both oneself and others, giving rise to great joy, it is named "Utmost Joy.

2. The Stage of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*): Because one possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and is far removed from the defilements of afflictions (*kleśa-mala*) that can give rise to even subtle transgressions, it is named "Freedom from Defilement.

3. The Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*): Because one accomplishes supreme meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and the great dhāraṇīs of the Dharma, and is able to bring forth [wisdom], it is named "Radiance."

Because of the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom, one dwells in the Fourth Ground, the Radiant (*Arciṣmatī*), where the most excellent factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) burn the fuel of afflictions as the flames of wisdom increase.

Because it is extremely difficult to master the union of the two modes of knowledge—ultimate and conventional—which are mutually contradictory in their activity, one dwells in the Fifth Ground, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*).
Because one dwells in the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*) that induces the [unconditioned], one dwells in the Sixth Ground, the Manifest (*Abhimukhī*).
7. The Far-Reaching Ground (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*) is so called because it brings the most excellent *prajñā* into manifestation through discernment;
and because it transcends the mundane paths of the two vehicles at the very limit of effortful application within the dwelling in signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*). 8.

The Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) is so called because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) continues spontaneously and uninterruptedly, such that it cannot be moved by the afflictions (*kleśa*). 9. The Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*) is so called because it accomplishes subtle... [text truncated]
Because one is able to skillfully preach the Dharma throughout the ten directions by means of the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge;
because on the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), the great cloud of Dharma-wisdom contains the waters of manifold virtues;

and because the body of reality (*dharmakāya*) is filled with the grossness [of afflictions] like space—thus, these ten stages collectively encompass all conditioned and unconditioned merits as their intrinsic nature. The meaning of this "intrinsic nature" is as explained extensively above.
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are explained in detail in works such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, the fourth chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī), and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. As these meanings are extensively expounded in the *Yogācāra-bhūmi-vyākhyā*,
I fear that a full account would be too prolix and thus shall not describe them here.
Furthermore, it proceeds to the first dhyāna to explain the ten vajras.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, proceeding to the first dhyāna to explain the ten vajras" refers to the seventh section below, which clarifies the explanation of the ten vajras.
Regarding these ten vajras, as stated in the fortieth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Ma..."
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of adamantine mind-arisings that adorn the Great Vehicle. What are the ten? They are as follows:
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms this thought: "All dharmas have no boundaries. The Bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind, thinking:
"I shall awaken to all dharmas of the three periods of time, leaving nothing remaining."
For the Bodhisattva who has first generated the adamantine mind, he reflects thus:
"Upon the tip of a single hair there are immeasurable Bodhisattvas preaching the Dharma of the Dharma-realm. Generating such a mind, he thinks:
"I shall generate the great adornment to adorn myself, and I shall transform and deliver sentient beings, causing them all to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
To attain parinirvāṇa through the Great Parinirvāṇa of Bodhi is the second arousal of the adamantine mind.
A bodhisattva arouses this thought: "The worlds of the ten directions are immeasurable, boundless, and without limit.
A bodhisattva makes such a great vow: 'I shall adorn all these worlds with unsurpassed, pure, and sublime ornaments.'"
The various adornments of those realms are all real and not false; this is the Bodhisattva’s third generation of the adamantine mind.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus: "Sentient beings are immeasurable, without limit, and inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva generates such a thought: "I shall dedicate all roots of goodness to all sentient beings with no [self-interest]."
The great light of supreme wisdom universally illuminates all sentient beings; this is the fourth generation of the adamantine mind.
A bodhisattva forms this thought: "All Buddhas are immeasurable and boundless. The bodhisattva generates such a mind as follows:
"I shall dedicate the roots of goodness I have planted to offer and provide for all Buddhas, and thereafter I..."
Thus one attains equal and perfect enlightenment; this is the fifth generation of the adamantine mind.
When a bodhisattva sees all buddhas and hears the Dharma they preach, they give rise to a heart of great joy.

They do not cling to their own body nor to the body of the Tathāgata, understanding that the Buddha-body is neither real nor false, neither existent nor non-existent (and so forth), and understanding that the Tathāgata is truly without any substantial existence.
Furthermore, they harbor no conceptual signs. Why? Because they encompass all things. This is the Bodhisattva’s sixth generation of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*).
If there are sentient beings who revile, abuse, or insult them, or even cut off their hands and feet, the Bodhisattva does not, on account of this, give rise to a mind of anger or malice;
rather, they continue to cultivate the bodhisattva path for unspeakable eons.
The practice of gathering in sentient beings without ever abandoning them:

Why? Because the Bodhisattva dwells in the non-dual Dharma, has well-trained himself in the Bodhisattva conduct, possesses a pure and straightforward mind, harbors no ill will toward any sentient being, endures all suffering with patience, does not retaliate against others, and is personally capable of enduring the sufferings of all sentient beings—this is what constitutes a Bodhisattva.
The seventh Bodhisattva, having generated the adamantine mind, reflects thus:
"In future ages, kalpas shall be immeasurable, boundless, without limit, and inexhaustible. Having generated such a mind, he thinks:
"I shall, throughout all future worlds and for as long as the realm of empty space endures, travel through all worlds to practice the Bodhisattva path and transform sentient beings."

For all sentient beings throughout a single world-system, as far as the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space—in all such worlds—one must likewise cultivate the bodhisattva practices for the sake of all sentient beings; this is the eighth generation of the adamantine mind.
A bodhisattva who has generated such a thought reflects: "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi takes the mind as its root."
Because the mind is pure, one is able to accumulate and fulfill all virtues;
if the mind attains mastery, one can achieve the practice of unsurpassed bodhi, fulfill all vows through the bodhisattva conduct, and ultimately transform and teach all sentient beings.
This is the ninth generation of the adamantine mind by a bodhisattva, who forms this reflection:
Knowing that the Buddha cannot be apprehended and that enlightenment cannot be apprehended— expounded at length up to the point of generating the mind of omniscience,
not abandoning the cultivation of bodhisattva practices, and not abandoning the teaching and transforming of sentient beings—

this constitutes the tenth generation of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) as an adornment of the Mahāyāna. It is not yet known whether these ten adamantine [resolutions] of this sutra correspond to those in the *Avataṃsaka*.
The ten adamantine minds (*vajracitta*) are identical to the inconceivable; alternatively, these may be the ten adamantine [minds] explained in the previous fascicle.
Furthermore, within the second dhyāna, the ten patiences (*kṣānti*) are taught.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, it is explained later in the Second Dhyāna. Regarding the ten types of patience (*daśa-kṣānti*), they will be discussed below following the eighth section.
As for these ten patiences, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, chapter thirty, states:

"When a Bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of patience, they are able to attain all unimpeded patience (*sarvāpratigha-kṣānti*). What are the ten? They are: first, the patience of conforming to sounds (*anuloma-ghoṣa*)."

Patience, the patience of compliance, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, the patience like an illusion, the patience like a mirage, the patience like a dream, the patience like an echo,
the patience like lightning, the patience like a transformation, and the patience like space— these are fully explained as such.
Furthermore, within the Third Dhyāna, ten dhyanas are explained.
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, reaching the Third Dhyāna, ten vows are explained. This is the ninth section from below, which explains the ten vows.

The self-nature of these vows consists of faith, superior understanding (*adhimukti*), and aspiration. Regarding the ten vows, as stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are to be compared and evaluated.
There are three kinds of supremacy: first, supremacy of aspiration; second, supremacy of practice; and third, supremacy of the benefit of the fruit.
What is supremacy of aspiration? It refers to the ten great vows. As the *Sūtra on the Ten Great Vows* states:

"When a bodhisattva thus dwells in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy, he gives rise to great vows as vast as the ocean. He accomplishes such fundamental skillful means and great practices, which are called 'without remainder.'"

Regarding the statement that "all Buddhas, all offerings, and all forms of reverence continue without cessation," the *Śāstra* explains that this first great vow being "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) has three aspects: first, the absence of remainder regarding all Buddhas;
second, the absence of remainder regarding all offerings; and third, the absence of remainder regarding all forms of reverence—and so on, as extensively explained.
The Sūtra says: Furthermore, one generates great vows, namely:
to receive and uphold all wheels of Dharma spoken by all Buddhas; to embrace the bodhi of all Buddhas;
and to protect and preserve all the teachings taught by all Buddhas—vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and extending to the end of the future.
Throughout all kalpas, for as long as all Buddhas attain enlightenment, if one protects and upholds the True Dharma, there shall be no rest.

The treatise states that the second great vow is "to receive and uphold them all," which means transcribing, making offerings to, reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding the teachings such as the sūtras, and expounding them for others; this is explained at length in the Sūtra, which says: "Furthermore, he makes the vow..."

The great vow is as follows: "May I go to make offerings to all Buddhas without exception, in all world-systems and dwelling places, from their descent from Tuṣita heaven and entry into the womb, until their parinirvāṇa; may I do so at all such times, without ever ceasing.
The Commentary says: "The third great vow is as explained extensively in the treatise. The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, he makes this great vow..."
May all that is called the vast and immeasurable conduct of all bodhisattvas— comprised of the stages (*bhūmi*) that do not depart from the *pāramitās*,
as extensively explained up to the path of the stages of reality and the skillful means of the *pāramitās* through which all are taught and led to practice,
so that their minds may attain increase; may all this be fulfilled.
The *Dīrghāgama-śāstra* states: "Regarding the fourth great vow, 'the mind attains growth,' by what practices does the mind grow?
It is through all the practices of the bodhisattvas that transform and teach others, causing them all to accept and practice [the Dharma], whereby the mind attains growth.
This is explained in detail as it says in that sutra: "Furthermore, one makes the great vow, namely, for all sentient beings without exception..."
"Born in the realms of form and formlessness, and so forth, until causing them to have faith and enter into all Buddha-dharmas. The *Treatise* says:
"The fifth great vow is to transform and guide sentient beings," and so on, as explained at length. The *Sūtra* says: "Furthermore, one makes a great vow, namely:
throughout all worlds without exception—vast and immeasurable, coarse or subtle, disordered, inverted, or upright, like [the arrangement of] Indra’s net..."

Because one knows with manifest presence the entry into the infinite distinctions of the world-systems of the ten directions according to their various classifications, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* states:
"The sixth great vow, 'without exception, in all world-systems,' has three aspects through which such knowledge of entering these world-systems manifests and is known:
first, all aspects, as extensively and infinitely described in the sutras."

...up to "because they abide correctly. Second, regarding the characteristic of the true meaning (*tattvārtha-lakṣaṇa*): as stated in the Sūtra, it is like the distinctions in Indra’s Net because it is the characteristic of the true meaning;
it is like the distinct performance of actions because [the true meaning] is differentiated by karma. Third, regarding the immeasurable characteristic:
the characteristic of the true meaning of the worlds of the ten directions can be known only by wisdom, whereas other characteristics can be perceived with the eyes. As the Sūtra says:
Furthermore, he makes a great vow: that all Buddha-fields—every single Buddha-field, every Buddha-field, all Buddha-fields, and all lands—are equal, pure, and so forth.
The Commentary says: "The seventh vow is to purify the Buddha-fields," and so on, as explained at length.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, he makes a great vow, namely that all Bodhisattvas shall be of one mind and one intent."
"Because of practice, one collectively gathers roots of goodness," and so on, up to "because of fully accomplishing the bodhisattva practices," etc.
The Commentary says: The eighth great vow is because one does not think of other vehicles. It is explained at length as that sutra says:
"Furthermore, one makes a great vow, namely, to mount the non-retrogressive wheel and practice the bodhisattva practices," and so on, up to "attaining suchness."
Regarding the "Treatise on the Body of the Intention-Jewel" (*Cittaratnagātra-śarīra-śāstra*), it states that the ninth great vow manifests the non-empty practice of the bodhisattva path;
furthermore, by practicing the bodhisattva path, it manifests the practice of the irreversible wheel of the vehicle.
The Sūtra says: "Moreover, one makes a great vow, namely: 'May I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in every world-system.'"
Because of their seeking of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do not depart from the path of ordinary beings;

yet, within the realm of all ordinary beings, they manifest the birth of a body, sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma, and delivering sentient beings.
They manifest Great Parinirvāṇa and display the realms of all Buddhas, the power of great spiritual wisdom, and even manifest Great Parinirvāṇa while never ceasing their bodhisattva practices.
The *Xing deng lun* (Treatise on the Equality of Practice) states: "The tenth great vow initiates Mahāyāna practice. The commentary explains this as follows:

"The principle of these ten great vows applies throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), yet because they are taught from the beginning, it is said that the first stage alone possesses the ten great vows;
alternatively, the 'ten great vows' refers precisely to the ten great vows found in the subsequent sutra."
Furthermore, he proceeded to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara within the Fourth Dhyāna,
where he preached the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as originally taught by Vairocana Buddha of the Lotus Treasury World.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, regarding the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground in the Fourth Dhyāna," this refers to what is explained below as the tenth [section], the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground.
*Maheśvara* is the Sanskrit term; in Chinese it is translated as "Great Sovereign" (*Dà Zìzài*).
He arises above the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca-śuddhāvāsa*). Because Bodhisattvas of the Tenth Ground are born in that heaven, there is this Great Sovereign. Thus, the *yú*... [text continues].

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle twelve, states: "Furthermore, beyond the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), there is the dwelling place of Maheśvara, where Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) who have reached the ultimate movement in the cultivation of the tenth stage are born.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains it in the same way. Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Stages of Mind (*cittabhūmi*), as explained in the preceding fascicle, these refer to the forty stages of mind.
The ten stages of setting forth (*daśa-prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*daśa-poṣadha*), the ten adamantine stages (*daśa-vajra*), and the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) are as described above.
The remaining thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are likewise identical and without distinction, as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Eon" (*Bhadrakalpika-parivarta*).
The Sūtra says: "The remaining billions" refers to the third section below, which clarifies the teachings of the ten billion Buddhas.
At that time, Śākyamuni, having first appeared from the Lotus Treasury World in the east and entered the celestial palace to preach the *Māra-parivarta-sūtra*, [departed].

At that time, from Śākyamuni’s initial manifestation until his arrival and entry into the celestial palace, the second section below explains the precepts cultivated on the stages, which consist of five parts:
first, birth in a celestial palace; second, entering the womb; third, leaving home;
fourth, attaining enlightenment; and fifth, turning the wheel of Dharma. This is the first: birth in a celestial palace.
Regarding the "Palaces of the Heavens of Form" (*rūpāvacara-deva-bhavana*): this refers to being born in the palaces of the fourth heaven within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
According to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, there are ten activities for dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven; thus, that sūtra’s forty-third fascicle states:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in Tuṣita Heaven, there are ten kinds of activities. What are these ten? Namely, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of all [beings] in the Desire Realm..."
The Deva preached the Dharma of detachment from desire, teaching that even sovereign freedom is impermanent and that all pleasures are ultimately suffering;
he exhorted and guided those devaputras to resolve upon Bodhicitta (this is the first matter).

For the sake of the devas of the Form Realm, the Bodhisattva explained the characteristics of the dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, and how the factors of those dhyānas arise in succession. There are three [types of these factors].
For those who are deluded, he even explains the wisdom of reality to them, exhorting, inspiring, and guiding those devaputras to resolve upon bodhicitta;
this is the second task of the Tuṣita Heaven. This is explained at length, up to:
while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, the Bodhisattva brings forth immeasurable and boundless dharma-gates, manifesting various forms within all worlds.
The various forms are explained at length, up to "in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to joy.
This constitutes the tenth activity of a Bodhisattva dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven, as fully described therein. Question:

For what reason is it that a Bodhisattva is born only in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita, and not in other heavens? Explanation: In the three lower heavens, [sentient beings] are submerged in the five [desires].
In the two heavens above [the desire realm], there is negligence regarding the five desires;

this fourth heaven is neither sunken nor negligent, and because it is easy to perceive and transform [beings], one is born in the fourth heaven and not in other heavens (as verified by the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 178, states: "Question: For what reason does the Bodhisattva receive his final birth in the Tuṣita heaven?"

Regarding the subsequent maturation (*vipāka*), it is said that it does not occur in other heavens because the lower heavens are characterized by negligence (*pramāda*) and the higher heavens have dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*).
Only in Tuṣita Heaven are both of these faults absent; thus, out of fear of negligence and aversion toward dull faculties, the Bodhisattva is born only there.
Some say that only in Tuṣita Heaven is the lifespan equal to the time it takes for the Bodhisattva to attain Buddhahood and for the Jambudvīpa... [to reach its full measure].

When the people of the state saw that the Buddha’s karma had matured and the timing was appropriate, and so forth, as extensively explained in the *Sūtra on Receiving Transformation*, it says in the forty-third fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"There are ten kinds of māras: namely, the māra of the five aggregates, because of attachment to the five aggregates;
the māra of afflictions, because of the defilement of afflictions; and the māra of karma, because it can create obstacles."
The demon of the mind arises from self-conceit; the demon of death arises from the separation of sensation and birth; the demon of celestial beings arises from the arrogance of negligence;
the demon of lost roots of goodness arises from a lack of remorse in the mind; the demon of samādhi arises from attachment to samādhi;

the demon of the spiritual friend arises from giving rise to a mind of attachment toward them; and the demon of not knowing the true Dharma of bodhi arises from being unable to give birth to the Great [Vows].
By virtue of this vow, there are ten demonic activities (*mārakarma*) and ten ways of abandoning demonic activities, such as associating with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

These are explained in detail as found in that [text]. Such categories are called the *Māraparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Sutra on the Questions of Māra), or perhaps there may be a separate section of a sutra titled the *Māraparipṛcchā-sūtra*; one should examine this.
"I shall descend to be born in Jambudvīpa in the kingdom of Kapilavastu; my mother’s name shall be Māyā, my father’s name Śuddhodana, and my own name Siddhārtha.
From the passage "descending to be born in Jambudvīpa... also named Siddhārtha," the second section below explains his descent to be born.

Regarding the signs of entering and emerging from the womb, as for the country of Kāpilavastu—also called Kapilavastu, which in Chinese is translated as *Siddhārtha*—the full Sanskrit term is *Siddhārthasiddha*.
*Siddha* means "accomplished," in the sense of achievement.
Westerners say that when one has mastered the recitation of scriptures, it is called *siddha*; this is translated into Chinese as "attained" (*bian*). This refers to...

Regarding the ultimate meaning of this matter, the intention here is as follows: the physiognomists prophesied that if he did not renounce the household life, he would become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*);
if he were to renounce the household life, he would achieve unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

It is for this reason that his name was established as "Saṃbodhi" (Accomplishment), because he would certainly accomplish the fruit of enlightenment. Nevertheless, before this prince had renounced the household life, he already had two names.
The first name is *Siddhārtha*; its meaning has been explained as before. The second name is *Devahrada*.

*Deva* here means "heavenly" or "god. This refers to when, seven days after his birth had been completed, the father-king sent him into *Devakula* (which means "abode of the gods") to visit Maheśvara and other deities.
At that time, the Prince entered *Devakula* to see Maheśvara.
Furthermore, because the other devas prostrated before the Prince, he was named "Devātideva" (God among Gods).

In this sutra, only one name is briefly mentioned, hence he is called Siddhārtha. According to the tradition of the Brahmins, as verified by the texts, the *Xi-yu-ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
*Sarvārthasiddha* (translated into Chinese as "One Who Has Accomplished All Meanings"). Question: Regarding the master of the Brahmins, the teacher says there are two types of Sanskrit sounds.
There are two types of vowels: the long and the short. In the Sūtras and Śāstras, they are distinguished based on the short vowel, which is called *siddhārtha*;
according to the tradition based on the long vowel, it is called *sarvārthasiddha*. Their meaning is one and the same.
However, regarding this Prince’s descent of the spirit and entry into the womb, the various schools differ. The Sthavira school states that the Bodhisattva...
On the thirtieth night of the month of Kṛttikā-Aśleṣā, he descended into his mother’s womb;

this corresponds to the fifteenth day of the fifth month. Other schools all state that he descended into his mother’s womb on the twentieth night of this month, which corresponds to the eighth day of the fifth month.
As for Māyā, she is Mahāmāyā, which means "Great Illusion" (Mahā-vidyā).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle fifty-six, states: "When Queen Māyā gave birth to the Crown Prince beneath the Śāla tree, ten rays of light appeared.
Whenever Buddhas were born in the worlds of the past, Queen Māyā was always their mother;
furthermore, from within Queen Māyā’s body, all the Buddhas of the past universally emerged."

Furthermore, in that same sutra, section forty-three states: "When the Bodhisattva enters the womb, a great light named 'Pure Realm' (*viśuddhaviṣaya*) issues from his right palm, capable of completely purifying the trichiliocosm.
If there are any outflow-free (*anāsrava*) pratyekabuddhas within this world who perceive this light, they immediately relinquish their life-span. If...
By the power of light, those who are unaware—namely all Māras, various non-Buddhists, and sentient beings with views—are all transferred to other worlds;
this excludes those sentient beings transformed by the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 178, asks: "For what reason does a Bodhisattva..."
Finally, there are those who pass away only from the heavenly realm and do not come from the human realm.
Regarding this, some say it is because among all the realms of existence, the heavenly realm is supreme; others say it is because those who come from the heavens are held in high esteem by humans;
and others say it is because among humans there is no such lifespan as that of Tuṣita, which is commensurate with the ripening of one's roots of merit. Question: For what reason?
Is it not the case that one attains perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) not immediately in Tuṣita Heaven, but must necessarily come to the human realm? Answer:

It is because this follows the nature of all Buddhas' teachings; that is to say, since the appearance of Buddhas in the world exceeding the sands of the Ganges has always occurred with their attainment of perfect enlightenment among humans.
Furthermore, it is only through the extremely sharp wisdom and vision of humans that one can attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There are ten reasons for descending into this world for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
At the age of seven, he left the household life.
The scripture states: "At the age of seven, he left the household life. This marks the third section below, explaining the characteristics of his renunciation, as found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The forty-fourth [chapter] says: "O Son of the Buddha, there are ten reasons why Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas manifest the act of leaving the home life (*pravrajyā*).
What are these ten? Namely: they manifest leaving the home life because they wish to cause sentient beings to feel weary of and detached from the household;

they manifest leaving the home life for the sake of sentient beings who are attached to the household; and they do so because they wish to manifest conformity with the path of all the noble ones (*ārya*)."
He manifests renunciation in order to proclaim and praise the Dharma of renunciation;
he manifests renunciation in order to cause sentient beings to abandon the two views; he manifests renunciation in order to cause them to abandon the pleasure of desire and the pleasure of self;
he manifests renunciation in order to manifest the characteristic of transcending the three realms; he manifests renunciation in order to manifest sovereign mastery.
He manifested renunciation because he was awakened by others; he manifested renunciation because he wished to accord with the Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses;
and he manifested renunciation because it is the natural law for all bodhisattvas in their final birth.
Question: Other sūtras state that he renounced at nineteen; why does this sūtra say he renounced at seven? How is this to be understood?
It is said that because the capacities of sentient beings differ, their perceptions and what they hear vary; therefore, one should not find this strange.

Furthermore, the *Western Regions Biographies* (*Xiyu zhuan*) states that when the Tathāgata left the city to renounce the world, the timing was not fixed: some say the Bodhisattva was nineteen years old, while others say twenty-nine.
He left the city on the eighth day of the latter half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to this [date].
On the eighth day of the third month— or as some say, on the fifteenth day of the middle half of the month of Śakha, which corresponds here to the fifteenth day of the third month—
he attained perfect enlightenment and was named by me Śākyamuni Buddha.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "thirty [kalpas] to achieve enlightenment" and so forth: this is the fourth section below, which explains the characteristics of achieving enlightenment, such as sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and subduing the various Māras.
These should be understood as they are explained in detail in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; fearing prolixity, I shall not describe them here.
It was taught in succession at ten successive dwelling places, from sitting upon the Vajra-flower-light-king throne in the site of the tranquil place of enlightenment,
up to the palace of the heavenly king Maheśvara.
The Sūtra says: At the site of the terrace of tranquil extinction, following the fifth turning of the wheel of Dharma, there is the abode of light;
that is to say, the ten kinds of abodes as described above.
At that time, the Buddha, observing the net-bannered standards of the Great Brahmā Kings, spoke for their sake regarding the infinite worlds as being like...
Just as the mesh of a net consists of worlds that are each distinct, different, and immeasurable, so too are the gateways to the Buddha’s teachings.
Having come to this world eight thousand times, I have sat upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King throne for the sake of this Sahā world,
even within the palaces of the heavenly kings up to Maheśvara, in order to briefly [expound] for all the great assemblies therein.
The joyful exposition concludes.
Next, the Buddha observes those devas who have gone to the palaces of the heavenly kings; this is the second turning of the wheel of Dharma by Śakra.
This refers to the Buddha observing the net of Mahābrahmā, wherein within a single net there are infinite distinct apertures.
For this same reason, it is taught that the distinctions between the infinite worlds are diverse;
just as the worlds differ from one another, so too are the gateways of the Tathāgata’s teaching.

Although there are infinite gateways of teaching with their various differences, they do not depart from the equal Dharma-realm, as is explained at length in the fifty-fifth chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, descending from the palace of the Heavenly King to the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa, he preached for all sentient beings upon this earth—

ordinary people and those shrouded in the darkness of ignorance— the original *Lushena Buddha’s Mind-Ground Sutra*, which is that which is constantly recited from the very first moment of generating the bodhicitta.
