The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, descending from the celestial palace to Jambudvīpa, beneath the Bodhi tree.
This marks the second section, which correctly elucidates the practice undertaken, namely the precepts (*śīla*). Within this, there are two parts: first, the introduction by the scribe;
second, the formal explanation beginning with "a single ray of light," of which this is the first. Regarding the benefit for humans, there are two aspects: the first concerns those on earth.

Regarding the second [point], the bodhisattvas who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are as can be seen from the text. From here below, the third [point] reveals what they recite:

namely, the precepts within the Forty Stages of Mind (*citta-bhūmi*) of the original Vairocana. These are the precepts recited by bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds (*prathama-cittotpāda*).
As for those who have first resolved their minds, according to this sutra and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the initial mind of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-vyākhyāna*) is called "the first."
Because this generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is the first among those that are non-retrogressive, it is called the "initial generation of the mind.

To speak according to the ultimate principle, the initial mind of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) is named the initial generation of the mind, for at that point one has already generated the unsurpassed bodhicitta.

Although there are many types of generating the bodhicitta, when summarized, they do not exceed two kinds: namely, the vow for oneself and the vow for others. Regarding the vow for self-benefit, it is the aspiration to cultivate [the path].
To forever abandon all unwholesome dharmas and to abide in all wholesome dharmas—this is called the aspiration for one’s own benefit (*svārtha-praṇidhāna*).

Regarding the aspiration for the benefit of others (*parārtha-praṇidhāna*), it is the aspiration to gather sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and to deliver them from birth and death;
this is called the great aspiration for the benefit of others. These two aspirations are termed bodhicitta; thus it is said in the *Yogācāra*.
The *Treatise* (Śāstra), fascicle 35, states: "Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas give rise to right vows and seek awakening, they produce such a thought and utter these words:
'May I certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, so as to be able to bring about all benefit and welfare for sentient beings.
If one can thus give rise to the bodhicitta, this is called a Bodhisattva."

That treatise states: "Furthermore, from the very first moment a bodhisattva generates the mind [of awakening], they are said to have entered upon unsurpassed enlightenment and are reckoned among the ranks of the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas," and so on at length.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 58, states: "The bodhicitta is the seed of all buddhas; it is able to give birth to all buddhas."
Because it is the Dharma, the bodhicitta is a fertile field that nurtures the pure dharmas of sentient beings;
because it is the great earth, the bodhicitta is able to support all worlds;
because it is pure water, the bodhicitta washes away the stains of all afflictions; because it is a great... [text ends]
Because wind is unobstructed throughout all worlds; furthermore, that same text at fifty-nine states:
"For example, just as a small vajra can destroy all things, so too is the bodhicitta:
by taking even a minor object as its focus, it can shatter all ignorance and delusion," and so forth at length. This refers to that which is produced upon the initial arousal of the mind.
The reciter explains that the first [term] constitutes the name. Why is this? Because even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) recite these precepts.
"The first is the light of the precepts, the vajra-jewel precept.
Regarding the phrase "the first is the light of the precepts, the vajra-jewel precept," from here below is the second section, the formal explanation of this passage.

There are two parts to the introduction: first, a brief indication of the characteristics of the precepts followed by the permission to explain them with the words "Listen attentively"; second, the detailed explanation of the characteristics of the precepts beginning from "At that time, Śākyamuni...
and so forth. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the enumeration of the names of the precepts used to manifest the granting of permission;

second, a brief praise of the merit of the precepts and an exhortation to uphold and listen attentively, beginning from "I, now as Vairocana... and so forth. Within the first of these [the enumeration of names], there are three points, the first of which is the manifestation...
The first [section], "The Names and Essences," reveals the fundamental source of all Buddhas. The second, "Manifesting Function," begins with "I now, for this...
and grants permission to speak; this is the first [part] which manifests the names and essences. Regarding the phrase "one precept": it refers to each individual precept among the ten heavy ones;
because its radiance can destroy delusions, it is called "precept-light. As stated in the sutra below: "Precepts are like the bright sun."
"Or one precept" refers to one among the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), namely the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint).
This is spoken of as "restraint" from the perspective of its predominance; however, if explained in detail, it is not that the other two are absent.

Alternatively, "one precept" means that such wondrous morality does not depart from the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), for it is free from existence and non-existence; thus it is called "one precept," or simply "one."
The term "precepts" (*śīla*) is used here to signify all [the virtues] within the six perfections. Regarding the "Vajra Jewel Precept": the term "vajra" has two meanings:
first, the sense of being firm and difficult to destroy; second, the sense of being able to shatter other things. The precepts are likewise so:
they are said to be difficult for non-Buddhist brahmins to destroy, and they shatter the darkness of saṃsāra as well as the defilement of broken precepts.
It is metaphorically named "Vajra.
It is the original source of all Buddhas, the original source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the phrase "the sūtra is the original source of all Buddhas," from here below is the second section, which reveals the original source of the Bodhisattva's function.
The original statement reveals the fundamental basis, meaning that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain the fruition of their results through this very precept.
As stated in a sutra below: "Multitudes of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust attain perfect enlightenment by means of this.
Regarding the phrase "seed of Buddha-nature," it means that the precepts constitute the Buddha-nature. Thus, these wondrous precepts act as the generative cause for the three bodies of the Buddha.

Alternatively, it may be that [Buddha-nature] acts as the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) for the fruit of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-phala*), or as the enabling cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*) for the attainment of the fruit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

This is what is called "Buddha-nature. As for the term "seed" (*bīja*), it carries the meaning of "cause"; that is to say, because ethical discipline (*śīla*) acts as the causal condition (*pratyaya*) to produce the fruit of conditioned phenomena.

Alternatively, "Buddha-nature" may be understood in relation to the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*), while "seed" is understood in relation to the conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛta-phala*). Within this context, there is the desire...
To manifest that there are two distinct fruits, two kinds of causes are explained:

either the Buddha-nature itself is called the seed, thus termed the "Buddha-nature seed," or it is said that the single light of the precepts is itself the adamantine jewel-precept. The intended meaning here is that the precepts are not separate from Suchness;

the precepts are Suchness, and Suchness is the characteristic of the precepts. This is because the characteristic is not separate from the essence, and the essence is identical to the characteristic. Therefore, they are one.
The term "precepts" (śīla) speaks of detachment but does not reveal their essential nature; the Vajra Jewel Precepts do indeed reveal this essence.

This essence is True Suchness (tathatā), and True Suchness is the fundamental source and basis of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. When one speaks of "Buddha-nature," it reveals that the essence of the precepts is the principle of Buddha-nature.
When one speaks of "seeds," this reveals that the characteristics of the precepts consist of conditioned practices.
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; all consciousness, form, and mind—whether emotional or cognitive—are entirely encompassed within the precepts of Buddha-nature.
As the Sūtra says, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature," this demonstrates that they are not separate from the precepts.
Regarding the explanation of the "Buddha-nature of True Suchness" (*tathatā-buddhadhātu*), there are two interpretations of this passage:

first, according to the various masters following the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and will certainly attain Buddhahood; this meaning is as commonly explained.
Second, Bodhisattva Dharmapāla and others state that "all" is of two kinds: first, "all of all," and second, "a small portion of all."
When all the sūtras state that "all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature," this is said with reference to a limited sense of "all.

Maitreya Bodhisattva, having ascended to the stage of the Regent (Bodhisattva of the Final Birth) and thoroughly penetrating the intentional language (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) of the Buddhas, established the five distinct spiritual lineages (*gotra*) in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to definitive knowledge; although there are two interpretations regarding this, [the following is] now...
Based on the views of Maitreya, Dharmapāla, and others— and not on those such as the ordinary person Nianboshi—
this statement that "all possess Buddha-nature" is spoken with reference to a limited sense of "all," or it is spoken in terms of the Buddha-nature of principle (*li*).
As for the statement that "all consciousnesses, form, and mind are sentient beings," they correspond respectively to the mental faculty (*manas*) and the six [sensory consciousnesses].

"Consciousness" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). As for "form" (*rūpa*), it refers to the five objects, the five sense faculties, and all that is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*);
these are all termed "form. As for "mind" (*citta*), this refers to the eighth consciousness; because the meaning of "mind" is preeminent there, it is specifically designated as "mind.

Alternatively, "mental consciousness" refers to the sixth [consciousness]. As for the term "mind" used here, it indicates that the five sensory consciousnesses are referred to as "mind" in contrast to their objects, form.
The statement that "sentiment," "mind," and so forth [enter the Buddha-nature precepts] clarifies that both form and mind are included within the Buddha-nature precepts.
"Sentiment" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), as explained above. "Mind"—referring to the intention (*manas*) and a portion of form—clarifies the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
"Entering the Buddha-nature precepts" clarifies that all minds and forms enter the *tathatā* (suchness) nature of the precept-substance (*śīla-tattva*).

Because it does not depart from suchness, and because the precepts, suchness, and the mind are without distinction, the meaning here is to reveal that not only do these precepts not depart from true suchness,
but all phenomena likewise do not depart from suchness; since they all enter the Buddha-nature of the precepts—
the very essence of the precepts— they are called "entering the precepts."
Because there is always a cause for the *dang-dang* (the eternal), the eternally abiding Dharma-body exists; thus, these ten *prātimokṣas* emerge in the world.
This is the Dharma-precept, which all sentient beings of the three periods of time wear upon their heads and uphold.
Because there is always a cause at every stage (*yad-yad-kāla*), one attains the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This means that the precepts themselves are the cause of the Dharma-body.
Because they are not limited to a single future [moment], it is said that "at every stage there is" (*yad-yad-kālam asti*);

because there is a cause for the future, it is said that "there will be a cause" (*bhaviṣyati hetuḥ*). Since there is a cause at every stage, there is the fruit of the Dharma-body at every stage. Question: How shall the Dharma-body be attained?

Regarding the statement that "there is the 'to-be-realized' (bhavya-bhavya)," the commentary explains: although the *dharmakāya* is eternal, its states of concealment and manifestation differ, as explained elsewhere where it is said that when concealed it is the *tathāgatagarbha*, and when manifested it is the *dharmakāya* fruit.
Since this passage establishes the meaning of the concealment and manifestation of the *dharmakāya*, it says "the to-be-realized.
Alternatively, all three bodies (*trikāya*) may be called the *dharmakāya*; what fault would there be in this? This is the intended meaning here.
It is said that because there exists the cause capable of producing merit that extends to the limits of the future, the Tathāgata’s virtues extend to the limits of the future without interruption;
thus, he is the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*. Since the *dharmakāya* is without birth or cessation, it is called "eternally abiding.
Furthermore, since the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* exist without end throughout the future, they are also said to be "eternally abiding."

Because of these bodhisattvas, it is said that they have emerged from the three realms and attained *mokṣa*. The old translation renders this as "separation" (*bie*). It is liberation (*vimukti*) in various places.

The Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang dynasty translates *brahmadatta* as "liberation" (*jie tuo*). *Mokṣa* means "liberation. *Vinaya* means "separation" (*bie*). If one were to follow this Sanskrit pronunciation, it would be called "separation";
however, here we conform to the Chinese terminology and thus call it "Prātimokṣa" (Separate Liberation). This refers to the seven classes of persons.
The distinct branches are called the Prātimokṣa (Individual Liberation). "Emerging from the world" means that by means of these precepts, one now emerges from the three realms of existence.
I shall now, for the sake of this great assembly, again expound the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Precepts, which are for all sentient beings.
The essence of the precepts is inherently pure. The Sūtra says:
"I shall now, for the sake of this great assembly of sentient beings... and so forth. This marks the second section, the promise to speak.
Regarding the term "repeatedly spoken," it is as explained previously in the *Vinaya-piṭaka-saṃgraha*; here too, it is said to be "repeatedly spoken. As for the term "inexhaustible," it means:

Because the Bodhisattva precepts are inexhaustible throughout the limits of the future, they are not like those of the Śrāvakas, who abandon their precepts as soon as they relinquish their common lot (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
To say that their fundamental nature is intrinsically pure means that these very precepts do not depart from suchness (*tathatā*).
I, now as Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal; Surrounding me, upon a thousand petals, there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis.

Upon each petal are ten billion lands, and in each land is a Śākyamuni, each sitting beneath a Bodhi tree, simultaneously attaining the Way of Buddhahood— thus are there a thousand times ten million times ten million.
From the *Vairocana-buddha-svabhāva-sūtra*, this is the second section, "Briefly Praising the Virtue of the Precepts and Exhorting Their Retention," which begins with the words "I, Vairocana, now...
and consists of twelve and a half verses. This section is further divided into three parts; first, there are two and a half verses that clarify the identity of the Teacher.
Next, following "The thousand billion Śākyamunis," there is a brief praise of the virtue of the precepts;

following this, from "Vairocana recites," there is an exhortation to uphold [the precepts] and a warning to listen attentively. Within the former section, there are two parts. First, there are two lines clarifying Vairocana.
Regarding "Vairocana," the Liang dynasty translation says "Pure and Full. He sits upon a lotus flower pedestal, as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Upon the fragrant water..."
In this world-realm of Padmagarbha, there are unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, all of which are places where Vairocana constantly turns the wheel of Dharma.
Next, surrounding [the central lotus], there are two rows of verses above and below the thousand petals, illuminating the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis.
Within these, there are three parts: first, the initial two lines clarify the thousand Śākyamunis; next, beneath each petal, there are hundreds of billions... [and so on].
The single verse clarifies that after the ten billion Śākyamunis, there are likewise thousands of billions below;
this explains what was taught by the thousand-billion-fold Vairocana Buddha. Question: How do these three types of Buddhas encompass one another? Answer:

Vairocana Buddha is the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body); the thousand-petaled Śākyamuni is the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (other-enjoyment body); and the ten billion [Śākyamunis] are the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation bodies).
Śākyamuni is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); therefore, the upper scroll of the sutra states: "At that time, Vairocana Buddha was filled with great joy and manifested the light of space;
from the fundamental source of his essential nature, he attained the eternal Dharma-body of Buddhahood and entered samādhi to manifest before the great assembly.
'O sons of the Buddha, listen attentively and reflect well upon this practice! I have [practiced] for hundreds of thousands of *kalpas*..."

Having cultivated the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*) for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, taking this as the cause, he first abandons the state of an ordinary person and attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, being named Vairocana Buddha.
He dwells in the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury World-Ocean; that terrace is surrounded by a thousand petals, each petal being a world-system.
I am the sovereign of these thousand world-systems, and I manifest as the thousand Śākyamunis who preside over them.
Beyond a thousand worlds, there is one leaf-world; within each world, there are ten billion Sumeru mountains,
ten billion suns and moons, ten billion sets of four continents, ten billion Jambudvīpas, and ten billion Bodhisattvas—
Śākyamunis seated beneath ten billion bodhi trees— each expounding upon the extensive *Bodhicittabhūmi* that you have asked about.
It is said that up to the Buddha atop the thousand-petaled lotus is my transformation body;

since these thousands of koṭis of Śākyamunis are themselves the transformation bodies of the thousand Śākyamunis, it is stated that such thousands of koṭis [of Buddhas] are the original body of Vairocana.
The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis, each receiving hosts as numerous as motes of dust, have all come to my presence to hear me recite the Buddha’s precepts; thus the Gate of Ambrosia is opened.
The scripture says: "The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis," and so forth; this is the second section, a brief praise of the virtue of the precepts, consisting of three and a half lines.
This is divided into three parts. First, one line and one phrase clarify that it was spoken by the True Buddha.

Second, from "At that time" onwards, one line and one phrase clarify that it was spoken by the thousand billion Buddhas. Third, from "The precepts are like the sun and moon" onwards, one verse-line correctly praises the virtue of the precepts;
this is the first part. It means that each of the thousand Buddhas and the hundred billion Buddhas, leading [their retinues]...
A multitude of subtle atoms all came together to the abode of Vairocana Buddha to hear me recite the Buddha’s precepts. They asked: "How does the self-enjoyment body perceive?
The Buddha replied: "Only a Buddha can know this. The assembly of Bodhisattvas then asked: "How do they see, hear, and understand? The Buddha said:

"Although the Bodhisattvas do not see or hear [it directly], that which they see as the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is not separate from the response body (saṃbhogakāya). Therefore, it is so described."

Regarding the statement "Listen as I recite the Buddha’s precepts," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) does not depart from the aspect of responding to sentient beings, or that the Buddha’s spiritual power causes one to see and hear it. Regarding the phrase "the gate of ambrosia immediately opens":
ambrosia (*amṛta*) is precisely nirvāṇa. Since these bodhisattva precepts serve as the gateway to nirvāṇa, it is said that "the gate of ambrosia immediately opens."
At that time, the thousands of billions [of emanations] returned to their original places of enlightenment;
each sat beneath a Bodhi tree and recited the precepts of my Original Teacher. The "Ten Grave Precepts and Forty-eight Light Precepts" state:
"At that time, the thousands of billions... This second section clarifies the manifestation and preaching of the Dharma, as can be understood from the text.
The precepts are like the sun and moon, and also like jeweled necklaces.

The Sūtra says: "The precepts are like the sun and moon," and so forth. This third section correctly extols the virtue of the precepts, first using metaphors and subsequently applying them to the Dharma.
This constitutes the first part, the manifestation of similes, which contains two types of metaphors: first, the metaphor of the sun and moon; second, the metaphor of the jeweled necklace.
The "ornament" (*ratna*) is used here as a metaphor for the essence of the first simile:
just as the sun and moon can dispel all darkness, so too can the precepts dispel all darkness. There are two kinds of darkness regarding the sun and moon as metaphors:

first, the violation of precepts is called darkness because it is conjoined with ignorance (*avidyā*) and because it brings about dark karmic fruits; second, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is called darkness because one has not yet attained [nirvana].
The light of wisdom that exhausts the outflows is the Bodhisattva precept; it shatters the two kinds of darkness, just as the sun and moon dispel them.
Regarding the phrase "removing the defilement of breaking the precepts," the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) states: "It is like a person with clear vision who can avoid dangerous and evil paths.

Regarding the ability to distance oneself from all evils and eliminate the darkness of birth and death, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the world, there are those of great intelligence who can remain far removed from all evils and eliminate the darkness of saṃsāra."
The thirteenth [simile] states that among great and grievous illnesses, the precepts are a potent medicine; amidst great terrors, the precepts are a protection;
and within the darkness of death, the precepts are a bright lamp. Thus, they are also like a necklace of jewels. This second simile is as follows:
just as a necklace of jewels can adorn the body, so too do these precepts adorn the bodhisattva. Furthermore...
Just as a precious gem can produce all manner of jewels and serves as their basis, so too is the precept. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"For example, just as the great earth is the support for all things that possess form, so too is the precept. The precept is the dwelling place for all wholesome dharmas.
This is explained at length, even to the point that if a person abandons this precept, although they may reside [in a certain state], [they lack its foundation].
Practicing asceticism in the mountains by eating fruit and taking medicinal herbs is no different from that of birds and beasts. Some people observe the precept of drinking only water;
some wear garments of grass or bark; they undergo ascetic practices and receive these disciplines, yet because they lack this true precept, they gain nothing at all.
On the other hand, there may be someone who, though dwelling in lofty halls and great palaces and enjoying fine clothing and delicious food, is nevertheless able to practice [the Way].
This precept enables one to be born in a favorable realm and to attain the fruits of the Path.
"A multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust / By this, they achieve perfect enlightenment.
From here on, the second section clarifies the Dharma, stating that a multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust achieve perfect enlightenment through this.
By means of this precept, all bodhisattvas attain perfect enlightenment. The term *brahma-svara* (Brahma-voice) remains intact [in the original]. Regarding *bodhisattva*:
in the Great Tang, *bodhi* is translated as "enlightenment" (*jue*) and *sattva* as "sentient being" (*youqing*).

The old translation, which rendered it as "beings with the mind of the Way" (*daoxin zhongsheng*), is erroneous. If one were to say "beings with the mind of the Way," the Sanskrit term should have been *mārga-manuṣya*.
Consulting the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*:
This was recited by Vairocana; I too recite it in this way. You, newly initiated bodhisattvas, should receive and uphold these precepts upon your heads.
Having received and upheld these precepts, you shall in turn transmit them to all sentient beings.
Listen attentively as I correctly recite the treasury of precepts within the Buddha-dharma, the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
This is what was recited by Vairocana. From here below, the third section clarifies the exhortation to uphold [the precepts] and the instruction to listen attentively;
herein there are three parts. The first two lines cite the words of the person who listens and recites. "I" refers to the thousand-billion Śākyamunis.

There is one verse that clarifies the exhortation to receive and uphold [the teaching] regarding the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), and four verses that serve as a warning to listen attentively.

Within the warning to listen, there are three lines that directly clarify the injunction to listen; next, from "The great assembly, believe with earnest attention" onwards, there are two lines and three phrases that clarify the injunction to generate faith;
finally, the last two lines provide the conclusion.
The great assembly, with minds of sincere faith, should believe: "You shall become a Buddha; I am one who has already become a Buddha.
Constantly maintaining such faith, they shall be fully endowed with the precepts.
All sentient beings who possess a mind should receive the Buddha-precepts. When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Having attained a rank equal to Great Enlightenment, you are truly the children of all Buddhas. The great assembly should all pay homage and listen with a sincere heart as I recite the Sūtra.

[The passage] beginning with "Great Assembly, believe with earnest attention" is the second section, which clarifies the instruction for generating faith. There are three kinds of faith: first, faith...
Because it is as stated in the sutra, "When one has already become a Buddha," and so forth;

because one is fully endowed with both faith and precepts, as the sutra says, "One constantly practices such that the categories of faith and precepts are already complete"; and because it is said, "If one receives these precepts, they encompass all precepts;
all sentient beings who possess a mind should embrace the Buddha-precepts"—this is an exhortation for all sentient beings to embrace them.

Regarding the three aspects of receiving the Buddha-precepts, the first is that one’s faith is identical to that of the Great Awakened One, as the sutra states: "When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the nature of all Buddhas.
The latter two phrases serve as a conclusion, which can be understood according to the text. Thus ends the second section, the exhortation to listen.
At that time, when Śākyamuni Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unsurpassed enlightenment, he first formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa:
the dharma of filial piety toward parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem; the dharma of filial piety toward the Ultimate Way.
Filiality is called the precepts, and it is also called restraint.

The Sūtra says: "At that time, Śākyamuni [spoke] up to the section on the Prātimokṣa. This constitutes the second major section, which extensively explains the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*).

Within this, there are two parts: first, explaining the meaning of the name to distinguish those capable of receiving the precepts; second, from "Then the Buddha said" onwards, the specific explanation of the characteristics of the precepts.

In the former part, there are three sections: first, summarizing and briefly explaining the general title; second, immediately emitting immeasurable light from the mouth; [and third, the actual exposition].
The emission of light below signifies an auspicious omen; hereafter, the Buddha’s son, listen attentively.

"If one receives the Buddha's precepts" is the first section, which serves to distinguish the person capable of receiving the Bodhisattva precepts. Within this, there are four parts: the first clarifies the Teacher, namely Śākyamuni.
*Śākyamuni* is translated in the Great Tang as "Able to Quiesce" (*Nengji*); formerly it was also translated as "Able to Fulfill" (*Nengman*).
Regarding the term "Cloud of the Buddha of Benevolence" (能仁佛): in its original Sanskrit sound it is *Buddha*, which here is translated as "The Awakened One" (覺者).
This is explained in detail in the eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vṛtti*. Second, to clarify the location: according to the sutra, he sat at the beginning beneath the Bodhi tree.
As for the "Bodhi tree," *bodhi* means awakening; this refers to the fact that all bodhisattvas attain awakening by relying upon this tree.
It is named the Bodhi Tree based on that which depends upon it, just as one speaks of "Devadatta’s robe.

Because the tree possesses awakening (*bodhi*), it is called the "Awakening Tree" (*bodhidruma*); this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive determinative). Alternatively, the tree of awakening is called the "Bodhi Tree";

among the six types of compounds, this is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative). Third, regarding the formulation of the precepts, it refers to the initial formulation of the Prātimokṣa as described. Fourth.

This is a brief explanation of the name "precept" (*śīla*), as stated in the sutra regarding filial piety toward one's parents and so forth. "Above, one accords with the Triple Gem, parents, teachers, and the Sangha";
"accordance" refers to the path to the ultimate Dharma. The "path to the ultimate Dharma" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Because the precepts accord with these factors conducive to enlightenment, they are called "accordance with the path to the ultimate Dharma. To name the precepts "filial piety" means that they follow and accord with the Buddha’s teachings.
This practice of filial piety is also called "precept" (*śīla*) and is further termed "restraint. To prevent wrongdoing and cease evil is what is meant by "precept.
Immediately, his mouth emitted immeasurable rays of light.
The Sūtra says: "Immediately, his mouth emitted immeasurable light. This marks the second section from here below, which concerns the emission of light as an auspicious omen (*prātihārya*).

Within this, there are three parts: first, the clarification of the emission of light; second, the passage beginning with "At that time," concerning the great assembly’s desire to hear [the teaching];
and third, the passage beginning with "He addressed the bodhisattvas," concerning the reason for emitting the light. This is the first part.
At that time, a great assembly of one hundred trillion bodhisattvas, the eighteen Brahmā deities, the sons of the six classes of desire-realm gods,
and sixteen great kings joined their palms and listened with single-minded devotion as the Buddha recited the Mahayana precepts of all Buddhas.
The Sūtra says: At that time, there was a great assembly of ten trillion beings. From this, we extract the second great assembly, whose members wished to hear [the teaching];
this assembly consists of four classes: first, bodhisattvas; second, the Brahmā hosts; third, the gods of the desire realm; and fourth, kings.
Regarding the "eighteen Brahmās," this refers to the three heavens within each of the lower three dhyānas, which constitute nine heavens; the fourth [dhyāna]...
The dhyānas consist of nine heavens. Within the first dhyāna there are three heavens: first, the Brahmakāyika Heaven; second, the Brahmapurohita Heaven;
and third, the Mahābrahmā Heaven. Within the second dhyāna there are three heavens: first, the Parīttābha Heaven; second, the Apramāṇābha Heaven;
and third, the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Within the third dhyāna there are three heavens: first, the [Parītta-]śubha Heaven...
The Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) consist of two: the Heaven of Ultimate Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*), the Heaven of Infinite Purity (*apramāṇaśubha*), and the Heaven of Universal Purity (*parīttaśubha*).

The nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna are: first, the Cloudless Heaven (*anabhraka*); second, the Heaven of Merit-Born (*puṇyaprasava*); third, the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*); fourth, the Heaven Without Affliction (*avṛha*); fifth, the Heaven Without Heat (*atapā*);

sixth, the Heaven of Excellent Manifestation (*sudṛśa*); seventh, the Heaven of Excellent Vision (*sudarśana*); eighth, the Heaven of the Ultimate Limit of Form (*akaniṣṭha*). Among these eight heavens, [the latter] is the lowest.
Beyond the three heavens where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, there are five subsequent heavens inhabited exclusively by sages. These surpass the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) heavens;
they are called Mahesvara, and Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are born therein.

The individual explanations of these names are as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 176, and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 22. [Next,] the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are explained.
These are: first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Heaven of the Thirty-three; third, the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven;
fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and sixth, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Regarding the sixteen great kings, as stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*:
first, the kingdom of Aṅga; second, the kingdom of Magadha; third, the kingdom of Kāśi; [and so forth].
4. The country of Kosala; 5. the country of Vṛji; 6. the country of Malla; 7. the country of Ceti; 8. the country of Vatsa;
9. the country of Kuru; 10. the country of Pañcāla; 11. Aśmaka; 12. Vatsa; 13.
the country of Surāṣṭra; 14. the country of Gandhāra; 15. Kaṃpilla; 16. [the country of] Śrāvastī.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 124, states that the sixteen great kingdoms are:

the kingdom of Aṅga, the kingdom of Magadha, the kingdom of Kāśī, the kingdom of Kośala, the kingdom of Vṛji, the kingdom of Malla, the kingdom of Puṇḍra, the kingdom of Suhyama, the kingdom of Aśmaka, and the kingdom of [A]... (text fragmentary).
In the kingdoms of Annadatta, Śyāmāvatī, Kambuja, Kuru, Pañcāla, Vatsa, and Śūrasena,
he addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Now, every half-month, I personally recite the Dharma-precepts of all the Buddhas."
The Sūtra says: "He addressed the Bodhisattvas... From here below is the third section, on the emission of light.
This is called "manifesting" because this precept is recited from within the mouth; thus, light is emitted from the mouth. Within the commentary on this passage, there are further two divisions:
first, the exhortation to recite and uphold it; second, from "Therefore," onwards, the conclusion regarding the reason for emitting light. This is the [third]...
First, the exhortation to recite and uphold: first it clarifies that one should recite oneself, and subsequently it clarifies the exhortation for others to recite; this is the first point.

"All of you Bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds should also recite, and even the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten bhūmis should also recite."
"From 'you all' onwards is the second exhortation for those who have resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment].

Regarding the Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds and are in the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), the ten 'aspirations for advancement' (*daśa-prasthāna*) are as stated in the previous fascicle: 'O Buddhas, you should know that within the stage of Firm Faith and Patience (*kṣānti*), there are ten aspirations for advancement toward the fruit:
first, the mind of relinquishment; second, the mind of precepts; third, the mind of patience; fourth, the mind of diligence; fifth, the mind of concentration;..."
Sixth is the mind of wisdom; seventh is the mind of aspiration; eighth is the mind of protection; ninth is the mind of joy; tenth is the mind of the summit.
Regarding the ten minds of long-cultivation, as stated above, they consist of the ten minds that enter from here into the stage of firm patience in the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

The ten minds directed toward the fruit are: first, the mind of loving-kindness; second, the mind of compassion; third, the mind of sympathetic joy; fourth, the mind of equanimity; fifth, the mind of giving.
1. The mind of six kinds of pleasant speech; 2. the mind of benefit; 3. the mind of harmony; 4. the mind of concentration; 5. the mind of wisdom.
O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten nurturing minds, one enters the firm cultivation of patience. Within this, there are ten adamantine minds directed toward the fruit:
1. the mind of faith; 2. the mind of mindfulness; 3. the mind of dedication; 4. the mind of penetration; 5. the mind of rectitude; 6. the mind of non-retrogression.

7. The Mahāyāna mind; 8. The signless mind; 9. The wisdom mind; 10. The indestructible mind—O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten adamantine minds one enters into the firm and holy patience (*kṣānti*).
Within this, the stages and fruits are as follows: the first stage is the Ground of Essential Nature Equality;

the second is the Ground of Good Wisdom of Essential Nature; the third is the Ground of Radiance of Essential Nature; the fourth is the Ground of *Jñeyalakṣaṇa* (Knowledge of the Characteristics of Objects) of Essential Nature.
The fifth nature of the Ground is the Wisdom-Illumination Ground; the sixth nature is the Flower-Light Ground; the seventh nature is the Fulfillment Ground;
the eighth nature is the Buddha-Roar Ground; the ninth nature is the Flower Ornament Sutra Ground; and the tenth nature is the Entry into the Buddha-Domain Ground.
The commentary explains that these forty minds explain, in successive order, the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), and the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Among the six types of lineages (*gotra*) on the stages, the subsequent ones—namely, the lineage of existence, the lineage of the nature-seed, the lineage of the path-seed, and the lineage of the noble ones—are each explained in detail as previously stated.
Therefore, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth; it has a cause and is not without a cause. Thus, these lights are neither blue, yellow, red, nor white.
Black is neither form nor mind, neither existent nor non-existent, and not a phenomenon of cause and effect;
it is the original source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the bodhisattva path, and the foundation for all the sons of the Buddha in this great assembly.
Therefore, all you sons of the Buddha in this great assembly should receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and study it well.
Therefore, the sūtra states that the light of the precepts issues from the mouth. From the second knot below, light is emitted;

herein, it is intended to signify that the precepts recited from the mouth are the precepts, and thus the light of the precepts issues from the mouth. Because this light represents the precepts, it is called the "light of the precepts.
Consequently, this light emerges due to causes and conditions, not without causes and conditions; the light is neither blue nor yellow.
Regarding "red, white, and so forth," because these characteristics are subsumed back into their fundamental nature, it is said that they are not blue, yellow, or the like;

alternatively, since the color of the precepts is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is now stated that they are not blue and so forth in order to reveal what is signified. The former explanation is superior.

Regarding "neither cause nor effect," this refers to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), which is neither cause nor effect, as it is free from the differentiated characteristics of cause and effect. This is precisely...
Because it is manifested by non-duality, it is said that the Buddha and Bodhisattvas share the same fundamental source. This means that both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas arise from this precept;
if this precept were absent, they would certainly not achieve fruition. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"For example, it is impossible for one who has no feet to wish to walk, no wings to wish to fly, or no boat to wish to cross over; likewise, it is impossible for one who lacks the precepts to [achieve the goal]."
Obtaining excellent fruits is likewise so. To the great assembly, he exhorted them to recite and uphold [this]:

"O Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! Whether one receives the Buddha’s precepts as a king, prince, high official, minister, bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, the eighteen Brahmā deities, the six classes of desire-realm devas, commoners, eunuchs, male or female libertines, or slaves—[all may do so]."
Whether they be spirits of the various classes, vajra deities, animals, or even transformed humans, as long as they understand the words of the Dharma Master,
they all receive the precepts and are called those of the foremost purity.
"Listen attentively, O Sons of the Buddha. From this point downward is the third section, which distinguishes the individuals capable of receiving the Bodhisattva precepts.

This exposition of the reception of the precepts is analyzed by means of four gates: first, clarifying the method of receiving the precepts; second, clarifying the conditions for relinquishing the precepts;
third, clarifying the distinctions between upholding and violating the precepts; and fourth, clarifying the methods of repentance. First, clarifying the reception of the precepts.

The Dharma further has two types: first, receiving the Dharma by relying on a teacher; second, receiving the Dharma through self-vow. Within the former, there are three parts: first, requesting the precept master;
second, clarifying the formal *karmavācanā*; and third, clarifying the request for witnesses. Within the section concerning the precept master, there are again two divisions:
first, clarifying the characteristics of the precept master; second, clarifying the manner of requesting him. This is the first [section], clarifying the precept master.
The master asked, "What kind of master may one receive the Bodhisattva precepts?

The explanation states that one must seek out a master who has already generated the great resolve (*mahācitta*), possesses wisdom and power, is skillful in speech, and is able to explain the principles of meaning; such is the Bodhisattva master.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 40, states: "If various Bodhisattvas wish to [study] these three kinds of Bodhisattva training..."

Those who diligently practice and study the treasury of the precepts—whether they be householders or those who have left the home life—having first generated the great aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, should carefully seek out fellow Bodhisattvas who have likewise made the great vow, who possess wisdom and power, and who are able to transmit and explain the meaning of the verbal expressions [of the dharma].
Master Kumārajīva said: "This is called receiving the precepts."

This Dharma originally emerges from the "Chapter on the Ordination of Kings" within the *Brahmajāla-vinaya*. It concerns the method by which Vairocana Buddha and King Miaohai, along with his thousand sons, received the precepts, with [Vairocana] acting as the Precept Master.
This Dharma is for those who have left the household life as Bodhisattvas and are fully endowed with five virtues:

first, they firmly uphold the pure precepts; second, their years since ordination are ten or more; third, they are well-versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka; fourth, they are exquisitely proficient in meditative contemplation; and fifth, they possess wisdom.
One who has exhausted the profound essence of the宗 (zong) is fit to be a teacher. Although this statement exists, that sutra has not yet been translated here;
therefore, I shall now provide a brief account based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Alternatively, regarding the second point, the formal request to the teacher, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:
"Having first prostrated at the feet of a superior Bodhisattva endowed with such qualities, one should make this request, saying: 'I...'"
Now, desiring to receive all the pure bodhisattva precepts from a son of good family, or an elder, or one of great virtue, I pray that you will, for a brief moment,
not decline this labor but out of compassion grant me their transmission. Having made such an unerring request,
one should bare the right shoulder and pay respectful homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The Bhagavat has already entered the great earth, attained great wisdom, and attained great supernormal powers.

The assembly of Bodhisattvas, being present before him, single-mindedly recollects those various merits; according to their respective capacities and causal power, they give rise to a profound and pure mind, or at least a slight degree of pure mind.
These wise and powerful, superior Bodhisattvas act with humility and reverence, resting their knees upon the ground.
Standing on the ground, or squatting or kneeling before the Buddha image, one should make this request:
"I pray only that the Venerable One—or say 'Elder'—or 'Noble Son,' out of compassion, will bestow upon me the pure bodhisattva precepts.
Having made this request, one should focus the mind on a single object and cultivate a pure heart, thinking: "Before long, I shall attain the inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed [state]."
The Great Treasury of Merit, having reflected upon these matters accordingly, remained silent.

According to this sutra, one should request two masters; therefore, the subsequent sutra states: "Upon seeing a person who wishes to receive the precepts, one should instruct them to request two masters:
an Upādhyāya and an Ācārya. The commentary explains: "If there are masters present, one should fully request both; if there are no masters..."
The location is not necessarily required to possess both [conditions]. Second, the explanation of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is further divided into two parts.

First, the explanation of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the harmony of the assembly; second, the formal explanation of the *karmavācanā*. Regarding the preceptor, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are two matters concerning the preceptor. That treatise states:
"At that time, a wise and capable Bodhisattva, regarding one who is able to practice correctly as a Bodhisattva..."
Therefore, with an undistracted mind, whether sitting or standing, one should speak these words:
"Listen, son of good family named so-and-so," or "Listen, Dharma-brother! Are you a bodhisattva? He should respond, "I have made the vow for Bodhicitta.
One should not yet say, "It has already been generated. According to this sutra, because the preceptor asks about the seven obscurations, the subsequent sutra [states]:
It is said that when one wishes to receive the precepts, the Dharma Master asks: "In this present life, have you not committed any of the seven heinous offenses?
A Bodhisattva Dharma Master may not confer the precepts upon one who has committed the seven heinous offenses in this present life. The seven heinous offenses are:

shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing one's Upādhyāya (Preceptor), killing one's Ācārya (Teacher), disrupting the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure), and destroying the Dharma.

Regarding those who have severed the roots of the Saṃgha or killed a noble person (*ārya*), if they possess the seven obstructions (*saptāvaraṇa*), they cannot receive the precepts in this very life; however, all others may receive them.
Yet, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that even for those with the seven obstructions, if they perform repentance, they may still receive the precepts.

Thus, it is not as [the case for] Śrāvakas, who, once they have committed a pārājika offense, can never again receive the precepts. These two positions do not contradict one another, as each is based on a different principle.

This means that within this sutra, the argument is presented that for one who does not repent, the commission of the seven heinous crimes results in the inability to receive the precepts in this very life;
however, since there is also the sense of receiving them through repentance, it is omitted here.
Next, regarding the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, from this point onward one should speak as follows: "You, son of good family named [so-and-so], or..."
"O Dharma-brother, you wish to receive from me all the training precepts of a bodhisattva and all the pure vows of a bodhisattva—
namely, the vow of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the vow of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the vow of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
Such training precepts and such pure vows have been fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past and will be possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future."
"One who is fully endowed with the present bodhisattvas of all ten directions now possesses these precepts;
regarding these pure precepts, all bodhisattvas of the past have already trained, all bodhisattvas of the future will train, and all bodhisattvas of the present are now training.
Are you able to receive them? He replied, "I am able to receive them. [The teacher] said, "I am able to bestow them upon you, O Bodhisattva."
The recipient of the precepts asks a second and a third time in the same manner; the donor of the precepts likewise answers a second and a third time.
The donor of the precepts asks the questions up to the third time, and once the pure precepts have been received, the recipient of the precepts gives the responses up to the third time.
One should request the witness [of the witnesses] as it is stated in the *Yogācāra-bhūmi-śāstra* regarding the reception of the pure precepts.
Having already been able to bestow the precepts upon a bodhisattva without rising from one’s seat, that bodhisattva may, before an image of the Buddha,
pay respectful offerings and prostrate at the feet of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas currently dwelling throughout the ten directions,
and make this declaration: "I, the bodhisattva named [Name], have now [received] from me, the bodhisattva named [Name], up to three times..."
"I, [Name], a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, have already requested [Name] as my witness.
I pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— the foremost true sages throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions—
who are fully awakened at all times and in all places regarding all sentient beings, both manifest and unmanifest, [bear witness] to this [Name]."
When receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, one also requests them to act as witnesses; this is stated likewise for the second and third times.

When the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) for receiving the precepts is completed, immediately thereafter, a natural manifestation (*dharmatā-nimitta*) appears before all the Buddhas currently dwelling in world-systems throughout the ten directions—boundless and limitless—as well as before all Bodhisattvas who have entered the Great Stages (*mahābhūmi*). By means of this, [the precepts are confirmed].

Having thus shown that the bodhisattva has received the pure precepts undertaken by bodhisattvas, at that time the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions give rise to mindfulness regarding this bodhisattva through the natural law (*dharmatā*) of phenomena. Because of this mindfulness, right knowledge and vision arise;
through right knowledge and vision, they realize according to reality that "in such-and-such a world, there is a bodhisattva of such-and-such a name."

All the pure precepts of the bodhisattva vows received by whichever bodhisattvas have correctly attained them shall, toward this bodhisattva who has received the precepts, give rise to feelings of affection, kindness, and compassionate concern as if toward a son or a younger brother.
Through the compassionate concern of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, this bodhisattva’s aspiration for wholesome dharmas shall increase manifold and never diminish. When...
Knowing this is called the formal announcement and request for witness when receiving the Bodhisattva precepts.
Having thus performed the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) for receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, both the bestower and the recipient together perform offerings;
they prostrate at the feet of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions and respectfully withdraw. Thus it is said.

The ethical discipline of restraint undertaken by a bodhisattva is the most excellent, unsurpassed, and immeasurably boundless treasury of great merit compared to all other forms of ethical discipline of restraint undertaken; it is the foremost and supreme.
To speak extensively, even when compared to all the *prātimokṣa* restraints, the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline of restraint does not equal even one hundredth part [of its merit].
And even one thousandth part, nor a numerical fraction, nor a calculable fraction, nor a countable fraction, nor a figurative fraction,
nor even a *upaniṣad* (proportional) fraction of it would not equal it,
because it encompasses all great merits. Second, the explanation of receiving the precepts through self-vow, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The forty-first [chapter] states: Furthermore, if a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) but does not encounter a person (*pudgala*) endowed with complete virtues, they should at that time personally receive the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline before an image of the Tathāgata.
It should be received in this manner: baring the right shoulder and placing the right knee on the ground...

Or, kneeling before the seat, one should speak these words: "I, who am named [so-and-so], respectfully address all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages.

I now wish, in the presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, to vow to receive all the bodhisattva training rules and to vow to receive all the pure bodhisattva precepts. That is to say:

The morality of restraint, the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the morality of benefiting sentient beings—such are the training rules and such is the pure morality that all bodhisattvas of the past have possessed, all bodhisattvas of the future shall possess, and all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions now possess.
Such are the training rules and such is the pure morality of the past... [and so forth].

Having departed from all bodhisattvas who have already trained, and regarding all bodhisattvas of the future who shall train, as well as all bodhisattvas currently training throughout the ten directions—this second and third [recitation] are also spoken in this same manner.

Having spoken thus, one should arise; all remaining [procedures] should be understood as previously described. However, for those who receive [the precepts] for themselves, they must first perform repentance. It is essential that...
One should take the appearance of a good omen as the limit; if one does not obtain a good omen, one does not receive the precepts. As this sutra states below:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when one wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts with a sincere mind, one should vow to receive them before an image of the Buddha.
One must repent before the Buddha for seven days; upon seeing a good omen, one then obtains the precepts. If...
If one does not obtain auspicious signs (lakṣaṇa), one should continue for two weeks, three weeks, or even up to one year until auspicious signs are obtained.
Once auspicious signs have been obtained, one may receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.

If one does not obtain auspicious signs, although one receives the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, one does not obtain the precepts. However, if one first receives the Bodhisattva precepts in the presence of others...
When receiving the precepts before a teacher, it is not necessary to see auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*), because this is a case of the Dharma-teacher transmitting the precepts directly.
However, if within a thousand *li* there is no one capable of acting as a precept-teacher, one may receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva;
in that case, it is necessary to see auspicious signs. Second, regarding the number of conditions for relinquishing the precepts: [the following] explains the relinquishment.
Regarding the causes and conditions for [losing] the precepts, there are either two or four. As for the two, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 40, states:
"Briefly, one abandons the bodhisattva's pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) due to two conditions: first, abandoning the great vow for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
second, manifesting superior-grade entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) by committing an offense that constitutes a defeat (*pārājika*). As for the four conditions:
As stated in the seventy-fifth fascicle of the *Śāstra*: "Furthermore, there are briefly four kinds of causes and conditions for relinquishing [the precepts]:
first, the arousal of a mind that is discordant with the mind of undertaking; second, intentionally uttering words of renunciation in the presence of a great person capable of discernment;
third, the total or partial violation of the four types of prohibitions; and fourth..."

Regarding the four factors that cause defeat: if one commits a total or partial transgression of any of these four types of factors that lead to defeat due to an intense degree of mental affliction (*paryavasthāna*), it should be understood that by this cause and condition, one abandons the bodhisattva vow.

If one subsequently attains purification through a mind of renewed commitment, one should receive the vow once again. The explanation of the latter four conditions is as follows: the first and second [of these] are...
Among the first two conditions, the first condition subsumes the latter two of the four; among the [latter] two, the second subsumes them.
Therefore, whether there are two or four, they are equal and without difference. Regarding the "four dharmas that surpass others," these are the final four among the ten grave precepts.
Because the latter four are not shared [with śrāvakas], only the four grave precepts are taught. Alternatively, it may be that the mental karma of a bodhisattva is intended.
Because they are grave, only four are designated as "offenses entailing defeat" (*pārājika-dharmas*). These refer to the first six among the ten grave offenses.
Since these six may be shared with the followers of the Two Vehicles, or may not be fixed [to them alone], they are called "concordant" (*anuloma*).

Alternatively, the term "concordant" may mean that anything which gives rise to an offense entailing defeat is termed "concordant. Although there are these two interpretations, the former is considered superior.

Why is this so? If it were the case that all instances of "conforming to" the defeats (*pārājika*) were termed "conforming offenses," then one would have to relinquish the precepts immediately upon engaging in the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) for a defeat.
This interpretation is incorrect. By this reasoning, it is clearly understood that only the first six among the ten [offenses] are designated as "conforming offenses";
it is not said that all cases of committing the first six grave precepts through intense fetters (*tīvra-paryavasthāna*) necessarily entail the relinquishment of the precepts.
The commentary states: "In this context, 'abandoning' refers only to abandoning the functional capacity (*vṛtti*), not the seeds (*bīja*).

Question: What constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) of these three categories of pure discipline (*śīla*)? The commentary states: "This consists of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) form. Regarding these, the "informative" is defined as the volition (*cetanā*) manifested at the time of the third *karmavācanā* (the final formal motion).
It is established as such by way of designation based upon that predominant volition and aspiration; thus, it is definitively categorized as form (*rūpa*).

Because it is not of the nature of karma (*karma-svabhāva*), if the unmanifest restraint (*avijñapti-saṃvara*) were to have the seeds of superior aspiration and volition as its nature, this would be because it is provisionally established based on those seeds of grace.

What has been explained above is stated from the perspective of "subsuming the provisional into the real," for apart from the seeds of grace and non-grace, the manifest and unmanifest actions have no separate essence.
If one analyzes the essence of the precepts (*śīla*) according to the categories of dharmas (*dharma-saṃkhyā*), [it is as follows].
This [matter] has as its nature the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), yet other passages state that manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) is the object of the eye;

this is said either by way of figurative description (*anuvṛtti-dvāra*) or as a provisional teaching (*pariyāya*). The *Abhidharmakarma-siddhi-śāstra* states: "The third section clarifies the distinctions between maintaining and violating discipline.

Regarding prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), one explains maintaining and violating; furthermore, regarding natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), one explains maintaining and violating. Thus it is with respect to prohibitive offenses.
Regarding transgressions, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 41, states: "If bodhisattvas abide in the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
just as the Bhagavān established prohibitions regarding transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) in the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya* for the sake of protecting others—
restraining śrāvakas from committing acts that would cause sentient beings who have not yet gained faith [to lose it]— "

Having caused those who have not yet developed pure faith to do so, and having caused those with pure faith to increase it further, within this regard, Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas should train equally without distinction.

Why is this? Because while Śrāvakas prioritize their own self-interest and constantly fail to abandon or protect the conduct of others, [Bodhisattvas act] in order to cause sentient beings who have no faith to gain faith, and those who already have faith...

This increases the training in the precepts one has undertaken; how much more so for a bodhisattva whose excellence lies in benefiting others? One should know that this statement is made from a general perspective.

If one were to follow the logic to its conclusion, there would also be non-common considerations regarding prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*), such as those concerning the code of conduct (*īryāpatha*).
For instance, if a bodhisattva perceives that by not keeping his robes uniform there would be some benefit, he would in that case not adjust his robes.
Categories such as these may be understood by analogy with this. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"If bodhisattvas abide in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, then just as the Bhagavān—in the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya*—established prohibitions for śrāvakas regarding minor matters, minor actions, and minor aspirations in order to cause them to dwell [in restraint], he likewise prohibits various śrāvakas from [certain acts]."
In this regard, Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas should not train in an identical manner. Why is this?

Because Śrāvakas regard self-benefit as supreme and disregard the benefit of others; thus, dwelling with few concerns, few activities, and few aspirations regarding the benefit of others may be called "excellent.
However, Bodhisattvas regard the benefit of others as supreme and do not disregard their own.
When one dwells with few affairs, few activities, and few expectations within the pursuit of benefiting others, this is called "sublime.

Such a bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting others, should seek various hundreds or thousands of garments from non-relatives—such as householders, lay devotees, or brahmins—and from families that give freely; they should observe whether those sentient beings have the means or not.
One should accept whatever is offered according to what is appropriate; as it is with seeking robes and begging bowls, so it is likewise for them.
Just as one seeks robes and bowls, so too may one personally seek various kinds of silk and thread to have a non-relative weave into a robe for the sake of benefiting others.
For the purpose of benefiting others, one should keep various *kauśeya* (silk) garments and various sitting and lying implements, each up to a maximum of one hundred.

From one thousand [verses] up to the full exposition, regarding the distinctions between maintaining and violating the precepts within the category of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), these shall be explained in the text itself.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra* states: The Buddha told Upāli, "You should now know that those of the Śrāvaka vehicle have distinct skillful means and a distinct profound intention for maintaining pure precepts; those of the Bodhisattva vehicle have distinct skillful means..."
There are those with divergent profound resolve who maintain pure precepts;

although these followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle maintain the precepts purely, they are not said to possess pure precepts according to the Bodhisattva vehicle. Although these followers of the Bodhisattva vehicle are said to possess pure precepts, they are not said to possess pure precepts according to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Why is this? It is because although these followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle maintain the precepts purely...
One who belongs to the Bodhisattva vehicle is not called one of pure precepts;
Upāli, one who belongs to the Śrāvaka vehicle should not, even for a single thought-moment, give rise to a single thought of desiring to receive another body.

This is what is meant by a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle maintaining pure precepts, whereas for a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle it constitutes the greatest breach of precepts and is not called purity. The explanation says: "This refers to all..."

When there is an opportunity to benefit others, a bodhisattva skillfully assumes a body and gives rise to various desires to gather in sentient beings, leading them out of unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states.
If a bodhisattva fails to gather in sentient beings through such desire and instead abandons them, this constitutes a breach of the precepts.
This is the intended meaning here, referring to both lay bodhisattvas and monastic bodhisattvas.
A bodhisattva who has gone forth must not engage in unchaste conduct for the sake of protecting the holy teaching.

Furthermore, it is said that a person of the Bodhisattva Vehicle such as Upāli, who is capable of enduring physical suffering through immeasurable eons without giving rise to weariness or aversion, is called a person of the Bodhisattva Vehicle who purely maintains the precepts;
whereas compared to him, one of the Śrāvaka Vehicle is considered to have the greatest breach of discipline.
It is not called pure. Why? It is said that those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle uphold the "open" precepts, whereas those who are Śrāvakas uphold the "unopen" precepts.

Upāli, when a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle commits an offense during the first watch of the day, they reflect during the middle watch of the day that they shall attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*); at that time, such a person does not break the precepts.

If a Bodhisattva has committed an offense during the middle part of the day, but then contemplates at a later part of the day that they shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), then at that time, the Bodhisattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) is not broken.

This is explained in detail up to the case where one has committed an offense during the final watch of the night, but then contemplates at the first part of the day that they shall attain all-knowledge; for such a Bodhisattva, [the aggregate of ethical discipline is not broken].

At that time, because of this principle, those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle uphold the open and flexible precepts, while those who belong to the Śrāvaka Vehicle uphold the non-open and inflexible precepts.
A Bodhisattva should not give rise to great shame, nor should they give rise to the entanglement of great remorse;
however, Upāli, one belonging to the Śrāvaka Vehicle who repeatedly commits offenses immediately breaks and loses [the precepts].
Regarding the aggregate of the śrāvaka’s precepts: why is this so? Because a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle should maintain the precepts and restrain all fetters as if their head were on fire;
they do so with a profound resolve for the sake of nirvāṇa. [This is] explained at length, until Upāli said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, there may be a mind associated with desire that violates the precepts, or one characterized by anger."

Regarding the transgression of precepts through the mind: when one transgresses a precept with a mind associated with delusion, World-Honored One, among the transgressions of a bodhisattva committed with a mind associated with desire, a mind associated with hatred, or a mind associated with delusion, which is the most grave?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli:
"If there is a bodhisattva who, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, violates the precepts with a mind associated with desire;

or if there is another bodhisattva who violates the precepts due to a mind of anger—among those abiding in the path of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, one who violates them out of anger should be known as the most grave. Why is this so?"
Because of anger, one is able to abandon sentient beings; because of desire, one gives rise to affection for sentient beings.
Upāli, regarding all fetters that give rise to affection, a bodhisattva should not feel fear;
regarding all fetters that cause one to abandon sentient beings, a bodhisattva should feel great fear. This is explained at length.
Even for a person of the Mahāyāna who commits an offense out of desire, I say that such a person does not commit a transgression [of the precept] through that desire;

however, I say that one who commits an offense out of anger commits a "great transgression. This is a great calamity and a great fall from within the Buddha-dharma, and it constitutes a major obstacle.
If there is a bodhisattva who lacks skillful means and possesses a mind associated with desire, [he is not thereby defiled].
If one commits a transgression against the precepts while giving rise to fear, yet does not give rise to fear when committing a transgression through anger;
if there is a bodhisattva who, possessing skillful means, commits a transgression against the precepts with a mind associated with hatred yet gives rise to fear,
whereas he does not give rise to fear when committing a transgression with a mind associated with desire.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddha, saying: "There are ten grave *prātimokṣa* precepts.
Following the Buddha’s statement that there are ten grave *prātimokṣa* precepts, this section below provides a detailed explanation of the characteristics of these precepts.
This part contains two sections: first, an explanation of the ten grave precepts; second, an explanation of the minor precepts; and finally, a general summary.
In the commentary on the tenfold structure of the text, there are three parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation; and third, a concluding summary.
Within the first part, there are four sections: first, indicating the number; second, exhorting recitation; third, exhorting study;
and fourth, exhorting upholding. This [passage] is the first [section].
If one receives the Bodhisattva precepts but does not recite these precepts, they are not a Bodhisattva and are not the seed of a Buddha;
I likewise recite them.
If one receives the Bodhisattva precepts and proceeds to recite them as well, this is the second section below, which is the exhortation to recite.
All bodhisattvas must necessarily recite the precepts; those who do not recite these precepts are not bodhisattvas and are not seeds of the Buddha.
Because one who does not recite and uphold the precepts will certainly be unable to attain the fruit of Bodhi, it is said that they are not seeds of the Buddha.
All bodhisattvas have already studied, all bodhisattvas shall study, and all bodhisattvas are now studying;
from this point downward is the third section, which encourages study regarding those who have studied up to the present among all bodhisattvas.
I have briefly explained the characteristics of the Prātimokṣa; you should train in them and uphold them with a reverent mind.
From the point "I have briefly explained" up to "uphold them with a reverent mind," the following section is the fourth: the exhortation to uphold [the precepts].
