*Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra*, Fascicle Lower, Part One.
Compiled by the Monk Shengzhuang of Chongyi Temple.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "I have already finished explaining the ten *pātimokkha* rules; the forty-eight minor precepts shall now be explained.

The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddha: from this point downward is the second section, the explanation of the minor precepts, which is divided into three parts. First, the summary of what preceded.
Following the introductory section, the subsequent detailed explanation consists of forty-eight parts; the final section is the exhortation to uphold [the precepts].
"If a Buddha’s disciple..."—from this point downward is the second part, the detailed explanation of the text, which is divided into five sections. The first is the ten precepts proper.

The explanation of the "Inclusion of the Dharmas Conducive to Wholesomeness" clarifies the precepts for benefiting sentient beings. In the second [section], there are ten precepts that clarify the precepts for benefiting sentient beings;

in the fourth, there are nine precepts that clarify both the precepts for benefiting sentient beings and the dharmas conducive to wholesomeness; and in the fifth, there are ten precepts that clarify the precepts for benefiting sentient beings.
These five sections are designated by their initial titles, or because they are described according to their predominant content, they are said to be "included."

Regarding the intermediate [category] such as "wholesome" and so forth, it is not that there are no further distinctions among the precepts and other factors; these shall be explained in the relevant passage.
This constitutes the first [section], the formal explanation of the "precept for gathering virtuous dharmas," which also reveals the "precept for benefiting sentient beings.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the exhortation to uphold [the precepts]. Within the first part, there are two sections. First, there are eight precepts that clarify the "precept for gathering virtuous dharmas," namely the six...

Following the section on the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), there are two precepts that clarify the precept of "beneficial action" (*anugrahaka-śīla*), which corresponds to the "beneficial conduct" (*artha-caryā*) among the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*).

Within the preceding section, there are three parts: first, two precepts that are hindrances to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); next, four precepts that are hindrances to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);
and finally, four precepts that are hindrances to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*). This is the first explanation regarding the precept against making offerings in an improper manner.

This is the section on obstructing the *dānapāramitā* (Perfection of Giving), which consists of three parts: first, the identification of the person; second, the clarification of the characteristics of the transgression;
and third, the conclusion regarding the offense if one does not act accordingly.
When wishing to accept the position of a king, when accepting the position of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), or when officials accept their positions, one should first receive [the precepts].
The Bodhisattva precepts protect the bodies of all ghosts and spirits, the bodies of kings and officials, and bring joy to all Buddhas.

Regarding those who wish to receive the rank of a king, from this point [the second section] below, there is a formal explanation of the characteristics of the precepts. This section contains two parts:

first, an exhortation to receive the precepts; second, following the practice of the precepts, the formal revelation of their characteristics. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections. First:
The sequence for exhorting others to receive the precepts: first, explaining the reason why all ghosts and spirits receive them;

this is the initial point, meaning that those who wish to assume positions such as kings must first receive the pure Bodhisattva precepts, as it is only by possessing these precepts that they may rule a kingdom or hold the offices of the hundred ministers.
Second, explaining the reason why all ghosts and spirits receive them: if one attains the precepts...
All ghosts and spirits shall protect the bodies of the king and his hundred officials, and the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas shall likewise bestow their grace upon them;
through these causes and conditions, their power of merit will increase, making them fit to be kings and officials.
Once you have received the precepts, you should give rise to a heart of filial piety and respect;

upon seeing elders, preceptors (upādhyāya), ācāryas, those of equal standing in study, those of the same view, and those who practice together, you should rise to welcome them, prostrate, and inquire after their well-being.

Having already received the precepts, the second section follows, which correctly reveals the characteristics of the precepts. This section is divided into two parts: first, clarifying what should be practiced;
second, clarifying what should not be practiced. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, clarifying the attainment of the precepts; second, generating a heart of filial piety;
and third, clarifying the reasons for this. This is the first [section]. Regarding the phrase "generating a heart of filial piety and a heart of reverence": this is the second [section].

Second, explaining the *Xiàosùnxīn jīng* (Sūtra on the Mind of Filial Obedience). From the section on the *zhǐshàngzuò* (senior monks) up to the "Great Fellow Students" is the third part, clarifying the objects of veneration.
Regarding the *hécháng* (upādhyāya): formerly called *héshé*, this means "power";

today it is said that the Sanskrit term is *upādhyāya*, which means "intimate instructor," or *upadeśaka*, which means "near-recitation master. (The text here appears to contain a scribal error regarding the latter term.)
The term *ācārya* was formerly translated as "one of correct conduct" (*zhèngxíng*). Now, according to the Sanskrit sound, it is called *ācārya*, which means "Teacher of Conduct" (*guǐfànshī*).
Regarding these four objects [of veneration], one should give rise to a mind of filial obedience; "filial obedience" clarifies the mental action (*manas-karman*).

"Reverence" clarifies the physical and verbal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*). What is intended here is that, upon seeing the *upādhyāya* and others, one should rise from one's seat and offer salutations.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states: "If one sees a mendicant who can treat them with the four kinds of hospitality—
first, looking upon them with kind eyes, welcoming and seeing them off, and respectfully inquiring after their well-being—
and yet the Bodhisattva, on the contrary, gives rise to arrogance, delusion, and pride, failing to rise to greet them or prostrate to them in each instance..."
One should provide offerings in accordance with the Dharma by selling oneself, one’s kingdom, city, sons, daughters, the seven treasures, and all manner of goods to supply them;
if one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

As for the passage stating that "the Bodhisattva goes to [them] and provides for them," this refers to the second section on what should not be practiced, which begins from the point where it says "if they appear."

If one knows that by making an offering there will be benefit for oneself and for sentient beings, one should offer with a sincere heart and inquire about the Dharma, even at the cost of one's body or life;
if, out of a mind of resentment or hatred, one does not make such an offering, this constitutes an offense.
However, if one currently lacks material goods, or if one intends to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue another and therefore does not make an offering, there is no offense.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If a bodhisattva, while dwelling in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), sees elders, virtuous persons, those worthy of respect, or fellow practitioners of the Dharma approaching, yet being constrained by pride and harboring resentment, fails to rise to greet them or offer them a superior seat, this is called an offense;
it is a transgression and constitutes an afflicted violation."

If one does not act out of pride, nor with a mind of resentment or malice, but solely due to laziness, indolence, forgetfulness, or a neutral state of mind, this is called an offense and a transgression; it is a non-afflicted violation.
There is no offense in cases where one has encountered a serious illness, or when the mind is deranged, or when one is asleep while another person perceives one as being awake.
They come to associate with one another, engaging in conversation, offering greetings and consolations, and inquiring after one's welfare;

or they themselves, or for the sake of others, proclaim the teachings on various dharmas, engage in discussion and analysis, and provide extensive explanations; or, as is elaborated at length, they may desire to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them;
or, as stated in this *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the first *Śīla-sūtra* regarding non-offering: "If it were not so..."
The third section below clarifies that the completion of the path of karmic action (*karmapatha*) occurs through the presence of four conditions, which constitute a defiled transgression:

first, the object (*vastu*), meaning the venerable person; second, the perception (*saṃjñā*), meaning the arising of the perception regarding that person; third, the affliction (*kleśa*), meaning a mind of pride or a mind of resentment;
and fourth, the culmination of the means (*upāya-paryavasāna*), meaning the completion of the act.
"If a Buddha’s disciple...
This marks the second section from below, which contains four precepts that obstruct the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). These four are explained as follows;
this is the first, clarifying the prohibition against drinking alcohol, as it is a gateway to negligence (*pramāda*), and thus it is regulated. The text is divided as follows:

This section has three parts: first, the identification of the person; second, the explanation of the characteristics of the karmic path; and third, the conclusion regarding the karmic path. This is the first part.

Therefore, if one gives food with alcohol and thereby generates the immeasurable faults of alcohol, and if one passes a vessel of alcohol through one's own hands to others to drink, they shall be without hands for five hundred lifetimes;
how much more so if one drinks it oneself? One must not teach any person to drink, nor even a single individual.

If one does not allow any sentient being to drink alcohol, much less drink it oneself, yet intentionally drinks it oneself or teaches others to drink it, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). According to the Sūtra,
regarding the phrase "intentionally drinking alcohol, how much more so for oneself," this second section below clarifies the characteristics of the karmic paths concerning alcohol.
Regarding the vessel and the person, there are two interpretations. One says that if one passes a wine vessel to encourage another, it constitutes an offense even if the vessel is empty.
Another says that merely passing an empty vessel also constitutes an offense. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three types of alcohol;
thus, the fifteenth fascicle of that treatise states: "There are three kinds of alcohol: first, grain-based alcohol (*surā*); second, [fermented fruit alcohol]; third, [fermented molasses alcohol]."
There are various kinds of fruit wines, such as those made from grapes (*mṛdvīkā*) and *ariṣṭa* trees.

Thirdly, there are medicinal wines, which are produced by blending various medicinal herbs with rice, malt, and sugarcane to transform them into liquor. Such types of substances cause the human mind to become agitated and lead to heedlessness;
these are called "alcohol" and should not be drunk under any circumstances (there are thirty-five faults associated with this, as recorded in the *Prajñāpāramitā*).
As the verse says: "The characteristics of the faults of alcohol are that it clouds the physical complexion and harms the intellect;
it agitates and confuses the mind, increases forgetfulness and anger, destroys joy, and ruins one's clan. It is truly drinking the poison of death. The commentary explains:

If one desires happiness for oneself, one should not drink under any circumstances. However, if one sees that drinking alcohol can be beneficial, one may employ skillful means to include others [in the act].
It is not an impediment for those sentient beings to emerge from an unwholesome state and be established in a wholesome state, even while drinking;

this is precisely yoga, established for the sake of protecting others as being free from fault. Some say that "five hundred lifetimes without hands" means five periods of five hundred years without hands:
one period of five hundred years in the *kṣāra* (salty dregs) hell, and two periods of five hundred years in... [the salt water hell].
In the Buddha’s excrement, one remains for three or five hundred years as a *kurukuccha* worm; for four or five hundred years as a fly or a gnat;
and for five hundred years as a dull-witted human—or perhaps this refers to the final five hundred years. (Note:
However, this drinking of alcohol constitutes an offense only when five conditions are fully met: first, it must be actual alcohol; second, there must be the perception [of it as such]...)

Third, the perception of liquor; fourth, the drinking, which refers to the desire to drink; fifth, the afflictions, which refer to the conjunction of hatred and delusion, whether present together or not;
and sixth, the culmination of the means, which refers to the completion of the drinking.
"If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally eats meat—no meat whatsoever may be eaten.
This is the second section from "If a Buddha’s disciple" onwards, which clarifies the precept against eating meat because it violates the mind of compassion;
the text is divided into three parts, and this is the first, identifying the person. From the scripture: "If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally eats meat—no meat whatsoever..."
Regarding those who consume [forbidden food], this section follows the second part, which clarifies the characteristics of the paths of action (*karmapatha*).

Within this, it first clarifies the prohibition against consuming such food, and subsequently clarifies that consuming it constitutes an offense. Of these two parts, the former consists of the prohibition followed by its explanation; this is the first.
Because it severs the seeds of the nature of great compassion and causes all sentient beings to see [the eater] and abandon them,
no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being.
The Sūtra states: "From severing the seeds of the nature of great compassion... to abandoning and departing. This is the second explanation of the reason why:
if one eats meat, it severs the nature of compassion; all sentient beings will conceive thoughts of enmity toward such a person and abandon them.
Furthermore, regarding this eating of meat, while the seven classes of followers commit the same offense, there is a difference between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Specifically, for the Śrāvakas:
While the teachings permit three kinds of pure meat, within the Bodhisattva teachings none are permitted at all.
Eating meat incurs immeasurable offenses; if one eats it intentionally, they commit a minor transgression.
Regarding the statement that eating meat incurs immeasurable sins, the second section below clarifies the faults and karmic causes and effects of consuming meat.
The *Cāṇakya-sūtra* states: "One who eats the flesh of a dog's entrails in this life will, upon death, fall into the Excrement Hell.
Regarding the third point, the formal conclusion on the path of karma: this is subsumed within the precepts as taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, as the sūtra says:
Meat does not arise from its own nature; it must be obtained by taking the life of a sentient being.
If you, O Son of the Buddha, do not eat the five pungent plants—garlic, leeks, scallions, onions, and *xingqu*—you must not consume them among any foods whatsoever.
If you intentionally eat them, you commit a minor offense (*āpatti*).
In the Sūtra, from the passage "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards, the third section clarifies the precept against the five pungent roots (*pañca-garadha*).
The five pungent roots are: first, garlic; second, leek (also called *fei-gan*; it resembles *fei* but is thicker); third, onion; fourth, *cong-lan*—traditionally said to grow in Lingnan;
its leaves resemble those of garlic but are broader, and its foul odor is like that of garlic; fifth, *hing-k’u*.
Regarding this, some say that the Sanskrit term is *hiṅgu*; because the syllable *gu* is elided, it is called "xing" (興), which corresponds here to the plant *yūnzhī* (芸薹).
In the language of the Brahmins, the mustard plant is called *hiṅgu*. Monasteries in the Western Regions and the monastic community do not permit the consumption of *yūnzhī*.
Furthermore, others say that *xingqú* (興渠) grows in the regions south of the [Five] Ridges.
Its shape resembles that of a *fei* (a type of onion), and its flavor is like garlic. Some say it grows in places such as Jiangnan and Guangzhou;

this should be further investigated. Regarding these three precepts, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that they are all categorized as prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) established for the protection of the holy teachings.
"O sons of the Buddha:
[This section] from 'If a son of the Buddha' onwards is the fourth, clarifying the precept against failing to instruct in repentance and the precept regarding violating commands for purity;

thus it is established. The text is divided into three parts: first, the person; second, the corresponding instruction to be given; and third, from 'And the Bodhisattva' onwards, the actual clarification of the karmic act."
This is the first [offense].

To see all sentient beings committing offenses against the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts; violating prohibitions; committing the seven heinous crimes or the eight difficulties;
or committing any other transgressions of the precepts—and yet the Bodhisattva does not instruct them to repent, but instead dwells with them and shares in the same monastic benefits.

If one participates in the *poṣadha* together with the assembly, yet when the precepts are recited, fails to expose their transgression and instruct them to repent, one commits a minor secondary offense (*laghu-pāyantika*).
From the phrase "throughout all sentient beings" up to "all offenses of violating the precepts," the second section clarifies what ought to be taught.

Regarding repentance within this [section], there are two parts: first, clarifying the commission of offenses; second, instructing on repentance and confession. This is the clarification of the commission of offenses.
As for the "eight precepts," these are the restraint (*saṃvara*) received in the *upavāsa* (fast-day) observance.

These eight precepts are analyzed through three gates: first, the method of receiving them; second, the method of relinquishing them; and third, an analysis through questions and answers. Regarding the method of receiving the precepts:
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, one must fulfill eight conditions to obtain the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*). What are these eight?
First, one must take refuge in the Three Jewels before receiving the precepts. As the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter fourteen, states:
"Is it only the lay follower (*upāsaka*) who can receive the one-day fast (*upoṣadha*), or can others also receive it? The verse says: "The one-day fast may be received by others as well."

There is one who, without having received the three refuges, says: "For those who have not yet received the lay devotee’s discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), if they take refuge in the Three Jewels for a single day and night and, after reciting the three refuges, receive the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), they obtain the discipline; otherwise, there is no such attainment.
The explanation is that if they have previously received the lay devotee’s discipline, it is not necessarily required that they first take the refuges, as they have already taken them.

Regarding the second point concerning the basis for receiving [the vows]: it means receiving them at dawn; that is, one must receive this precept at the time of sunrise, as this precept must last for one full day and night.

For those who have previously made such a formal commitment, saying, "I shall always receive this *upavāsa* discipline on the eighth day of the month and so forth," if there are obstructing conditions in the morning, they may still receive them once the fast has concluded.

Third, regarding the three types of receiving [the precepts]: "lower seat" means being in the presence of the teacher while occupying an inferior seat—either squatting or standing with the body bent and palms joined—except in cases of illness;
if one is not respectful, the restraint (saṃvara) is not generated. Fourth, "receiving from a teacher":

this refers to receiving from another teacher, as there is no such thing as spontaneous reception. Fifth, "receiving according to the instruction": one who receives these precepts should follow the teacher's instructions.
The instructor should explain [the precepts] afterwards, not before, nor simultaneously; only in this way is the formal reception from a teacher accomplished.

Otherwise, both the giving and the receiving of the precepts fail to be established. Sixth, regarding the "possession of factors": it means that only when the eight factors are complete is the *upavāsa* (fast-day observance) established.
If any factor is lacking, the *upavāsa* is not established. What are these eight? First, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from taking what is not given.

1. Refraining from unchaste conduct; 2. Refraining from false speech; 3. Refraining from intoxicants; 4. Refraining from using perfumes, garlands, ointments, dancing, singing, and watching performances;
5. Refraining from sleeping or sitting on high, broad, and ornate beds or seats; 6. Refraining from eating at improper times; and 7. Refraining from adornments.

One who receives this discipline must necessarily abandon adornments, because they are the basis for vanity and negligence; however, one does not necessarily have to abandon the habitual articles used for adorning the body.
Regarding the necessity of abandoning eight things: because it lasts for one full day and night, as stated in a verse of the *Abhidharmakośa*:

"The *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) is received at dawn while seated below the teacher; it is received according to the instruction, complete in its limbs, free from adornment, and lasts for a day and night.

According to the Sautrāntika school, abstaining from eating at improper times is the essence of the fast (*upoṣadha*), while the remaining eight items are called the "fasting observances" (*upavāsa*).

Because the categories of anointing the body, wearing ornaments, perfumes, and garlands, and watching or listening to dancing and singing are divided into two [groups], and so forth as explained at length;

thus, these eight precepts are not necessarily limited to a single day and night, as they may also last for a month, a year, or more. As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 37:
"In this regard, the Sautrāntikas say that between the two limits, it may be for the duration of one's entire life."

Although you have made a formal commitment after the end of your life, you cannot generate the Pratimokṣa vows within that distinct body because there is no preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and no recollection (*smṛti*).
Why is it that when one receives the Upavāsa vow for a period of one day and night,
or five or ten days and nights thereafter, what factor acts as an obstacle to those numerous Upavāsa restraints?

It is not that they cannot arise; as for such a statement, does it not contradict the sūtras? Having examined all the sūtras, I have never seen it stated that one may receive the *upavāsa* discipline at night.
For what reason do you, with your inferior intelligence, disparage the omniscient domain of the Buddhas?
The rest is as previously explained. According to the Mahāyāna, these eight precepts have not [yet been fully established].
One must necessarily follow a teacher, yet there are also cases of self-initiated reception; as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53:

"Regarding this ethical discipline (*śīla*), there is that which is received from another through one's own volition, and furthermore, there is that which is received solely by oneself, with the exception of the bhikṣu-vinaya.
Why? Because not everyone is capable of receiving the bhikṣu-vinaya. If [one were] a bhikṣu..."

It is not necessary to receive [the precepts] from another; whether one is fit for renunciation or unfit, as long as one desires to go forth, one should simply go forth spontaneously according to one's own wish.

If this were so, the holy teaching would lack any standard of conduct, and there would be no *dharma* or *vinaya* that could be understood. Therefore, there are no bhikṣus [who have gone forth in such a manner].
Question: If there is such a thing as "natural undertaking" (*svarasavāhana*) apart from the *bhikṣu* vows, for what reason must one further receive them from another?

Answer: Because there are two kinds of factors that support the undertaking and preservation of the abstention from immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*), namely, shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
When one commits an offense, whether in the presence of others or in private, these two produce a profound sense of shame.

Thus, because one can only fulfill the precept of guarding the auxiliary branches by receiving them from another after having abandoned immoral conduct, if shame (*hrī*) is truly present before one, there must necessarily also be dread of blame (*apatrāpya*);
for one who lacks dread of blame certainly possesses shame. Therefore, the dharma of shame is the most powerful condition.
Regarding the subsequent fulfillment of the auxiliary branches, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is not necessarily the case that all eight are complete.
Regarding what one is able to undertake, it may consist of one, two, three, or even up to eight precepts of the *upavāsa* (fasting) observance (*śīla*).
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, one must possess all eight types to be designated as the *upavāsa-saṃvara* (the restraint of fasting); thus, that treatise (vol. 53) states:
"The restraint of fasting is comprised of five factors. What are these five? First, undertaking the factor of abstaining from harming others..."
1. The branch of abstaining from harming oneself or others; 2. The branch of cultivating the practice of not transgressing what has been undertaken; 3.
The branch of maintaining right mindfulness so as not to transgress what has been undertaken; 4.

The branch of not harboring thoughts that harm the lives of others or covet the wealth of others—this is called the first branch; 5. The branch of abstaining from unchaste conduct—this is the second branch.
Why is this? Because by being free from these [first two], one does not cultivate one's own delusions and thus does not harm oneself;
nor does one cultivate [affection for] the wives and concubines of others and thus does not harm others. To abstain from false speech is the third limb.
To abstain from all intoxicants, which are the basis of negligence, and to abstain from the other three [bases of negligence] is the fourth limb. Why is this? Because...

The fifth limb is: to repeatedly reflect upon oneself, "I now abide in the definitive fast (upavāsa)," and at all times to maintain right mindfulness while remaining far removed from singing, dancing, music, perfumed ointments, garlands, and high beds; to abstain from eating at improper times;
and to distance oneself from all intoxicants and sources of heedlessness that one was formerly accustomed to.

Why is this? Although one abides in the factor of right mindfulness, thinking, "I now abide in the definitive fast and precepts," if one becomes intoxicated by various liquors, one will become deranged and lose self-mastery. Regarding these two passages, how are they to be reconciled?
The explanation states that there are two interpretations. One says: "Only when the factors are complete is it called 'near-dwelling' (upavāsa)."

Receiving [the vows] for one day, two days, and so forth is also called "near-dwelling" (*upavāsa*). If one wishes to receive [the vows] for one or two days and so forth, what factor acts as an obstacle such that one does not obtain the precepts?
Regarding this, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that those who fully receive [the vows] for eight periods of time are "encompassed by the five branches.
This does not mean that they must necessarily be encompassed by all five branches; some say that one only attains what is encompassed when one necessarily possesses all eight branches.

Regarding the statement that "the undertaking of the precepts is not accomplished if there is any deficiency in the restraint," the phrase "a single portion" and so forth refers to the description of the corresponding conduct.
Second, concerning the conditions for the relinquishment of the precepts: according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) restraint is relinquished through five conditions.

First, it is relinquished by means of intention, because one relinquishes the training by generating an informative act (*vijñapti-karman*) directed toward a person capable of understanding. Second, by...
1) Because of abandoning the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*); 2) because of the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs;

3) because of the severance of one's own roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*); 4) because of night and day. The Sautrāntika masters say that "night and day" are not mentioned [in the definition], as they accept [the loss of vows] through a month, a fortnight, and so forth.
The other four conditions are the same as those held by the Sarvāstivādins. If one follows the Mahāyāna itself...
There are two interpretations. The first states that it is relinquished due to four conditions, which is the same as the Sautrāntika position;

this is because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also permits [the observance] for one month, half a month, and so forth. The second states that it is due to three conditions; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53, says:
"Regarding the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) discipline, it should be known that it is relinquished either after sunrise, or by the arising of a discordant state."

The mind (meaning intentional relinquishment) may, at an intermediate stage, relinquish the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class), even though it has already been acquired; it must necessarily be relinquished again.

The commentary explains that this does not refer to the time of severing the roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*) or the arising of both sexual organs (*ubhaya-vyañjana*), because their timing is constrained. Regarding the question and answer:
the question asks whether there are karmic conditions for which the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) discipline should not be conferred. The answer is as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "If..."
It should be understood that the *upavāsa* restraint (near-dwelling discipline) must not be conferred upon those whose intention (*āśaya*) is impaired. Why is this?
Because some act out of compliance with others, or because some falsely claim they wish to receive the *upavāsa* restraint for the sake of obtaining wealth, profit, or honor;
yet, in reality, they lack the intentional desire to receive it. It should be known that such cases are termed "impairment of intention."

These questions and answers are omitted for fear of being too prolix; the meaning of the five precepts and ten precepts is as explained elsewhere. Regarding the "seven reverses," they shall be explained in the subsequent scripture.
As for the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), this is simply a scribal error where the character *nàn* (difficulty) was written instead of *zhòng* (grave).

Some say that the "eight difficulties" refers merely to the transgression of the precepts, which is called the "eight difficulties" because one is born in the eight difficult states; thus, the name of the result is applied to the cause.
This is called the joy of the Buddhas appearing in the world for yoga. It is said:

"If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), harbors a mind of resentment or a mind of malice toward violent and immoral sentient beings, and because they have fundamentally transgressed the precepts, abandons them through such means and fails to provide them with benefit—this is called [having a fault]."
To commit a transgression that involves a violation is a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*).
If one abandons [beneficial action] due to indolence or laziness, or fails to act for the benefit of others due to lack of mindfulness, this is called an offense that is not defiled (*akliṣṭāpatti*).

There is no transgression in cases such as when the mind is deranged, or when one intends to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue another, or when acting to protect the minds of many sentient beings.
Alternatively, there is no transgression if one sets aside [the task] through skillful means to protect the monastic regulations and does not provide benefit;
in such a case, one should instruct them to confess. To "instruct" means to cite what the other has said to cause them to remember, and subsequently teach the method for confession.
To "cite the offense" means that when Bodhisattvas see sentient beings violating their vows, they abide in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
One should carefully examine the person whose fault is being pointed out before pointing it out, and one should act with mindfulness;
that is to say, one should observe whether the *pudgala* being pointed out has affection and respect for oneself. This is explained at length in the sutras.

Furthermore, this pointing out of faults is consistent with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Briefly, there are two types of methods for repentance (*deśanā*): the first is the repentance of grave offenses.

Second, regarding repentance for light offenses and repentance for grave dharmas: if one commits a *pārājika* offense with a superior degree of entanglement (*saṃyojana*), one loses the bodhisattva precepts;
one should be taught to repent and should be granted the precepts again. If one commits a *pārājika* offense with a middling degree of entanglement, one should repent before three persons.
If one commits a *pārājika* offense or a light offense with an inferior degree of entanglement, one should repent before a single person.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 41, states: "If a bodhisattva violates any of the aforementioned *pārājika* offenses due to an intense degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), they shall forfeit their ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) and must receive it again.
If they violate the aforementioned *pārājika* offenses due to a medium degree of entanglement, they should confess before three persons or more."
The ritual for the disclosure and removal of misdeeds (*duṣkṛta*) is as follows: First, one should state the offense committed and speak thus:
"Venerable One, [or: O Great Virtue], I, who am named so-and-so, have transgressed the Bodhisattva Vinaya rules.
Regarding the matter as stated, I have committed a misdeed (*duṣkṛta*). The remainder is like the disclosure and repentance for the removal of misdeeds performed by a Bhikṣu."

The rules regarding offenses should be explained as follows: if one commits an offense such as those involving defeat (*pārājika*) or other violations due to minor entanglements (*parittakleśa*), one should confess and repent before a single person (*pudgala*). It should be understood that this procedure is as previously described.
However, if there is no suitable person (*anulomika-pudgala*) before whom one may confess and eliminate the transgression, at that time the Bodhisattva...
With a pure intention, one generates the resolve: "I shall certainly guard myself against future [transgressions] and never commit them again.

In this way, regarding the restoration from and purification of a transgression—and as for other violations—this indicates that even light offenses, whether heavy or light as described above, must not be concealed;
rather, they should be confessed before a bodhisattva capable of receiving the confession.
Regarding "vowing by oneself and repenting in one's heart for what was transgressed also results in returning to purity before a single person," etc.:

this refers to the general principle applicable to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practitioners. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "One should know that all violations are subsumed under *duṣkṛta* (misdeeds);
one should confess them before a person of sufficient power who is capable of understanding and accepting the meaning of the verbal expression."
The *Lùchànhuì jīng* (Sūtra on the Confession of Transgressions) continues with the third section, which correctly elucidates the paths of action (*karmapatha*).

Because they possess five conditions, these paths of action are fully established. First, the object (*vastu*): this refers to a person (*pudgala*) who has committed a transgression. Second, the perception (*saṃjñā*):
this refers to the arising of that very perception regarding the transgressing person. Third, the intention (*chanda*): this refers to the arousal of a [corresponding] desire toward them.
The four [factors] regarding the desire to bring forth charges and the desire not to instruct toward repentance are: first, the bodhisattva’s mind of anger and mind of resentment;
fifth, the culmination of the means, which refers to neither bringing forth charges nor instructing toward repentance.
If a Buddha’s disciple— this marks the third section from below, which explains the three precepts; these three are explained as three,
the first of which is the precept against failing to provide support and failing to request the Dharma, which violates the benefit of superior progress, and is therefore proscribed.

Furthermore, all seven assemblies commit this offense equally; it is prescribed for both major and minor transgressions, and within the Śrāvaka teachings, it constitutes the seventh category of offenses (*saptama-nikāya*). The text is divided into three parts;
this first section identifies the individuals involved:
Mahāyāna Dharma masters, as well as those who share the same Mahāyāna study, views, and conduct, enter monasteries, private residences, or cities.
If someone comes from a hundred or a thousand *li* away, one should rise to welcome them and see them off.
The Sūtra says: "Upon seeing a Mahāyāna Dharma Master arrive at one's residence, city, or village... This begins the second section, clarifying what should be practiced therein; it has two parts:
first, manifesting that which is to be revered, and second, from "if [someone comes] from a thousand *li*," the actual clarification of reverence and respect. This is as follows:
The first point is as can be seen from the text. The Sūtra says: "If one goes a hundred or a thousand *li* to welcome and see off [the teacher]," and so forth.
This begins the second section, which correctly clarifies respect and reverence; herein there are three parts: first, clarifying welcoming and seeing off; next, clarifying providing for needs;
and finally, clarifying requesting instruction. This is the first of these.
He shall pay homage and make offerings three times every day, providing daily sustenance of three *liang* of gold, food of a hundred flavors, seats, bedding, and medicine.

He shall provide for the Dharma Master all that is required. He shall constantly invite the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma at the three sessions of the day, prostrating three times daily without giving rise to anger or a mind of affliction, doing so for the sake of the Dharma’s extinction.
The body requests the Dharma.
The Sūtra says: "From prostrating and making offerings up to giving them everything one possesses"—this clarifies the second point, providing for others.

Regarding the phrase "two or three pieces of gold," this is an expression of extreme urgency; it means that those who listen to the Dharma do not regard even their own bodies or lives [as more important].
If this is so for sentient beings, how much more so for material wealth? It is like the Bodhisattva Bālāha, the Prince of the Snowy Mountains, who cherished the Dharma above all;
or like the Brahmin who loved the Dharma. Why is this? Material wealth does not transcend the realm of desire, whereas the gift of Dharma brings about liberation from birth and death.
Material wealth is finite and exhaustible, but the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible and never-ending, until one attains perfect and complete enlightenment.
Bodhi. If one does not act thus, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

If the sutra were not otherwise, this would mark the third section below, which correctly clarifies the determination of offenses; the five conditions for committing an offense are to be understood according to what precedes.
It should be understood that this is precisely the third aspect subsumed under the second precept of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, as previously explained under the first precept.
If, O sons of the Buddha:

The Sūtra says: "If a Buddha’s disciple... This is the second section, concerning the precept against not listening to the Dharma. The text is divided into three parts, which may be understood according to the previous model;
here, first, the person is identified.
[The disciple] sees that in every place there is the preaching of the Dharma—the Vinaya, Sūtras, and Śāstras—and that within great houses there are places where the Dharma is being taught.
"Wherever one goes, upon arriving at a place where the Dharma is being preached... This is the second section, clarifying what should be practiced therein.
It contains two parts: first, clarifying the place for preaching the Dharma; second, clarifying how one should listen to the Dharma. This is the first part.
"Dharma" (dharma) here refers to the Sūtras and the Vinaya-piṭaka; "Vinaya" (vinaya) refers to the Vinaya-piṭaka, with the Sanskrit term preserved in its original form.
Vinaya is here translated as "Discipline" (tiáofú). It is called "Discipline" because it disciplines the body, speech, and mind, subduing unwholesome karma;
the term *vinī* used here is likely an abbreviation of *vinaya*.
A newly initiated bodhisattva should take a scroll of the sūtras and the vinaya to the place where a Dharma teacher resides to listen, receive, and inquire about it;
they should likewise go to all places where the Dharma is preached, whether in mountain forests, beneath trees, in monastic quarters, or elsewhere, to listen and receive it.
The Sūtra says: "From 'a newly initiated bodhisattva' up to 'one who listens and receives'—this is the second [section], clarifying the statement on how one should listen to the Dharma.
Regarding listening to the Dharma, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 82:
"Listening" means that when a speaker of the Dharma preaches the true Dharma, one should establish others in a state of respect so that they may listen without error. How so?
"Abiding securely" refers to either a single cause or even up to eleven causes;
that is, listening to the Dharma with reverence so as to be able to realize benefit and well-being in the present.

Regarding this, there may be four permutations—such as being beneficial but not bringing well-being—as already explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the section on the "Acceptance of the Dharma. As for the "two causes," they refer to the first [of the two], which is "well-established."
Because all phenomena are well-established, they are free from all faults and possess great significance;
furthermore, because the exertion undertaken by both the speaker and the listener yields a superior fruit.

Were it otherwise, the efforts of the speaker and the listener would be in vain, and their further exertion would result in no fruit. As for the three causes, [the first is] listening to the Dharma with reverence.

To cause sentient beings to abandon the evil destinies, to attain the good destinies, and to be able to swiftly attract and grasp the causes of *nirvāṇa*—these three matters are essential and can only be obtained through listening with reverence. Regarding the four causes:

first, by listening to the Dharma with reverence, one is able to thoroughly understand the teachings of the *sūtras* and other scriptures; second, such true Dharma enables sentient beings to abandon [the evil destinies].
All unwholesome states are subsumed within [the category of] wholesome states; if one listens well, one will be able to apply oneself with diligence.

Whether it be relinquishing or adopting, these three arise through the relinquishment and adoption [of states]. Because of this relinquishment and adoption of wholesome and unwholesome causes, one swiftly realizes *nirvāṇa*.
To speak extensively, there are ten causes, the first of which is listening to the Dharma with reverence.

One attains the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*), by which one is able to experience the benefits of hearing the Dharma and seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma rather than through unrighteous means, while perceiving deep faults and disadvantages in doing so.
Second, one is skilled in knowing renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*): that is, when losing wealth and treasures, one is without sorrow or grief, nor does one lament or resent it;
this is explained at length, including the state of mind regarding separation from one's kin, as well as when encountering illness.
1) Not being deeply sorrowful or lamenting over suffering, nor being distressed by it, and so forth, as explained at length;

2) Deeply perceiving the defects within all sensual desires and seeing the supreme merit of renunciation, one leaves the household life in purity, abandoning attachment to excellent bedding and seats, and is even able to realize the various sublime meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*);
3) Listening to the Dharma with reverence, one quickly accords with it.

They realize and understand the vast and profound, as well as the seemingly profound, laws of dependent origination; furthermore, they are able to give rise to vast roots of goodness and the joy of renunciation.
As the Blessed One has said: "My noble disciples, with single-minded devotion and attentive ears, listen to the True Dharma;
they are able to sever five things and cultivate seven things, swiftly and completely fulfilling the five [factors] of the noble ones."
The disciple listens to the Dharma with reverence; all conditioned phenomena that have arisen are subject to cessation.
Having understood the True Dharma through these six aspects, they become free from dust and transcend suffering, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

They are able to attract and gather the most excellent provisions for realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and even for attaining the fruit of arhatship, as well as for attracting and gathering the state of an arhat.

10. It is capable of inducing all mundane and supramundane meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and attainments (*samāpatti*); as fully explained therein. It is the most excellent of the fruits of the Śrāvaka stage;

it is capable of inducing the provisions for the Pratyekabuddha stage; it is capable of skillfully inducing the provisions for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It is capable of inducing all mundane and supramundane meditative concentrations, liberations, and attainments, as fully explained therein.
If one does not go there to listen and receive [the teaching], one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
The Sūtra says: "If one does not go there... This concludes the third section, the formal conclusion of the path of action (*karmapatha*). As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:

"If various Bodhisattvas, dwelling securely in the Bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*), hear the exposition of the True Dharma, the treatises, or the analytical determination (*viniścaya*)," and so forth.
If, being constrained by pride, one harbors a mind of resentment or a mind of malice and does not go to listen, this is called an offense and a transgression.
If one does not go to listen because of being obscured by laziness or indolence, it is an unafflicted offense;
there is no transgression if one does not perceive [the teaching], or if one is ill, lacks physical strength, or knows that [the teacher] is mistaken.
It is said that if one correctly understands the meaning of what has been spoken—having heard it repeatedly, retained it, and comprehended it;
if one is well-learned, fully endowed with hearing and retention, and has accumulated such learning; if one desires to dwell the mind uninterruptedly upon the object;

if one strives to induce the sublime meditative concentration (*bodhisattva-samādhi*) of a bodhisattva; and if one recognizes for oneself that one is of an extremely dull faculty and that one’s wisdom is turbid.
It is difficult to receive and difficult to maintain the Dharma one has heard; it is difficult to collect the mind and cause it to abide upon its object of focus.
There is no transgression in not going to listen [if one is unable]. One should understand that the five conditions for committing an offense are as previously explained.
If a Buddha’s disciple—
this is the third section from below concerning the precept of turning one's back on the Great and heading toward the Small, as explained in the ten grave precepts above—
the precept against slandering the Triple Gem does not distinguish between the Great and the Small; yet to slander everything taught herein while clinging to the Small is a violation.

Because they slander the Great [Vehicle], there are those who lead [others astray]; this is a prohibition because it violates the fundamental practice. The text is divided into two parts; this first section identifies the person.

Their minds turn away from the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas that abide eternally, claiming these were not spoken by the Buddha, while instead accepting and upholding the teachings of the Two Vehicles and non-Buddhist paths.
To see all prohibitions, precepts, heterodox views, sutras, and vinayas as [merely] minor defilements constitutes a transgression of a light stain (*laghu-āpatti*).

This is because their minds turn away from the Mahāyāna; this is the second section, the formal explanation of the paths of action (*karmapatha*) which all seven classes of followers (*saptasaṃgha*) equally commit, though they differ in magnitude.
Because their natures are dull and because they have long been habituated to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, they lack faith in the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the profound sūtras, one slanders them by saying they were not spoken by the Tathāgata. As it says in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:

"If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the ethical discipline of restraint, hear the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and, with respect to its profound points—those most sublime and profound meanings of the true Dharma and the inconceivable spiritual powers of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas—fail to give rise to faith and understanding, but instead feel aversion, turn away, and slander them."

That which does not lead to the meaning, does not lead to the Dharma, was not spoken by the Tathāgata, and does not benefit or bring happiness to sentient beings is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled offense. The explanation says:
if one has not yet studied the Mahāyāna and practices exclusively according to the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, this constitutes an offense. If, regarding the Mahāyāna...
Having mounted [the Great Vehicle], one should thoroughly investigate it while also practicing the Hinayana teachings; thus, there is no transgression. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"If a bodhisattva, while dwelling in the code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), fails to diligently investigate the Bodhisattvapitaka and instead abandons it all to study exclusively the Śrāvakapitaka, this is called a transgression that is non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*) and constitutes a violation against outsiders."
"Scriptures and Vinaya" refers to the teachings of non-Buddhist paths, such as the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* or the *Sāṃkhya-kārikā*.
If one has not yet trained in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, yet diligently practices and studies the treatises of other paths, this constitutes an offense.

However, if one wishes to subdue the false views of non-Buddhists and establish the Tathāgata’s True Dharma, it is permissible to engage in discussion regarding the treatises of those non-Buddhist paths.
To study this is itself non-offensive, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:

"If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), has the Buddha’s teachings currently available and has not yet mastered them through thorough study, yet diligently applies himself to the study of heterodox treatises and the scriptures of outsiders, this is called an offense;
it is an afflicted transgression. There is no transgression [in the following case]: [text continues].
If one is exceptionally intelligent, quick to grasp, able not to forget when hearing the sūtras,
capable of reflecting upon and penetrating their meaning, and has achieved the unshakable awakening that arises from investigating the Buddha’s teachings according to principle—
such a person should always devote two parts of each day and night to training in the Buddha’s words, and one part to studying external [teachings].

There is no transgression if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), studies and seeks mastery in the treatises of other paths and the various non-Buddhist (*bāhya*) treatises, provided that he does not do so out of a deep-seated attachment, cherishing them as precious gems or finding pleasure in their flavor;
rather, he approaches them as one would use a bitter medicine. This is called a transgression, a violation, and it is defiled.
Regarding the transgression termed "wrong view," this refers to abandoning the superior [teachings] outside [the tradition], as the violation of the precepts may be understood from what precedes.
If, O Son of the Buddha, the Sūtra says:

"If a Son of the Buddha"—this marks the second section below, which contains two precepts clarifying the *anuśaṃsa-śīla* (precepts for benefiting others), namely the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*).

This is the second part of the explanation on obstacles to beneficial conduct, divided into two sections; this is the first, clarifying that the precept against neglecting the sick violates the mind of compassion, and is therefore established as a prohibition.
The text is divided into three parts: first, the person [to whom it applies]; second, the proper course of action; and third, the conclusion regarding the path of karma.
This is the first part.
Upon seeing anyone afflicted by illness, one should honor them no differently than a Buddha. Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of tending to the sick is the foremost.

Whether it be one's parents, teachers, monastics, or disciples who are ill, or those with impaired faculties suffering from the hundred varieties of maladies, one should nourish and care for them all until they are restored to health.
From "passing through all illnesses" up to "nurturing them until they are healed," the second section below explains the practice of gathering the eight fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*):
first, the Buddha; second, holy persons (*ārya*); third, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); fourth, the instructor (*ācārya*);

fifth, the Sangha; sixth, the father; seventh, the mother; eighth, the sick. These fields of merit are briefly categorized into two groups of three; expanded, there are eight, and so on, even unto infinity.
The statement regarding the two types of fields is brief: first, the field of merit; second, the field of the poor.
Thus, the third fascicle of the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states: "When a bodhisattva practices giving, they contemplate two fields of merit: first, the field of merit; second, the field of the poor.
The bodhisattva gives to those who are impoverished and suffering in order to increase their dharma of merit, and to realize unsurpassed wondrous [enlightenment]."

"Because of wisdom, one gives to the field of merit. The commentary explains: this means that because it constitutes the unsurpassed and wondrous characteristic, one gives to the field of merit of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, that sutra says: "Because of repaying kindness, one gives to [the field of merit];
because of giving rise to compassion, one gives to the poor; because of abandoning afflictions, one gives to the field of merit; and because of accomplishing merit, one gives to the poor."
The *Qiongjie* (Exhaustive Explanation) states: Among the eight fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), the first seven are called "fields of merit" because they produce superior merit;
thus they are named "fields of merit. The eighth type is called the "field of the destitute. Regarding the three mentioned therein:
the first is the "field of qualities" (*guṇakṣetra*), referring to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones (*ārya*) because they possess supreme virtues; or alternatively, it refers to the Saṃgha.
Second is the field of gratitude (*upakāra-kṣetra*), namely parents, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), and teachers (*ācārya*). Third is the field of the destitute.
Broadly speaking, there are eight such fields, as previously described among the eight fields of merit (*puṇya-kṣetra*); each of these possesses distinctions that are immeasurable and boundless.

Regarding the acquisition of merit from these, there are two interpretations. One states: "The amount of merit obtained corresponds to the excellence or inferiority of one's intention; it does not depend on the [objective] field of merit itself."
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 35, states: "Although the object given may be the same, the amount of merit varies according to the superiority or inferiority of the mind.
Śāriputra offered a bowl of rice to the Buddha, but the Buddha immediately turned and gave it to a dog, then asked Śāriputra:
'You gave this rice to me, while I gave this rice to a dog; who obtained more merit? Śāriputra [replied]."
Regarding the statement, "As I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma, the merit obtained by the Buddha giving to a dog is greater than that [obtained by giving] to Śāriputra":
although Śāriputra is the most supreme in wisdom among all humans and the Buddha is the foremost field of merit, the merit obtained by the Buddha giving to a wicked dog is far greater.
Therefore, one should know that great merit arises from the mind and does not reside in the field. One interpretation says:
The merit of giving resides in the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), not merely in the intention of the giver. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:

"Sometimes the merit of giving resides in the field of merit; for example, the Arhat Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa once offered a single flower to a Buddha-stūpa, and for ninety-one kalpas he experienced happiness among humans and devas before attaining arhatship. Furthermore, there is the case of King Aśoka.
When the boy Wang was a child, he offered soil to the Buddha; when King Yaṃvudhi erected eighty-four thousand stūpas, the material offered was most humble.
Although the boy’s intention was slight, because the field of merit was sublime, he obtained a great reward.
One should know that great merit arises from a fertile field. Thus, these two explanations each rely on one aspect of meaning and do not contradict one another.
"Contrary" refers to giving with fierce and superior great compassion to those in poverty and suffering, and giving to the field of the Tathāgata with a mind of fierce and profound pity;
although there are differences [between these recipients], the merit obtained is no different.
Thus, the fifth fascicle of the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "If one can, with a sincere heart, give rise to great compassion and bestow gifts upon animals with single-minded devotion..."
The merit of making offerings with reverence to all Buddhas is exactly equal and without distinction;

this statement is intended to show that there is no superiority or inferiority in the mind of giving, and thus it says the merit is without distinction. In reality, while one obtains merit through giving with an equal mind, it is not the case that there is no distinction [in the amount of merit].
Therefore, that sutra states: "If one gives to an animal, one obtains a hundredfold reward."
Giving to one who breaks the precepts yields a thousandfold reward; giving to one who upholds the precepts yields a hundred-thousandfold reward;
giving to a non-Buddhist who has abandoned desire yields a millionfold reward; giving to one who is directed toward the Path yields ten billionfold rewards, as explained at length.
Furthermore, giving with a mind that grasps at something results in little merit, whereas giving with a mind that grasps at nothing results in great merit.
Because it is immeasurable and boundless, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle twenty-four, asks: "How does a bodhisattva not contemplate the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and the non-field of merit?
What is the field of merit? From the heterodox practitioners who maintain the precepts up to the Buddhas—these are called the field of merit.
If one should harbor the thought that such individuals as these are the true field of merit, you should know that this mind is then [defiled]."
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva of limited capacity perceives all immeasurable sentient beings as being none other than fields of merit. Why is this?

Because they have well cultivated the application of mindfulness toward diversity (*nānātva-smṛtyupasthāna*). One who has well cultivated the application of mindfulness toward diversity observes that among sentient beings there is neither one who maintains the precepts nor one who violates them.
Furthermore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "In the east..."
"Can the expanse of space be measured, or not? "No, World-Honored One. [The Buddha] spoke at length until:

"The merit of giving a gift without signs (*animitta*) is likewise so. Based on this principle, it was said, Śāriputra, that the merit obtained from giving food to the Buddha is small because there is something obtained;
whereas the merit of the Buddha giving to a dog is very great because there is nothing obtained."
Therefore, when the sutra states that the field of merit for nursing the sick is foremost, it means that because the great compassion of all bodhisattvas is primary,
they manifest the excellence of benefiting others and thus make this declaration.
If a bodhisattva, out of a mind of resentment and hatred, fails to provide relief to those who are ill when encountering them within a monastery,
a city, a wilderness, a mountain forest, or on a road, they commit a minor offense.
Next, the third section concludes the path of action (*karmapatha*). An offense becomes defiled when four conditions are met:
first, there is a sick person who is without support or protection; second, one perceives the sick person as being sick; third, there is affliction, namely anger and so forth;
and fourth, the act is completed, meaning one fails to go and visit them. As it says in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

If a bodhisattva, dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, sees sentient beings afflicted by serious illness and, harboring a mind of resentment or a mind of malice, fails to go and attend to them, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted offense.
However, if one fails to go and attend to them because of being obscured by laziness or indolence, it is not [an afflicted offense].
Regarding stained offenses and non-offenses: if one is ill; if one lacks physical strength; if one has requested another who is capable and compliant to go and provide service;
if one knows that the sick person has someone to rely upon and protect them; if one knows that the sick person has the personal strength to provide for themselves;
or if one wishes to protect and maintain the wholesome qualities one is cultivating so that they do not decline.
If one is aware of being hindered by extreme dullness and obtuseness such that it is difficult to receive, difficult to retain,
and difficult to collect the mind upon an object for meditative concentration; or if one has previously promised to act as a companion to another—
such as for a sick person or one who is suffering— to assist them in removing their pain, one should know that the same applies in those cases.
"If a Buddha’s disciple...
This marks the second section from below, concerning the precept against possessing instruments for killing.

Because this violates the meaning of compassionate conduct, the text is divided into two parts; this is the first, which identifies the person [subject to the rule]. It is established as a prohibition because it violates the mind of compassion.
The seven classes of followers equally commit this offense.
One must not possess any swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, axes, or instruments of war; nor any evil nets or traps that are tools for killing living beings.
All such things are forbidden to possess. Furthermore, even if a Bodhisattva were to have their parents killed, they would still not seek retaliation.
How much more so for one who kills all sentient beings; if one intentionally keeps weapons such as knives or staves, one commits a secondary offense (light defilement).
The Sūtra says: "One must not keep [weapons]; to do so constitutes a secondary offense. From this point downward, the second section clarifies the paths of karma (*karmapatha*).

An offense is established through four conditions: first, the object (*vastu*), namely knives, staves, and so forth; second, the perception (*saṃjñā*), namely the perception that they are knives and so forth; third...
The afflictions refer to the four [unwholesome roots] such as malice and so forth; "to the ultimate" means to actually carry weapons and staves.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind, as will be explained in detail within the following six chapters.
The Sūtra says: "These ten precepts," which will be explained in detail in the sixth fascicle below, are here summarized in the third section as a forward reference to what follows.
That is to say, if one breaks the precepts, one cannot even obtain the body of an animal, much less that of a human or a deva.
As the *Sāṭhā-Nigaṇṭha-putra Sūtra* states: "If one does not uphold the precepts, one cannot even obtain the body of a scabby jackal."

How much more so for one who has attained a body of merit? Furthermore, the *Candrapradīpa-samādhi* states: "Though one possesses a noble appearance, lineage, and extensive learning, if one lacks ethical discipline and wisdom, one is but a bird or beast.
Though one may dwell in a lowly station and possess little learning or insight, if one can maintain pure ethical discipline, one is called a superior person."

The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, for the sake of gain or out of an evil mind, one must not act as a messenger between nations to join military arrays or incite armies to wage war and slaughter immeasurable sentient beings.
A Bodhisattva must not enter military camps to come and go, much less intentionally act as a traitor to the state;
if one does so intentionally, they commit a minor offense."
The Sūtra says: "If a Buddha’s disciple... This marks the second section, which contains ten precepts clarifying the precepts for benefiting others (*anugrāhaka-śīla*).

Among these, the fourth, fifth, and seventh [precepts] are obstacles to *priyavāditā* (loving speech); the seven types [of conduct] are subsumed under *samānārthatā* (common purpose) and *arthacaryā* (beneficial action). The text is divided into two parts:

first, the individual explanation of the ten [precepts], and second, a concluding summary that points forward to the location where they will be explained. Within the first part, the ten are explained individually.
This is divided into ten sections. This first section clarifies the person who receives the precepts; the subsequent section, beginning with "Furthermore, a bodhisattva should not...
and ending with "the path of karmic action," concludes the exposition, as can be understood from the text itself.
If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally buys and sells free persons, male or female slaves, or six kinds of livestock; or trades coffins, wooden planks, or other implements for containing the dead;
or intentionally does these things themselves or teaches others to do so, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The Sūtra says: "If a Buddha’s disciple... This is the second section, clarifying the precept against buying and selling. Because it violates the path of cultivation, it is thus prohibited.
It is equally an offense for both the Great and Small Vehicles; it is regulated for all seven classes of practitioners. There are two types:

first, causing harm and distress to others, which violates the mind of compassion—this refers to what the Sūtra describes as buying and selling slaves and so forth; second, for the sake of worldly profit—this refers to trading...

Regarding the prohibition against selling coffins or staffs, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these were established as prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) for the sake of protecting others;

in this regard, Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas should train equally. The conditions required to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed, and the number of such factors, should be understood as previously explained.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders another good person, a virtuous person, a Dharma master, a teacher, a monk, a king, or a noble person without cause,
saying that they have committed the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses; or if, toward parents, brothers, and the six classes of kin,
one ought to give rise to a heart of filial piety and compassion, yet instead inflicts further harm and rebellion, thereby falling into an undesirable state— this constitutes a light offense.

Defilement and transgression. The Sūtra says: "If a Buddha’s disciple... This is the third section, clarifying the precept against slandering; the text is divided into two parts, the first of which identifies the person.
The Sūtra says: "With an evil mind... This is the second part, clarifying the path of karma. Some say that this does not distinguish between [the presence or absence of]...
Regarding the transgressions involving roots, lack of roots, or confessing to those outside one's own group, these are all said to be grave and not light.

Among these ten grave offenses, speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly to those within the same group is said to be light and not grave. However, for the sake of gain and honor, praising oneself and disparaging others is grave and not light;
thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If a bodhisattva, for the sake of seeking gain and honor..."
To praise or disparage others is called the first *pārājika* offense.
However, if one praises oneself and disparages others not for the sake of seeking gain or honor, it is minor rather than grave. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline, possesses a mind of attachment toward another or a mind of malice toward them..."
To praise or disparage others is termed an offense and a transgression; it is an afflicted offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
if it is for the purpose of subduing various evil non-Buddhists; if it is for the purpose of maintaining the holy teaching of the Tathāgata;
or if one desires to use skillful means to discipline and purify those with faith—such as Dharma masters, teachers, monks, kings, and parents—and thereby cause their [faith] to increase even further.

To disparage those who have been kind to one—whether by subduing them or through other means as explained extensively above—or to cause those who have not yet developed pure faith to lose that faith because one has already contemplated harming those who were kind to oneself, constitutes an offense.

Toward those who have been kind, one should give rise to filial obedience and repay their prior kindness; to act otherwise and instead commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) against such persons is a defiled transgression.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), harbors a mind of resentment toward sentient beings who have previously bestowed kindness upon them—failing to recognize that kindness and failing to understand its significance—and thus refuses to provide appropriate recompense in their presence, this is called an offense;
it is a defiled transgression. If [this occurs] due to laziness or indolence..."
There is no offense if one is obscured by negligence; if there is no recompense due to lack of defilement;
or if there is no offense because one has applied diligent effort but lacks the power or ability to obtain the recompense.

Furthermore, there is no offense if one intends to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue another—as explained at length—or if one wishes to repay a kindness but the other person does not accept it. These constitute an offense only when five conditions are met.

Regarding the path of action of slandering: first, the object of the slander, such as one's parents; second, conceiving the notion that they are such persons; third, giving rise to the intent to disparage them;
fourth, the arousal of afflictions, namely hatred and so forth; and fifth, the completion of the preparatory means, which is the utterance of words understood by the other person.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, sets a great fire to burn mountains, forests, or wilderness from the fourth month to the ninth month;

If they do so intentionally, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
