The generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is so called because it involves the arising of a desire for faith and resolute conviction, the arising of a mind of aspiration, and the arising of a mind of profound faith that gives rise to certainty.

Some say that the nature of the generation of the mind is wisdom (*prajñā*), because one must first discern all the merits of enlightenment (*bodhi*) and discern all the faults of saṃsāra before engaging in practice.
In my current interpretation, the generation of the mind consists of the desire for faith and resolute conviction.

The essence of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) consists of volition associated with understanding; it is called the "arousal of the mind" because one generates a superior volition and aspiration to realize enlightenment.
If one discusses its auxiliary companions, the simultaneous mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with it constitute the essence of the arousal of the mind.

Regarding whether the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) and the arousal of the mind are identical or distinct, Master Yuan explains: "The essential fruit of Bodhi itself is termed 'aspiration'; [the volition] that acts toward it is the arousal of the mind."
The intention-fruit is termed "generating the mind" (*cittotpāda*); however, this current interpretation is not correct, because there is no distinction between generating the mind and the vow.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 35: "Therefore, generating the mind has the initial right vow as its intrinsic nature.
The characteristic of the second generation of the mind refers to the two kinds of right vows—namely, those for one's own benefit and those for the benefit of others—as its characteristic."
The aspiration for self-benefit refers to the generation of the vow to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; as the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Furthermore, all bodhisattvas give rise to the mind of right aspiration, vowing: 'I shall certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The aspiration for the benefit of others refers to the act of benefiting all sentient beings; as the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "It is able to act [for their welfare]."
Because it is for the benefit of all sentient beings, the generation of the mind [of awakening] takes the aspiration for that goal as its defining characteristic.
The two types of great vows mentioned above encompass all the vows of Bodhisattvas;
the realization of enlightenment is itself the benefit of others, because sentient beings seek enlightenment, and thus the Bodhisattva’s benefiting of others is precisely his own self-benefit.
Benefiting sentient beings is for the sake of one's own benefit; as stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:

"When a bodhisattva does not allow their mind to become inferior or weak regarding the affairs of others, generating the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), the benefit of others is precisely the benefit of oneself.
Third, regarding the objective referent (*ālambana*) of the generation of the thought of enlightenment, there are briefly two: first, enlightenment (*bodhi*); second, [sentient beings].

Because it concerns sentient beings, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Therefore, the generation of the mind takes great enlightenment (*bodhi*) and the welfare of all sentient beings as its objective referent.
In this context, enlightenment is the objective referent for one's own benefit, while sentient beings are the objective referent for great compassion.
This is because the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* identifies ten types of sentient beings as its objective referents; thus, that treatise...
The ninth fascicle states: It is asked, "With what kind of sentient beings does great compassion take as its object? The verse says:
Those who are burning, those who are hostile, those overcome by suffering, And those shrouded in darkness;

those dwelling in the aggregates, those bound by great fetters, Those who eat poison, those who have lost the path, Furthermore, those dwelling on non-paths, and those who are emaciated and parched— These ten kinds of sentient beings are the objects of the mind of great compassion.
The commentary states: Briefly, the great compassion of a bodhisattva takes ten types of sentient beings as its object.

First, sentient beings who are ablaze, meaning those who are attached to and delight in the defilements of desire. Second, sentient beings overcome by enemies, meaning those whom Māra obstructs when they are practicing virtue.
Third, sentient beings oppressed by suffering, meaning those who dwell in the three miserable realms. Fourth, sentient beings shrouded in darkness...
First, those who constantly engage in unwholesome conduct, because they do not recognize the retribution of karma;
second, those who abide in the aggregates (*skandha*), meaning those who do not delight in *nirvāṇa*, because the path of the aggregates of birth and death is not severed;
third, those who are bound by great fetters, meaning those with heterodox and deviant views, because their desire for liberation is tightly bound by various kinds of deviant views.
1. Those bound by fetters (the seventh type) are beings who consume the poison of nutriment; that is, those who relish the flavor of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Just as delicious food mixed with poison can harm a person, so too is wholesome concentration: when one becomes attached through craving, one then falls away and loses it. 2.
Those who have lost the path (the eighth type) are those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*); because they are deluded and mistaken regarding true liberation.
Ninth, those who abide in what is not the path refers to those who are indeterminate regarding the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), because they are subject to regression.
Fourth, the distinctions in the arousal of the bodhicitta are briefly fourfold: first, the entry; second, the root;
third, the outflow of great compassion; and fourth, the basis for the bodhisattva’s training. Regarding "entry," it means:
The initial stage of the ten levels of faith is called "entering," because one enters into the vast practice of bodhi and enters into the vast fruit of bodhi;

thus it is called "entering. Once having entered, by practicing the bodhisattva conduct with intense diligence through three incalculable great eons, one will certainly realize the fruit of sublime bodhi. If...
One who is able to enter the initial stage of the ten faiths is already included among the number of great bodhisattvas; thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 35, states:
"Furthermore, as soon as bodhisattvas first resolve their minds [on awakening], they are said to have entered into unsurpassed bodhi and are included among the number of bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna.
It says "fundamental" because it is only by relying on the arousal of the mind that [the path] subsequently arises.

Regarding its practice, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "Furthermore, it is only after a bodhisattva has generated the resolve (*cittotpāda*) that they can gradually and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
it cannot be done without having generated the resolve. Therefore, the generation of the resolve serves as the root of unsurpassed enlightenment.
As for the phrase "the natural outflow of great compassion," it means that one generates the resolve for enlightenment with the desire to rescue sentient beings.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, all bodhisattvas, out of compassion for all sentient beings who suffer, give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) with the desire to rescue and deliver them;
therefore, this arousal of the mind is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of compassion. Furthermore, the seventh fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:
"First, they do not seek their own peace, but rather aspire for worldly renown and fame, so as to eliminate the suffering of sentient beings until it is completely exhausted."
There are others who vow to deliver such classes of beings; for a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (*prathamacittotpādika*), this is the basis for their training.

As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Furthermore, based upon and established by the initial resolution for awakening, a bodhisattva’s training consists universally in all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and in performing what is beneficial for all sentient beings."
Because they are all able to cultivate [the path] therein, the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is that upon which the training of all bodhisattvas relies.
Fifth, regarding the explanation of the causes and conditions for arousing the mind, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 35:

"It should be known that the initial arousal of the mind by a bodhisattva arises from four kinds of conditions. What are these four conditions? Namely, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family..."

Having seen the inconceivable, most marvelous, and rare supernormal powers and majestic might of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or having heard of such matters from a trustworthy source, and having thus seen and heard them, one then forms this thought: "Unsurpassed Bodhi possesses great majesty and virtue;
it brings about the accomplishment of such visions for those who abide in it and those who practice in accordance with it."

Through the superior power of having seen and heard such inconceivable miraculous transformations and majestic might, one generates profound faith and understanding toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*);
by means of this, one gives rise to the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*). This is called the first causal condition for the initial arousal of the mind.
Alternatively, there may be a certain class of beings who, although they have not seen or heard the aforementioned miraculous transformations and majestic might...
Having heard the teaching of the subtle and sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, which relies upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they develop deep faith.
By the predominant power of hearing the true Dharma and that deep faith, they give rise to profound conviction and understanding regarding the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
and because they have attained the subtle and sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata, they resolve their minds upon bodhicitta. This is...
This is called the second causal condition for the initial arousal of the mind.

Alternatively, there may be a certain class of persons who, although they have not seen, heard, or known the sublime Dharma, nevertheless see that the entire Bodhisattva-piṭaka is about to perish. Having seen this, they form this thought:
"The Bodhisattva-piṭaka, by remaining long in the world, can extinguish the immeasurable suffering of sentient beings; I ought [to protect it]."

Abiding in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Dharma and generating the bodhicitta for the purpose of extinguishing the great suffering of immeasurable sentient beings—due to the superior power of protecting and upholding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Dharma, one gives rise to deep faith and understanding in the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
for the sake of attaining the subtle and wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata, one generates the bodhicitta. This is called the third initial generation of the mind.
Furthermore, there may be a certain class of people who, although they do not perceive that the True Dharma is about to perish,

nevertheless see during the final eon, the final age, and the final time, that sentient beings of defiled and evil nature are afflicted and disturbed by the ten secondary afflictions of body and mind—
namely, that they are full of ignorance, full of shamelessness and lack of dread of blame, full of stinginess and envy, full of sorrow and suffering, and full of heaviness and rigidity.
Having seen that there are many afflictions, many evil deeds, much negligence, much indolence, and much lack of faith—

and having explained this at length up to— "I should now resolve to attain great bodhicitta so that the immeasurable sentient beings of this degenerate age may follow my example and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment"— this was because he perceived the hardships of the final eon.
By virtue of having attained the superior power of the resolve for awakening (*cittotpāda*), one develops profound faith and understanding toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*);
from this cause, one gives rise to the mind of great enlightenment. This is called the fourth condition for the initial arousal of the mind.
Furthermore, there are four causes and four powers for giving rise to the mind of great enlightenment, as fully explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
The remaining five gates are as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter 25; fearing prolixity, they shall not be described here.

This statement is intended for those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta to understand the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) as the basis for generating that mind. Why is this? There are two types of generating the mind:
first, the indeterminate generation of the mind, which refers to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). As the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* (Renwang jing) states: "A Bodhisattva of the ten faiths..."
Like light feathers following the wind to the east or west, there are two types of the resolve for awakening (*cittotpāda*): the "definite" and the "indefinite.

The definite refers to the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*), which, for the sake of emphasis, are termed "definite"; the indefinite refers to the ten [stages of] mind, which are called the "ten nurtured" (*daśa-poṣa*).

As for the "vajra," it refers to the ten vajra-stages as previously explained. Alternatively, "resolve for awakening" may refer to the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), which are omitted here for brevity.
As previously stated, "generating the mind" refers specifically to the initial generation of the mind within the ten stages of faith;
thus, the "ten minds" are so called because they transcend the ten stages of entering and the ten stages of nurturing. The remainder is as previously explained. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If bodhisattvas, abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, see sentient beings seeking [benefit] in the present life or the future..."

If, for the sake of the Dharma, one extensively practices what is unreasonable, harboring a mind of resentment and a mind of malice, and fails to proclaim the correct principle as it truly is, this is called an offense.
The commentary explains that "failing to proclaim the correct principle as it truly is" means not teaching the Mahāyāna sūtras of correct principle;
rather, the Bodhisattva [proceeds] to the third section below, which concludes the equipment of the path of karma.
The details of the conditions may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
"If a disciple of the Buddha," and so forth, is the sixth [section], which clarifies the precept against preaching the Dharma erroneously;
it is established because such action violates the teachings and instructions. Seven.
The section on the common transgressions unique to the Mahāyāna and not shared with the two vehicles consists of three parts:

first, the person; second, that which should be practiced; and third, the conclusion regarding the path of action (*karmapatha*). This [first part] identifies the person; as the Sūtra says: "One should, with a good mind, explain and resolve the meaning and flavor.
Below this is the second part, clarifying that which should be practiced. Within this, there are two sections: first, clarifying what should be studied; next, clarifying...
To speak of this to others is the first [requirement].

When seeing newly initiated bodhisattvas who have come from a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, one should preach to them according to the Dharma all forms of ascetic practice, such as burning the body, the arms, or the fingers;
or, if they do not burn their bodies, arms, or fingers, [one should teach] making offerings...
To nourish all Buddhas, a renunciant bodhisattva— even at the cost of their own body, flesh, hands, or feet— should provide offerings to everything from starving tigers,
wolves, and lions to all hungry ghosts; only then should they teach the True Dharma to each one in succession,
causing their minds to open and their intentions to be liberated.

The Sūtra says: "Seeing that new students have arrived and are making offerings [to him]," and so forth. From this point downward, the second section clarifies his teaching for others; herein there are two parts:
first, describing ascetic practices to cause them to resolve their minds toward enlightenment; second, correctly expounding the Dharma. This is the first part, wherein he describes ascetic practices.
For those who are not bodhisattvas who have left the household life, there are two subsequent interpretations. The first says: "If..."
Not burning one's body and so forth as an offering to the Buddhas is neither the way of a renunciant nor that of a bodhisattva.
One interpretation states that a householder bodhisattva may burn his body even to the point of sacrificing his life, whereas a renunciant bodhisattva cannot perform such an act. Why is this?

Because it is not in accordance with the proper conduct (*ācāra*). However, for the sake of protecting the holy teachings and benefiting sentient beings, one does not burn the body [in ordinary cases].
Based on the claims of newly initiated bodhisattvas, it is said that "the bodhisattva burns the body and abandons the body" is merely an expression of the ultimate;
it does not necessarily mean that one must abandon the body to become a bodhisattva.

Subsequently, each person’s mind will gradually open to understanding. This is the second section below, which clarifies the correct teaching; although there are two textual passages, they constitute a single point.
Second, the meaning of what should be practiced:

If a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and honor, fails to answer, answers erroneously, or speaks with inverted order regarding the words of the Sūtras and Vinaya— neither preceding nor following them properly—
and thereby slanders the Triple Gem, the speaker commits a minor offense.

[This concludes] the third section of the Sūtra on the Bodhisattva, which establishes the causal conditions for the equipment of karma; the extent [of these conditions] may be understood by analogy with what preceded. Question:
What is the difference between this case of not teaching the Dharma and the previous case of being stubborn and not teaching? Answer:

It is explained that in the former case, one does not teach the Dharma because of an inherent stinginess regarding the Dharma (*dharmamātsarya*), which constitutes a defeat (*pārājika*). In the latter case, it is not due to a nature of stinginess regarding the Dharma.
To refuse to teach the Dharma out of a desire for gain and honor or out of a mind of resentment is a minor offense, not a grave one; thus there is a distinction between them.

As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, harbors a mind of resentment or a mind of malice and anger, or is transformed by envy, and does not bestow the Dharma upon another who comes seeking it, this is called an offense."
To commit a transgression that constitutes a violation is an afflicted offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*).

If, due to laziness, indolence, forgetfulness, or a neutral state of mind, one fails to bestow the Dharma, this is called an offense that is not an afflicted violation (*akliṣṭāpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases:

when encountering non-Buddhists seeking out faults and shortcomings; when one is ill; when the mind is deranged; or when one intends to employ skillful means for the purpose of training [the recipient].
He subdues them and leads them out of unwholesome states, establishing them in wholesome states, and so forth, as explained at length.
If a disciple of the Buddha, for the sake of food, drink, money, material gain, or reputation, associates with kings,
princes, ministers, and officials, relying on their power and influence to beg, seize, beat, drag, or forcibly take money and goods from anyone— [this is a transgression].

To seek profit is called "evil seeking," "excessive seeking," or "seeking through others. To do so entirely without a heart of compassion or filial piety constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).

According to the Sūtra, from this point downward is the seventh precept, clarifying the prohibition against evil seeking; it is also known as the precept against begging by means of intimidation or influence. It is a precept for study.

First, the paths of action (*karmapatha*) are explained in sequence; this is the first [section]. From the passage "for one's own gain and support" onwards, the second section explains the formation of the paths of action, which contains three parts:
First, becoming closely attached for the sake of gain, as the sutra says, "for one's own gain and support," up to "becoming closely attached to kings and others.
Second, seeking through unrighteous means, as the sutra says, "relying on [one's] physical form... [and so forth].

Regarding the three cases such as seeking through intimidation and so forth, these are cited as non-bondages (asaṃyojana) as explained in the Sūtra: "All seeking for profit is called 'evil seeking'...
and so on at length. If one acquires wealth through improper means, one commits a pārājika offense; if the object has not yet been acquired, it is a light rather than a grave offense.
The full set of conditions is as previously described.

If a disciple of the Buddha who studies and recites the precepts observes the Bodhisattva precepts during the six periods of day and night, they must understand their meaning and the nature of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

If a Bodhisattva does not understand even a single sentence or a single verse of the causal conditions of the Vinaya, yet falsely claims to understand them, they are deceiving themselves and likewise deceiving others; for they do not understand any of the dharmas.
If one acts as a teacher to bestow precepts upon others [without qualification], one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
In the *Sūtra*, from the passage "If a Buddha-son... onwards, the eighth section clarifies the precept against being a teacher to others when possessing no knowledge;

that is, to forcefully provide instruction despite having no understanding carries the fault of error. This offense is common to all seven groups of practitioners, and it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Third, regarding the first person, one should next practice the subsequent points and conclude with the formal confession of the offense; the initial text is clear.
Regarding the passage "reciting the precepts until reaching the nature of Buddha-nature," this is the second section, which clarifies what should be practiced: "six times every day.
For those who have not yet become proficient, they should recite the precepts six times every day and maintain the Bodhisattva precepts according to their teachings and principles during the daytime.

There are three periods each night, making six periods in total; however, if one has previously practiced [this discipline], it is not strictly necessary to observe all six periods, as the meaning and principle have already been understood.

Thus, understanding this sublime precept as the *Buddhatva-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva proceeds from here to the third section, which cites transgressions and defines the offenses, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "If a Bodhisattva abides in the code of pure Bodhisattva ethical discipline..."
To give rise to deceitful speech, empty talk, and the display of signs; to employ expedients to investigate and seek profit for the sake of gain;
to live by a livelihood that tastes of such things; and to persist in this without shame or remorse—this is called an offense, a transgression. It is a defiled offense.
There is no offense if one gives rise to the desire to eliminate [such behavior], exerts diligent effort, and applies oneself to the task.
When afflictions burn fiercely and suppress the mind such that it occasionally manifests as deceitful displays, this is explained as "ignorance acting as a teacher for others.
The number and conditions required are to be understood according to the previous [explanation].
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, sees a precept-observing bhikṣu holding an incense burner and practicing the bodhisattva path,
yet instigates discord between two parties, slanders and deceives this worthy person, and commits every kind of evil— this constitutes a minor offense of defilement.

In this sutra, from "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards, the ninth section clarifies the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*). First, it identifies the person; subsequently, it explains the karmic result.
This constitutes the heading for the person. From "If with an evil mind... onwards, the second section clarifies the path of action (*karmapatha*).

If there is one who, with an evil mind, [approaches] a bhikṣu upholding the precepts who carries an incense burner while practicing the bodhisattva path—even though he is a bodhisattva upholding the precepts—yet...

Causing two parties to fight by reporting their faults to one another and their faults to the other—because this causes quarrels and disputes to arise between the two sides—the remainder of the text is easy to understand.

When a Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings, even if they speak words that cause division, they commit no offense at all and instead generate much merit; as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva sees..."
When a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have been taken under the influence of evil friends and who cherish them without relinquishing them,
he gives rise to a heart of compassion and the intention to benefit and bring them peace. According to his capacity and strength,

he speaks words of separation so that they may part from those evil friends and abandon their mutual intimacy, lest those sentient beings suffer for a long night due to their proximity to evil friends.

If a bodhisattva, with a mind intent on benefiting others, speaks words that cause division to separate those who love one another, provided it is without purpose or benefit, there is no transgression;
rather, much merit is produced.
Thus, O Son of the Buddha:
The Sūtra says: "If a Buddha’s disciple... This is the tenth section, clarifying the precept on releasing living beings. The text consists of three parts: first, the person;
second, the practice to be performed; and third, the conclusion regarding the offense. This [first part] identifies the person:
"Out of a mind of compassion, one practices the act of releasing living beings."

This sutra, through the power of a compassionate mind, prescribes the practice of releasing living beings. Within this, there are two parts: first, a general statement; second, a detailed explanation.
This is the general statement:
"All men have been my fathers, and all women have been my mothers; there is no birth in which I have not been born from them."
Because of this process of taking birth, the sentient beings of the six realms have all been my parents; thus, to kill and eat them is to kill my own parents and to kill myself.
Since all earth and water are my former bodies and all fire and wind are my fundamental substance, one should constantly practice non-killing, so as to receive birth after birth.
"Throughout all men, up to those who have been my parents in birth after birth"—this is the second section, which specifically explains this [practice].
Within it, there are two parts: first, delivering animals; second, delivering those who have been kind. In the former, there are two sub-sections: first, generating the mind of compassion;
second, explaining the actual rescue. This is the first [of those two]. "All men are my parents," and so forth.
This means that since beginningless time, all sentient beings have successively served as one another’s fathers, mothers, sons, and daughters.
Thus, the ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Regarding the difficulty of birth, as the Bhagavān said:
'For a long time you have galloped through saṃsāra, and the blood flowing from your bodies has exceeded the four great oceans. Regarding the uncertainty of birth, even if one were to take..."

Regarding all the grasses, trees, roots, stalks, branches, and leaves upon the great earth, were they to be cut into fine counting-sticks the length of four fingers, you would calculate that throughout the long night of transmigration, the parents you have passed through are as follows:
such beings have once been my mother, and I too have throughout the long night been their mother; such beings have once been my father, and I... [have likewise been their father].
Furthermore, if one were to calculate for as long as that night with counting-sticks the thickness of four fingers, they would quickly be exhausted;
yet I do not say that the limit of the number of parents you have had throughout the long night can be reached. Moreover, I declare:
"I observe that there is not even a small portion of this great earth where you have not been born during the long night."

Furthermore, it is said: "I have observed that among the sentient beings in the world, it is not easy to find anyone who has not already undergone immeasurable births and deaths throughout the long night;
they have not failed to become your mother, father, brother, sister, preceptor, teacher, or other venerable ones, or those equal to venerable ones. As it is also said:

It is said that if a single person were to accumulate the bones from the bodies they have received throughout a single kalpa, and if someone were to pile them up without allowing them to decay, the height of that heap would surpass Mount Vipula near Rājagṛha.
When it says "my own body," it refers to the body formed by the five aggregates of all sentient beings; that is what is meant by "me."
Because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the body are similar, killing another is killing one's own body;
or, based on the great compassion of the same essence, that person is my body and I am that person’s body, so when killing that person, one also kills one's own body.

Or, because earth, water, fire, and wind are none other than the bodies of former lives, it is said that "life after life one receives birth" refers to the practice of releasing living beings (*prāṇa-mokṣa*); therefore, in the future, there shall be no [rebirth].

Because it is singular, it is said that "life arises from life. Alternatively, some say that because one receives birth as a human or a celestial being through the practice of releasing living beings, and because these distinctions between human and celestial births differ, it is said that "life arises from life."
If one sees people of the world killing animals, one should employ skillful means to rescue and protect them, liberating them from their suffering and hardship;
one should constantly teach and preach the Bodhisattva precepts to save and deliver sentient beings.
The Sūtra says: "If one sees worldly people... From this point, the second section clarifies the correct salvation of sentient beings.

This means that Bodhisattvas, through skillful means, rescue and protect sentient beings from life-threatening dangers, causing them to be free from all suffering, regardless of their own bodies or lives, just like that Deer King.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle eighteen, states: "King Brahmadatta of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī was out hunting."
In a forest grove, he saw two herds of deer, each herd having its own leader. One leader had five hundred deer in his herd;
this leader was the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni. The other leader was the Bodhisattva Devadatta.
When the Deer King saw that the king’s great assembly was slaughtering his followers, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion and went straight to them.
Before the King, the royal archers vied with one another to shoot flying arrows like falling rain.
Seeing that the deer was advancing directly forward without any hesitation, the King commanded his attendants: "Withdraw your bows and arrows; do not interrupt its intent to come.
Once the Deer King had arrived, he knelt and addressed the King: "Your Majesty, for the sake of a minor matter of pleasure and amusement, the entire herd of deer has [been gathered] at once..."
"All must undergo the suffering of death; if we provide the meal by rotation, it will suffice. The next day, he sent a deer to supply the royal kitchen.
The king approved of his words and allowed it to be done as he wished. Thereupon, the two leaders of the deer herds assembled and established a rotation, with each taking their turn for one day.
Among the herd of Devadatta, there was a doe who was pregnant, and her turn eventually arrived.
"She should have been sent here to inform her master that my body must be delivered for death today; however, I am pregnant, and this child is not yet due.
I beg you to grant me justice, so that the one who should die may die in their turn, and the living one be spared.
The Deer King, enraged, said, "Who does not cherish their life? But when it is one's turn to come, one must simply go; how can there be an excuse? The mother deer reflected upon this: "I..."
"The King is unkind and does not respond with reason; he does not examine my words but instead gives way to reckless anger, such that it is not worth reporting.
I shall go at once to where the Bodhisattva-king is and inform him of the situation in full. The deer went and reported everything to the king. The king asked, "This deer, what did its master say?
The deer replied, "My master is unkind and does not perceive the principles of justice, yet he gives way to wrath. Your Majesty’s benevolence extends to all beings."
Therefore, he has come to take refuge as I do today; though heaven and earth are vast, there is nowhere else to appeal.
The Bodhisattva reflected: "This is truly pitiable. If I do not intervene, his son will be killed unjustly.
If I were to appoint someone else in his place, those who have not yet reached their turn would be passed over—how could this be right? Having resolved that he himself must take his place, he then...
"Sending me away to escort the doe back, I shall now take her place; do not worry. The Deer King went straight to the king’s gate.
When the people saw him, they marveled at his coming of his own accord and reported the matter to the king.

The king was likewise surprised and immediately ordered him to come forward, asking, "Are all the deer exhausted? Why have you come here? The Deer King replied, "Great King, your benevolence extends [to all]."
"In this district, there is not a single deer that has been harmed; they only flourish and multiply—how could there ever be an end to them?

However, I have heard from another division that there is a doe in the district who is pregnant and about to give birth. Her body is destined for the carving block, and her fawn would likewise lose its life.
When she returned and reported this to me, I felt compassion for her. Yet, to replace her with another of a different kind is also improper. If she returns and..."

To save those who are no different from wood or stone—this body will not long remain, for death is inevitable; yet the merit of compassionately rescuing others from suffering and distress is immeasurable.
If a person lacks compassion, they are no different from tigers or wolves. Upon hearing these words, the King rose from his seat and spoke this verse:
"I am truly a beast, though called a 'human-headed deer. Though you possess the body of a deer,"
He was named Mṛgaśiras; yet, speaking according to principle, he was not a human by virtue of his physical form.
If one can possess compassionate kindness, though they be a beast, they are truly a human being. "From this day forward, I shall no longer eat any flesh.
By bestowing upon you the gift of fearlessness, you may set your minds at ease, and all the deer shall find security."
On the anniversary of the death of one's parents or siblings, one should invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra;
by dedicating this merit to the deceased, they shall attain the vision of all Buddhas and be reborn among humans or in the heavens.

In the Sūtra, following the section on "Seeing One's Parents," the second part clarifies that for a newly initiated bodhisattva, one first gives rise to loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) toward those who have been kind, gradually extending it to all sentient beings.
This is just as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter thirty-two, states: "I shall now demonstrate the practice based on the contemplation of loving-kindness."
A beginner, having correctly apprehended the signs within the categories of friends, enemies, and neutral persons, sits in the proper posture and,
through a mental application belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-manasikāra*) accompanied by the superior intention for their benefit and happiness,
generates resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) toward one friend, one enemy, and one neutral person; regarding these three categories, [he views them] with equanimity.
Accompanied by a resolute intention for benefit and happiness, one attends with the desire to grant them happiness, thinking thus:

"May all those sentient beings who seek happiness obtain happiness"—that is, either faultless sensual pleasure, or faultless sensual pleasure accompanied by joy, or faultless pleasure devoid of joy; subsequently, or toward one's two parents.

Whether toward three kinsmen, four kinsmen, five kinsmen, ten, twenty, or thus throughout all directions and intermediate points, one fills those categories of kin without interval and generates resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) therein;
such that not even a space the size of a staff-tip remains within them.
Just as it is with the category of kin, so it is with the categories of enemies and neutral persons.
One should know that it is likewise so.
If one does not act thus, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

As for the sutra, if it were otherwise, this would be the third section [dealing with] the raising of faults and the causes and conditions for the determination of offenses; the number of these is to be inferred from what precedes.
It should be understood as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "If a bodhisattva, dwelling in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
sees that sentient beings could obtain great benefit through various harsh applications or intense applications,
yet he protects them from distress and does not manifest those actions, this is called an offense, but there is no transgression, provided he perceives that by means of this..."
Regarding those who, having obtained little benefit in this present life, give rise to much distress and fail to rescue their parents— as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:
"If one does not recognize the kindness of sentient beings who have previously shown one favor, fails to understand that kindness, harbors a mind of resentment,
and is unwilling to repay them appropriately in the present, this is called an offense and a transgression."
This constitutes a defiled transgression.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind, as each individual precept is explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Extinction of Sin."
Following these ten precepts, the second section below provides a forward reference to what will be explained later.

The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha:

This section, beginning from 'If a son of the Buddha,' constitutes the third part, which elucidates the ten precepts of the *śīla* of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) and the *śīla* of benefiting others (*anugrāhaka-śīla*).

Within this, there are two sections: first, the individual explanation of the ten precepts; second, a forward reference to their place of exposition. Regarding the first, the individual explanation..."
Furthermore, there are two divisions: first, five precepts that explain the obstacles to the six perfections; second, six precepts that clarify the benefits.

This is the first [division], which explains the inclusion of the retribution for wholesome deeds (*kuśala-vipāka*) in three parts: the first is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*); the next two are the obstacles to wisdom (*prajñā*);

and the last one is the obstacle to ethical discipline (*śīla*). This is the first [explanation]: using the retribution of anger to restrain the mind from violating patience through the retribution of breaking the precepts.

The textual division has three parts: first, the person; second, the characteristics of the karmic path; and third, from "If a bodhisattva" onwards, the citation of faults and the determination of the offense.
This [first part] identifies the person:
if one responds to anger with anger or strikes back in response to a strike, yet does not retaliate even if one's parents, brothers, or six types of relatives are killed—[this is the case].
If a ruler of a state is killed by another, one must not seek retribution through killing; for the cycle of killing begets killing, which is contrary to the way of filial piety.

One should not even keep slaves, let alone beat, strike, or revile them, resulting in immeasurable verbal offenses arising daily from the three karmas of body, speech, and mind—how much more so for intentionally committing the seven heinous crimes?

The Sūtra states, "Repaying anger with anger," and below this, the second section clarifies the characteristics of the paths of action (*karmapatha*). This text is divided into two parts: first, the prohibition of anger;
second, a detailed re-explanation of this, which constitutes the prohibition of anger. Next, the Sūtra says, "If one kills one's own parents...

and so forth; this is the second part, the detailed re-explanation. It means that if one sees another coming to kill one's parents and yet cannot retaliate against them, how much less could one do so intentionally?
Regarding those who commit the seven heinous offenses and so forth, even if a sovereign ruler is killed by another, one must not seek retribution through killing.
There are two interpretations of this: first, it is said that even if a sovereign ruler kills his own parents, a Bodhisattva still must not kill in retaliation;
second, it is said that if a king is killed by another state, one likewise must not dwell upon or carry out retributive killing.
Regarding the practice of repaying killing with compassion following the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it is like the lion king repaying a lethal arrow with compassion;

this account is as explained in the "Chapter on the Lion’s Vow" of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra*). Because killing living beings creates enmity that leads to rebirth in the evil realms, one does not keep slaves or servants.
This rule was established for ordained bodhisattvas out of compassion, while for lay practitioners, it refers to the six types of kin.

If a renunciant bodhisattva lacks compassion and seeks revenge— even against their own parents, paternal uncles, brothers, or other members of the six relations— and thus retaliates, they commit a minor offense.
The third section, following the sūtra, concerns the bodhisattva who has gone forth: raising the faults and defining the offense. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:

"If bodhisattvas dwelling in the code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) respond to another’s abuse with abuse, respond to another’s anger with anger, respond to another’s striking with striking, or respond to another’s grappling with grappling, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted violation."
"If a Buddha’s disciple...
From this point downward, the second section contains two precepts that explain the obstacles to wisdom;

these two become three [in the broader context], and this is the second part, clarifying the precept against arrogance and refusing the Dharma. This section is divided into two parts: first, explaining the person, as stated in the text.
The Buddha’s disciple next clarifies the path of karma.
At the very beginning of his renunciation, before having attained any realization, he may rely on his own cleverness and intelligence;

or rely on his noble status, advanced age, or long-standing lineage; or rely on his great learning, high social standing, abundant merit, or wealth in the seven treasures. Out of such arrogance, he...
One should not fail to consult and receive from a Dharma Master who has mastered the Sūtras and Vinaya; even if such a Dharma Master is of humble lineage,
young, from a low station, poor, or lacks physical faculties, yet actually possesses virtue and understands all the Sūtras and Vinaya,
a newly initiated Bodhisattva must not disregard the Dharma Master’s lineage and fail to come to consult and receive from him the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This constitutes the offense of a light defilement (*āpatti*).
In the sutra, this section following the first—concerning the renunciant bodhisattva—clarifies the paths of action (*karmapatha*). The text is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying that one does not receive the Dharma out of self-reliance; second, clarifying that one does not receive the Dharma out of disdain for others. This is the first part. Within this:
There are two [sections]: first, clarifying reliance on one’s own superiority; second, clarifying the refusal to accept the Dharma. Within the former, there are two parts:

first, clarifying that one has not yet attained understanding; second, clarifying reliance on one’s own superiority. This is the first [part], clarifying that one has not yet attained understanding, as indicated by the scripture:
"while relying on oneself... The second part clarifies reliance on one's own superiority, which contains five phrases. The first is relying on cleverness.
Second, relying on intelligence; third, relying on high status and seniority; fourth, relying on great lineage and noble birth; fifth, relying on great learning;
sixth, relying on great wealth—these are the six [prideful attitudes] by which one does not consult or receive [the Dharma]. Below this, secondly, it clarifies the sutra on not receiving the Dharma.
Regarding "the Dharma-preacher," below this, secondly, it clarifies disparaging others for not receiving the Dharma, meaning that when consulting and receiving the Dharma, one does not examine [it].
Whether old or young, one does not look upon others with pride or disdain because of the law of reverence.

As it is said, regarding those who possess the Dharma of wisdom—whether they be old or young—they are like the devas who serve Śakra. If a Bodhisattva despises another as being inferior and does not go to listen to the Dharma, they fail to transmit and benefit through transformation;
thus, a transgression is committed. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "One harbors a mind of arrogance and does not approach the teacher."
"To request instruction [in such a manner] is called a transgression," and so forth, as explained at length.

From this point downward, the second section clarifies the meaning of teaching the precepts with a mind of pride, which contradicts the principles of instruction.

Therefore, this regulation was established. Regarding the common transgressions of the seven classes of followers, the text has three parts: first, it clarifies the persons; second, it clarifies the reception of the precepts;
and third, it clarifies the paths of karma. This [section] identifies the persons:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when one wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts with a sincere mind, one should do so before an image of the Buddha or a bodhisattva.
When receiving the precepts through self-vow, one should repent before the Buddha for seven days; if one beholds a favorable sign, one then obtains the precepts.
If a favorable sign is not obtained, one should continue for two weeks, three weeks, or even up to a year, until a favorable sign is attained.

Once a favorable sign has been attained, one may receive the precepts before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva. Even if a favorable sign is not obtained, one may still receive them before an image of the Buddha.

The precepts are not said to be "attained" [in the same way as worldly things]. When one first receives the Bodhisattva precepts before a Dharma Master, it is not necessary to see an auspicious sign (*lakṣaṇa*).
This is because the Dharma Master has received them through a lineage of successive transmission; thus, there is no need for an auspicious sign.

Therefore, when receiving the precepts before a Dharma Master, one attains them immediately because of the arising of a profound mind of respect; one attains them simply by that. If, within a thousand *li*, there is no...
When one who can bestow the precepts receives them before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, they must perceive a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*).
For those who receive the Bodhisattva precepts after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, this constitutes the second section clarifying the method of receiving the precepts: first, the self-vow reception;
next, the reception from a teacher. Within the former, there is first the clarification of the timing of the precepts, followed by [the clarification of]...

This is the first section concerning the ritual for self-initiation. Following this, the second section concerning the ritual for self-initiation begins before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
Regarding "repentance" (*chànhuì*): the Master of Dharma says that since the character for "repentance" (*huì*) is not written [in the text], it should instead read "to polish away" (*mò*).
This refers to enduring and repenting one's actions; thus, every half-month, one increases the roots of virtue (*śīla-mūla*).
This refers to the vow of self-acceptance: first, before an image of the Buddha or an image of a Bodhisattva, one repents for all evil and unwholesome deeds committed.
If, after seven days have passed, one perceives an auspicious sign (*lakṣaṇa*), then those transgressions are extinguished.

If no auspicious sign is perceived, one must continue for three weeks, or even up to one year, until an auspicious sign is seen. If no auspicious sign is perceived, then the precepts are not obtained.
Regarding what is called "auspicious signs" (*lakṣaṇa*), as stated in the sutra below:

if there is one who has violated the ten precepts, they should be taught to repent before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, reciting the ten precepts and the forty-eight minor precepts six times each day.

If they reach the point of performing the prostrations to the three thousand Buddhas, they will see auspicious signs—whether after one seven-day period, two or three seven-day periods, or even up to one [month].

In the year [of the ritual], one must see auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*). These signs include the Buddha coming to touch one’s head with his hand, seeing various extraordinary phenomena such as radiant light and flowers, thereby causing the extinction of transgressions.
Regarding the *Jie jing* (Sūtra on Precepts), if it appears first, this is the second section following the preceding part: receiving the precepts from a teacher.
Although there are two textual passages, the second clarifies the conclusion of receiving the precepts.
If a Dharma Master, relying on his own mastery of the sutras, vinaya, and Mahayana precepts, acts as a virtuous friend to kings, crown princes, and high officials,
yet when newly initiated Bodhisattvas come to inquire about the meaning of the sutras or the vinaya, he answers each question poorly with a light mind,
a malicious mind, or a conceited mind, he commits a minor offense (light defilement).
In the Sūtra, following the section on the person of the Dharma-preacher, the third part correctly clarifies the paths of action as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"If someone comes to engage in conversation, discourse, consolation, or inquiry, and one— restrained by pride,
harboring resentment, or harboring malice— responds with words that do not accord with correct principle, this is called an offense and a transgression."

This is an afflicted transgression, not one committed through pride; it is done without a mind of resentment or a mind of malice, but solely due to laziness, indolence, forgetfulness, and a neutral state of mind. This is called a transgression that is not an afflicted violation.
There is no violation in cases such as when one is afflicted by a serious illness, or when the mind is deranged, and so forth, up to when one acts for the sake of protecting many.
There is no transgression when one does not respond to sentient beings; this constitutes a course of action (karmapatha) through five conditions:
first, there is an object; second, one abides in one's original state of mind; third, the other has not asked; fourth, afflictions arise, namely pride and so forth;
and fifth, one provides an answer that is unreasonable.
"O Sons of the Buddha.
This marks the person [who commits the offense]. From "O Sons of the Buddha" downward, this third section on the precepts for training in heterodox paths is divided into two parts: first, the person;
second, the characteristics of the action, followed by the summary of the offense. This [initial phrase] designates the person.
If one possesses the Buddha’s sutras and vinaya, the Mahāyāna Dharma, right view, right nature, and the true Dharma-body, yet fails to diligently study and practice them,
instead abandoning the seven treasures to study the false views of the two vehicles, non-Buddhist paths, secular classics, Abhidharma, miscellaneous treatises, records, and chronicles—
this is to sever the Buddha-nature and create the causes and conditions for obstructing the Path; it is not the practice of the Bodhisattva path.
In the Sūtras, from the Buddha’s Sūtras and Vinaya up to the section on the habituation of anger, this is the second [section] clarifying the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
First, it clarifies not habituating to the Mahāyāna; next, it clarifies studying heterodox paths—this is the first [point], "not habituating to anger.

Regarding the term "right view" (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), it refers to wisdom (*prajñā*) induced by correct principle. Regarding the term "right nature" (*samyaktva*), it refers to the two kinds of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*): both principle and practice.

The "True Dharma-body" refers to the fruit obtained from the two preceding causes. Regarding the passage on "discarding the seven treasures," this refers to those who abandon the Mahāyāna Sūtras of Śākya and instead study heterodox views, even down to committing them to writing;
this constitutes the second [section] concerning the practice of heterodox paths.

First, the practice of heterodox dharmas is clarified, and next, their faults are revealed; this is the first [of those two]. Both the followers of the Two Vehicles and the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are so named.

Because wrong views are contrary to the views corresponding to the Mahāyāna, those who study the vehicles of the two [Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha] and exclusively reject the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya while exclusively delighting in practicing the sūtras and śāstras of the two vehicles are said to have committed an offense. *Gāyu* says:
"Regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one has not yet studied it with thorough precision; regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one exclusively rejects it; regarding the Śrāvaka-piṭaka..."

To study exclusively [in this manner] is called an offense that is non-afflicted yet a transgression of the training. Regarding those who study outside the Buddhist teachings, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:

"While the Buddha's teaching currently exists, to fail to investigate it thoroughly and instead to diligently study the treatises of heterodox paths and various non-Buddhist works is called an offense;
what is thus transgressed is an afflicted violation. The details are as fully explained therein.
The previous statement that "the sutra says this severs the Buddha-nature" constitutes the second point, which reveals the fault.

"If one acts intentionally, one commits a minor offense (duṣkṛta)" and "if one acts intentionally according to the sutra, one commits a minor defilement offense (mṛdudauṣṭhulya-āpatti)" constitute the third point, which clarifies the formal determination of the offense (*āpatti-samāpti*). [This concludes] the section on the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*).
One should understand this according to the principle to some extent.

"If a Buddha-son" refers to the second section, which contains six precepts clarifying the precepts for benefiting others; the first four concern the gathering of others through *samānārthatā* (common purpose).
Regarding the obstacles to the next two [perfections], which are the obstacles to beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), the first four [obstacles] are divided into four parts; this is the first:

the precept against improperly gathering a following, also called the precept regarding the use of the Three Jewels. The text is divided into three sections: first, the person [who commits the offense]; second, the explanation of what should be practiced;
and third, citing the improper act to conclude with the transgression. This is the first section.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you shall serve as the master of the Dharma, the master of its practice, the master of the monastic quarters, the master of instruction, the master of seated meditation,
and the master of conduct. You should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness, skillfully reconcile disputes, and properly guard the property of the Triple Gem,
never using it recklessly as if it were your own.

Following the passage "after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa," the second section clarifies what should be practiced. Within this, there are three parts: first, the time, as indicated by the phrase "after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa";
second, the person capable of practicing, as indicated by the phrase "acting as a master of the Dharma" and so forth;

and third, the six types of masters. First, the master of preaching the Dharma (*dharmabhāṇaka*), meaning one who is able to preach the Dharma is called a master of preaching the Dharma, or one who is able to establish [the teaching].

Regarding the assembly for establishing the Dharma, there are two types of "Dharma Master" (*dharmasvāmin*): first, it refers to one who possesses wisdom regarding the Dharma; second, it refers to one who is capable of expounding the Dharma.
The commentary explains that one who is the master of the Dharma is called a "Dharma Master," though this does not necessarily mean they must be able to expound it to be so named;
alternatively, one who is able to expound the Dharma is called a "Dharma Master. Third, the "Monastery Manager" (*vihārasvāmin*) refers to one who performs maintenance and repairs.
Regarding the assignment of dwellings: there are four types of masters of dwellings.

Fifth, the master of meditation (*dhyāna-ācārya*), which refers to one who, having previously known all the methods of meditation, is able to instruct others; such a person is called a master of meditation.

Sixth, the master of arrivals and departures (*āgantuka-ācārya*), which refers to one who attends to guests, welcoming them upon arrival and seeing them off when they leave. These three duties should be performed as prescribed in the sūtras, and one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Because the mind skillfully reconciles disputes and the like, it is intended here that one should, as appropriate,

give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward the six aforementioned leaders to skillfully reconcile their disputes and guard the property of the Triple Gem; this concludes the second [section] on what should be practiced.
"Yet, on the contrary, one disturbs the assembly, engages in strife, and uses the property of the Triple Gem according to one's own whims; this constitutes a minor offense.

Regarding the phrase "on the contrary, one disturbs the assembly," the following is the third section, which cites the transgression and concludes with the definition of the offense. There are two types of such transgressions:

first, disturbing the assembly by failing to rely on the principles of the teachings and thus causing disorder in the distribution [of resources]; second, using the property of the Triple Gem according to one's own whims.
"Objects" refers to the property of the Sangha master; thus, one who guards the property of the Triple Gem must also manage its distribution and usage.

When using such objects, if one does not inform the Sangha assembly and uses them according to one's own whims, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). Question: Does not the use of the property of the Triple Gem constitute a grave offense? Answer:

It is explained that the owner of these objects does not act out of a thieving mind, nor for their own personal gain, but solely for the sake of the Sangha’s use; therefore, [it is not a grave offense].
Not informing the Saṃgha is a light offense, not a grave one. In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, if one engages in quarreling or disputing, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
Regarding the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptadharmāḥ saṃghaprakaraṇasamathāḥ*), if one applies a remedy [inappropriately], it is subsumed under a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

If, acting as the leader of the Saṃgha, one uses the property of the Triple Gem without informing the Saṃgha, this is explained according to its specific meaning as being subsumed under a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). (Examine the text.)
"If a Buddha’s disciple..."—from this point below, the second section clarifies the precept on receiving offerings exclusively. This specifically restricts monastics, not laypeople;
it means that regarding the bedding and furniture of the monastery or when a donor invites the Sangha, both the host and the guest must share in the portion.

However, the resident monks alone received [the offerings] without sharing the portion belonging to others who were not residents; for this reason, the rule was established. The text is divided into three parts: first, the persons involved;
second, the proper procedure to be followed; and third, the raising of the fault. This section identifies the persons.
If a guest Bodhisattva bhikṣu first arrives at a monastery, a dwelling, a city, a royal residence,
or even a place for the summer retreat or a great assembly, the monks who were already residing there should welcome him upon his arrival and see him off upon his departure;
they should provide him with food and drink, as well as housing, bedding, and rope-seated couches, supplying him with everything he requires.
There is no object that should not be sold; even one's own body, the bodies of one's sons or daughters, or whatever else is required for their needs, may all be given away.

If a donor comes to invite the assembly of monks or visiting monks, and there is a share of offerings to be distributed, the monastery superintendent should assign the visiting monks to receive the invitation in due order.
The phrase "in the dwelling of a resident monk" appearing earlier in the sutra clarifies the second duty to be performed. Following this, there are three parts:
first, it clarifies the role of the host of the room, as indicated by the passage "in the dwelling of a resident monk";

second, it clarifies the arrival of visiting monks, as indicated by the passage "he also sees visiting bodhisattva bhikṣus arriving, etc."; and third, it clarifies the provisions for supporting visiting monks, which includes the following...
First, one should welcome them when they arrive and see them off when they depart, for as the Sūtra says, the resident monks should welcome and see them off.
Second, one should provide all necessities, for as the Sūtra says, from providing food and drink up to supplying whatever is required, one should give it all to them.
Third, if someone comes to invite [the Sangha], one should assign [a monk] according to the Sangha, for as the Sūtra says, "If there are donors who come to extend an invitation..."
Because the community of monks must be appointed in successive order, there are briefly six types of such appointments. First, identifying the person who appoints:
this refers to one who has completed five years of *varṣa*, has not violated any of the grave precepts (*pārājika*), and does not carry out the practice of giving;
when the Sangha appoints him to handle administrative affairs (*kāyavastu*), he is one who does not carry out [the practice of] *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Second, clarifying those who are appointed.

People say that the five groups of renunciants who do not commit a *pārājika* offense and are not subject to burial—if they possess a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and practice the *śikṣādattaka* (probationary) rules—shall always remain at the bottom of the third [category].
Regarding the three locations for the appointment of monks: first, a village monastery such as a *saṃghārāma*;
second, an *araṇya* (forest hermitage); and third, a place where the Saṃgha resides. These exclude the aforementioned [first two].
Regarding the dwelling places of the Saṃgha in these two locations—and likewise in the third location—one must first establish the boundary (*sīmā*) and only then appoint the succession of monks.

Furthermore, there is another explanation stating that even if the boundary has not yet been established, one may appoint the succession of monks based on the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*); this also presents no hindrance.
Fourth, as for the method of appointing the monks, it proceeds from the fully ordained monks (*upasampanna*) down to the novices (*śrāmaṇera*), completing one cycle before beginning again.
The *Upādhyāya* (Preceptor) may appoint anyone from the lowest rank down to a *śrāmaṇera*.

Whether for a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*), an assembly (*huì*), the reception of the precepts, the summer retreat (*an-jū*), or a Dharma discourse, appointments are made according to circumstances. When leading the *Upādhyāya* or during a lecture session, the order of monks is appointed;

this is specifically termed "inviting the present Sangha" (*xiànqián-sēng*). This is distinct from other names. Fifth, regarding the timing of written invitations (*shūqǐng*) among the ten directions: as follows...

Regarding the sequence of letters received, they are arranged according to their order of arrival; if they arrive simultaneously, it is understood that those from a distant location are considered "prior" and those from a nearby location are considered "subsequent.
If the distance is equal and they arrive at the same time, it is understood that the one delivered first by the official in charge is "prior.
Regarding letters from a prior person whose boundary has not yet reached the official in charge, there are two interpretations: the first says...
Entering the *dhātu* (elements) constitutes one sequence; some say that seeing [the object] first constitutes another.

Generally, when discussing the order of the Saṃgha, one does not distinguish between Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, but rather establishes an equal hierarchy based solely on the status of those who have left the household life. If there is an invitation for the Śrāvaka Saṃgha, only the Śrāvaka Saṃgha is appointed;
if there is an invitation for the Bodhisattva Saṃgha, the Bodhisattva Saṃgha should be appointed. Regarding the six types of accepting and relinquishing invitations:
Question: Regarding the case where one renounces a previous invitation and accepts a subsequent invitation, there are two interpretations because it is not clearly explained.

One interpretation states that one renounces the previous invitation by first forming the intention to do so. Another interpretation states that one renounces the previous invitation upon accepting the subsequent invitation, and then renounces that [subsequent one] as well;

this is also unobjectionable, as it belongs to me in portions. A third interpretation states that if one first forms the intention, "I shall renounce the previous [invitation]," [then one may accept the subsequent one].

Regarding the question of whether one may accept a later invitation after having renounced a previous one, yet subsequently renounce that later one as well—whereas it was previously understood that once an invitation has been accepted and renounced to another, it cannot be taken back—the following two interpretations exist:
The first states that one must renounce the previous invitation in the presence of a person before one can accept the subsequent one;

furthermore, the previous acceptance must be renounced and given to someone outside the boundary (*sīmā*). The second states that it is not permissible to give it to an outsider, because the assignment of monks is based on the original [invitation].
Regarding the question from the perspective of the *dhātu* (elements/realms): "May one give [the food] to those who have not received a share of the meal for the Saṃgha? It is not understood;

some say this may not be given to those who have not received a share of the meal for the Saṃgha. Others say that since the Buddha permitted the relinquishing of the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), once the relinquishing is complete, it may be given to those who have neither received an invitation nor a share of the meal for the Saṃgha. The remainder of the text is understandable.
If the resident monks alone accept the invitation without dispatching guest monks, the master of the monastery incurs immeasurable sin;
he is no different from a beast, neither a śramaṇa nor of the Śākya lineage, and commits a minor offense.

Regarding the phrase "the resident monks and others" and so forth, this is the third section, which raises the faults and establishes the offenses. The number of requisite conditions (*pratyaya*) may be understood according to reason;

as the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If various bodhisattvas, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), accept disciples yet harbor a mind of resentment and fail to provide them with timely, unerring instruction and unerring teaching..."
If, knowing that the community is in need, one does not seek for their sake— in accordance with the Dharma—
from faithful laymen, householders, or Brahmins, clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, medicinal requisites for illness,
or various articles for the support of the body, and fails to provide them at the appropriate time, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted offense.
If, due to laziness, indolence, or negligence, one does not go to provide instruction or admonition, nor seeks out the requisites for the Dharma, there is no offense,
provided it is not a transgression born of defilement. There is also no offense if one intends to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue that person—
as explained in detail previously— or if one is observing a monastic regulation, or if one suffers from leprosy or other ailments, or lacks the physical strength.
Whether he himself undertakes the preparatory application, or requests others who possess great power;
whether he knows that the assembly is widely known in the world as having great merit and each being individually capable of seeking clothing and other requisites for the body;

whether he has already provided instruction and admonition to each according to what is appropriate, doing so correctly; and whether he knows that there is someone originally present within the assembly.
If non-Buddhists enter among the assembly for the purpose of stealing the Dharma— being incapable, untamable, and entirely without transgression—
if they do so, O Disciple of the Buddha: [there is no offense].

In the Sūtra, from "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards is the third section concerning the precept against accepting special invitations, which harms the offerings of others and violates the principle of equality;

therefore, it is established as a rule. The text is divided into two parts: first, the identification of the person, and second, the conclusion regarding the path of karma. This [first part] identifies the person.
"One must not, under any circumstances, accept individual invitations for offerings; once received, these offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions.
Regarding the phrase "under no circumstances," the second section below, which concludes the discourse on the paths of action, is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying what should not be done; second, defining the offense. This is the first part, clarifying what should not be practiced; within this, there is first the formal statement.
The subsequent explanation of this constitutes the heading of the sutra.

Regarding the second explanation, "And these offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions," why is it asked here whether one should not accept individual invitations? This statement was made to resolve such doubts.
It clarifies that these offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions.

If one separately accepts an invitation and takes property belonging to the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself— using for personal purposes items intended for the eight fields of merit, such as those belonging to the Buddhas,
the holy ones, individual teachers and monks, parents, or the sick— one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the passage, "If one separately accepts an invitation and takes the property of the Sangha of the ten directions," etc., this marks the second section:

citing the transgression and establishing the offense. The meaning here is that whether it be an invitation for the Sangha to a meal or an offering of goods to the Sangha, none of these may be accepted as a separate invitation.
Some say that if among four people there is even one who belongs to the monastic succession (*saṃgha-krama*), then [the rule] does not apply.

Regarding the offense of committing [a transgression] when there is no formal sequence of the Saṃgha, this is precisely what is being regulated; one should understand the number and conditions of the factors involved according to reason. Question:
It is not understood why it is an offense even when one does not accept an invitation. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"When others come to invite one, or when one goes to a household, or goes to another monastery to receive offerings of food, clothing, and other requisites..."

If one is overcome by pride and arrogance, harbors a mind of resentment, does not go to that person's place, or does not accept their invitation, this is called an offense and a transgression; it is a non-afflicted violation.
There is no violation if one is ill, lacks physical strength, is mentally deranged, is in a remote location, the path is dangerous, or if one intends to employ skillful means.
To discipline them, to subdue them, to lead them out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states; or because of other prior requests;

or for the sake of uninterrupted cultivation of various wholesome dharmas, desiring to protect these wholesome qualities so they are not temporarily abandoned; or for the sake of attracting hitherto unattained meanings;
or so that the meaning of the Dharma heard does not decline—just as one would for the sake of ensuring the meaning of the Dharma heard does not decline through discussion.

It should be understood that the determination regarding this case is likewise. Alternatively, if one knows that the person has come with a mind of malice and harm to invite [the practitioner], or if it is for the sake of protecting others who harbor much resentment, or to uphold the monastic regulations, and thus does not go to that place nor accept the invitation, there is no transgression in any of these instances.
Question: Is it not a defiled transgression to fail to go to that place out of a mind of resentment? Answer: No.
Therefore, the *Dharmasaṃgraha-śāstra* asks: "Is this a violation that constitutes defilement? The commentary explains: "This is merely an error made by the scribes of the earlier translators;
there is no need to be alarmed. Regarding the eight fields of merit, they have already been explained as previously stated.

"O Sons of the Buddha. This marks the person [to whom the precept is addressed]. From this point downward, the fourth section explains the specific precept regarding requests made for one's own benefit, which violates the merit of equality; therefore, it is established as a prohibition.

The text is divided into three parts: first, the person; second, the practice that should be followed; and third, the citation of faults and the determination of the offense. This is the identification of the person.
When ordained bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, and all donors invite the Sangha as a field of merit to fulfill their vows, they should enter the monastery and inquire with the administrative officers.
If one intends to invite according to the sequential order of the assembly, one thereby obtains the holy and sage Sangha of the ten directions.
This is superior to the worldly practice of separately inviting five hundred arhats or bodhisattva monks; it is not equal to a single invitation made according to the monastic sequence.

If an ordinary person invites monks individually, this is the practice of non-Buddhists; the Seven Buddhas had no such custom of individual invitations, as it does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety.
If one intentionally invites monks individually, one commits a minor offense.
Following the section on "The Bodhisattva Who Has Left Home," the second part clarifies what should be practiced, as can be understood from the text.

Regarding the third part, which cites faults and defines the offense following the passage on "the worldly people making separate invitations": the seven Buddhas mentioned all reside here [in this assembly].
Their offenses were committed within the past hundred kalpas; thus, the long-lived devas have personally seen and heard of them. For now, I shall speak only of the path of these seven Buddhas.
In principle, all Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise not subject to separate invitations;

nevertheless, this separate invitation is a transgression common to the seven assemblies, though the gravity differs between the Great and Small Vehicles, as the Small Vehicle also permits the practice of separate invitations (verify the text). Regarding this, there are two interpretations:
first, it is said that if there is no monastic order at all within a single assembly, one commits an offense; second, if within a single assembly there is... [text breaks off].
