If one requests the monks in sequence for the remainder [of the meal] and then makes separate invitations, there is no offense. One opinion states that making separate invitations for both [groups] constitutes an offense.
Regarding what are called the "Seven Buddhas," this refers to the three Buddhas of the past and the four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa; these constitute the Seven Buddhas.
Thus, the *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), fascicle nine, states: "In ninety kalpas there were three Buddhas, and in the subsequent kalpa there will be a thousand."
At the beginning of ninety kalpas, there was the Buddha Vipaśyin. During the thirtieth kalpa, there were two Buddhas:
the first named Śikhin and the second named Viśvabhū. At the beginning of the ninety-first kalpa, there were four Buddhas:
the first named Krakucchanda, the second named Kanakamuni, the third named Kāśyapa, and the fourth named Śākyamuni.
Kāśyapa Muni explained that Vipaśyin is also called Vipaśa and also called Vyuṣita;
these are variations of the Sanskrit pronunciation due to differences in lightness and heaviness of articulation, yet their meaning is one and the same.

This [Vipaśyin] is translated as "Victorious Vision" (Śreṣṭhadarśana), also as "Diverse Vision" (Nānādarśana), and also as "Extensive Vision" (Vistīrṇadarśana). As for Śikhin, he is also called Śikhi; this is translated as "Victorious" (Śreṣṭha).
Regarding "Supreme" (*Anuttara*), it is also called *Vipula*, *Viśvabhu*, *Utpala*, or *Suvrata*;
in Chinese, these are translated as "All-Victorious" (*Sarvajaya*) or "Extensive Birth" (*Vistara-janman*).
Regarding "Kālakaraṇḍa," it is also called *Krakucchanda*, *Krakutsunda*, or *Kālakaraṇḍa*.
Regarding "Great," this is translated as "Crown" (*mūrdhan*). As for *Kanakamuni*, some say it is *Kanagamuni*;
*kanaka* here means "knotless tree" (*nirgranthi-vṛkṣa*), and *muni* means "endurance," "fulfillment," or "quiescence.
Regarding *Kāśyapa*, this is translated as a clan name; derived from the name of the clan, he is called Śākyamuni. The old translation was "Capable of Endurance" (*Nengren*).
It is also called "Able to Fulfill" (Nengman); in the current translation by the Great Tang, it is rendered as "Able to Quiesce" (Nengji).

If a disciple of the Buddha—this marks the second section from below, which contains two precepts clarifying the obstacles to beneficial conduct (*kuśalacaryā*). These two are further divided into two parts.

This is the first [section], clarifying the precept against wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). It concerns the violation of the rule against taking life and the violation of the rule against improper conduct for gain;

it applies equally to all seven classes of followers, yet the text specifically addresses those who have left the household life. The passage is divided into two parts: first, the mention of individuals, followed by the citation of their misconduct. This [initial part] serves to identify the individuals involved.
Out of an evil mind, for the sake of profit and sustenance, they trade in the sexual favors of men and women; they prepare their own food by hand, grinding and pounding it themselves;
they practice physiognomy on men and women, interpret dreams for good or ill fortune, and determine whether a child will be male or female;

they employ incantations and crafts, train hawks, and concoct mixtures of a hundred kinds of poisons and a thousand kinds of poisons, including snake venom, raw gold and silver, and *gūḍha* (sorcery)—all utterly devoid of compassion.
The mind incurs a secondary offense of defilement (*laghu-mala-pāpa*).
According to this sutra, because of an evil mind, the second [section] cites the transgression and concludes with the penalty.

Based on this sutra, there are twelve kinds of methods of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*): first, trafficking in the sexual favors of men and women for profit, which all seven groups of practitioners (*saptāṅga*) commit equally; second, oneself...
1. Preparing food by hand for ordained monastics; 2. allowing householders to grind and pound their own grain (the same applies to these);
3. interpreting the physical marks of men and women; 4. interpreting dreams regarding good and bad fortune; 5. incantations and sorcery; 6. mechanical arts and crafts;
7. methods for training hawks; 8. compounding a hundred kinds of poisonous drugs; 9. snake venom; 10. producing gold and silver; 11. *gū* poison (insect-based toxins).
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the four kinds of "mouth-food" (*mukhabhojana*) are termed wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). The fourth fascicle of that treatise states:
The woman Viśuddhamati asked Śāriputra, "Is there not such a thing as living by impure means?

Śāriputra replied, "There are those among the renunciants who compound medicines, sow grain, plant trees, and so forth; these who live by impure means are said to have 'downward-facing mouth-food' (*adhomukha-bhojana*)."
If a renunciant observes the stars, the sun, the moon, wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and hail as a means of livelihood, this is called "upward-facing" (ūrdhvamukha) food.

If a renunciant flatters those of power and influence, acts as a messenger between the four quarters, and seeks much through clever speech as a means of livelihood, this is called "four-sided" (caturmukha) food. If a renunciant studies various... [text truncated]
Practicing incantations, calculating fortunes and misfortunes, and other such various forms of impure livelihood—these are called the four types of "sister-mouth-food.
I do not fall into these four impure foods; I sustain my life by seeking alms through pure means.

Due to the conditions involving the five families, one immediately violates this precept. First, regarding the matter: the matter at hand refers to the specific activity being performed, which is appropriate.
1. The object, such as medicine; 2. The perception, which is the mental conception of that object; 3.
The arising of desire, which is the aspiration for an impure livelihood; 4. The affliction, which is either greed for gain and honor, or anger, or delusion, whether present in full or incomplete;
5. The culmination, which is the completion of the act. Herein, the intended meaning is that if—
If one engages in various forms of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) with a virtuous mind, it constitutes a defiled transgression;
however, if one practices such things as compounding medicines for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, there is no offense. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, gives rise to deceit, empty talk, hinting, or the employment of expedient means..."
To seek gain through pretense, to seek the taste of gain, to engage in modes of livelihood that are wrong, and to persistently hold to these without shame—this is called an offense, a transgression.

It is a defiled offense. There is no offense if, while one has generated the desire to eliminate them and exerts diligent effort, the afflictions are so intense that they overwhelm the mind and manifest from time to time.
"If a Buddha’s disciple...

This marks the second section, explaining the precept against disrespecting auspicious times. It is a violation for all seven assemblies; one interpretation holds that it is restricted only to laypeople.
The three long months were originally established for the sake of laypeople, which is why they are mentioned first as being superior.

Regarding the statement that "a bodhisattva who has not yet left the household life commits evil and employs evil means, thereby also violating the precepts," the textual division consists of two parts:
first the person, then the offense; this [section] designates the person.
Out of an evil mind, one slanders the Triple Gem oneself while feigning intimacy; one speaks of emptiness with the mouth while practicing within the realm of existence;
one acts as a go-between for laypeople to facilitate sexual intercourse between men and women;

and being bound by lustful attachments, one commits killing, robbery, or theft on the six days of fasting or during the three long months of fasting, thereby violating the fast and transgressing the precepts—such a person commits a minor offense.
The Sūtra states that for one who, with an evil mind, performs the second type of transgression during the months of fasting when they are advanced in years—there are three such months:
first, the first month; second, the fifth month; and third, the ninth month. This means that the first month is the beginning of the manifestation of all classes of sentient beings;
the fifth month is the period of their flourishing; and the ninth month is when all classes of sentient beings desire to store away [their provisions].
Because it was at the beginning [of the year], these three months are called the "Month of the Long Fast.

Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* commentary states that when cultivating merit for the deceased, there are three periods: the second month of spring, the fifth month of summer, and the ninth month of autumn.
According to this sutra, the second month is the first, the fifth month is the middle, and the ninth month is the last; thus, the present text aligns with these three.
Regarding the "long months": from the latter half of the first month to the first half of the second month constitutes the initial month;

from the latter half of the fifth month to the first half of the sixth month constitutes the middle month; and from the latter half of the ninth month to the first half of the tenth month constitutes the final month of the *upavāsa*.
Thus, because these scriptural passages each rely on a specific meaning, they do not contradict one another, O Great Wisdom.
The *Dulun* (Śīla-saṃgraha-śāstra), fascicle 15, states: Question: Why is it that on these six fast days one receives the eight precepts and cultivates merit?
Answer: On these days, malevolent spirits pursue people, seeking to snatch away their lives; they cause illness, misfortune, and decline, making people inauspicious.
Therefore, at the beginning of the kalpa, the sages taught people to observe the fast. Question: For what reason do the various classes of ghosts afflict and harm [beings] on these six days?

A person replied: "As stated in the *Benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Original Arising of Heaven and Earth), when the kalpa was first formed, there was a prince of a certain Brahmā heaven who was the father of various spirits and ghosts.
He practiced the asceticism of a brahmacārin for twelve celestial years;
during six days of this period, he cut his flesh and drew his blood, placing them into the fire. For this reason, these spirits and ghosts invariably possess power during these six days."

Furthermore, the *Lì yòu jiù jí jīng* (Sūtra on Saving the Sick through Power) and the *Sì tiānwáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Four Heavenly Kings) state that on these six days, Śakra, the Four Kings, their princes, and their messengers descend to bestow blessings or calamities.
The *Chūshòu zāi jīng* (Sūtra on Receiving the Fast) says:
"During the fast day, spend one part in meditation, one part in reciting the sūtras, and one part in lying down; this is the correct method for the Bodhisattva’s day of fasting."
Receiving [the precepts] on the fourteenth day and releasing them on the seventeenth; receiving them on the eighth day of the fourth month and releasing them on the fifteenth;

receiving them on the first day of the seventh month and releasing them on the sixteenth; and receiving them on the fourteenth day of the ninth month and releasing them on the sixteenth—according to this sutra, there are these four long fasts (*caturmāsa*).
Depending on the capacities and conditions of individuals, their perceptions and understandings differ, so one should not find this strange.
The remainder of the text is understandable. Thus concludes the first section, the formal explanation of the ten precepts.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind; they are explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Formulation of the Precepts" (*Śīlasaṃvara-vinaya*).

Regarding the phrase "having passed through these ten precepts, etc.," from here below is the second section, which clarifies the exhortation to uphold [the precepts] by pointing forward to subsequent chapters.
The Buddha says, "O Son of the Buddha.

From the words "The Buddha says" onwards is the fourth section, the Precept of Benefiting Others (*anugraha-śīla*). First, it is explained; later, there is a conclusion. Within the former, there are two parts: first, [the explanation].

There are three precepts that clarify obstacles to meritorious conduct; next, it is clarified that there are six precepts which constitute the precept for gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
Within the preceding section, these three are explained and divided into three parts. This is the first [part], clarifying the precept against failing to provide ransom.
The text is divided into three sections: first, the person; second, the response; and third, the conclusion of the fault. This is the identification of the person.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, if one sees non-Buddhists, all manner of evil persons, or bandits who sell images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one’s parents;
who sell the sūtras and the Vinaya; or who even sell bodhisattvas who have resolved for enlightenment—making them servants or slaves for officials or for anyone at all.

Following the section on "After the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa," the second part clarifies that one should practice within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This section has two parts: first, it clarifies the timing;
second, it clarifies the objects toward which one should act. This is the first part, clarifying the time period:

namely, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the ages of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) and the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*), amidst an evil world, if one encounters non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), wicked people, or the like...
From here below is the second section, clarifying the objects that ought not to be dealt with; these are of five kinds: first, selling images of Buddhas or Bodhisattvas;
second, selling images of one's parents; third, selling the Sūtras and Vinaya; fourth, selling Bhikṣus or Bhikṣuṇīs;

and fifth, selling those who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment—namely, practitioners on the path of a Bodhisattva—referring to those who sell people who have newly resolved their minds to serve as slaves to others.
When a bodhisattva sees such things, they should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and employ skillful means to rescue and protect them,

teaching and transforming others everywhere to purchase with their own wealth Buddha and Bodhisattva images, as well as all the sūtras and vinayas belonging to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and those who have resolved to attain enlightenment.

After the Bodhisattva has witnessed these matters, the second section follows, which correctly clarifies what ought to be practiced; although there are two passages, the second clarification of what ought to be practiced is now concluded.
If one does not redeem [the person], one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

If one does not redeem [the scriptures], this is the third section from below, which defines the transgression common to the seven classes of practitioners, though the gravity differs between the Great and Small Vehicles.
Specifically, according to the Śrāvaka teachings, if one sees a relative being sold by others and fails to redeem them, one commits an offense of the seventh category (saptama-varga).
[Note: The text should be verified. Regarding scriptures, images, and other items, no separate rules are established. This precept is violated when five conditions are met. What are they?
These constitute the five factors: first, the object (*vastu*), which refers to objects such as scriptures and images, or the act of selling them, or even [selling] one's own slaves and servants;

second, the perception (*saṃjñā*), which refers to generating the perception that they belong to another; third, the intention (*chanda*), which refers to giving rise to the desire not to redeem them;

fourth, the affliction (*kleśa*), which refers to greed, hatred, and delusion, whether present in their entirety or partially; and fifth, the culmination (*niṣṭhā*), which refers to failing to go and redeem them, whether by oneself or [through others].
If one is ill; or lacks physical strength; or knows that one can accomplish the task oneself;

or knows that what is to be done would lead to what is unreasonable or what is contrary to the Dharma; or if one is diligently cultivating virtuous qualities and does not wish to abandon them even for a moment;
or if one is by nature dull-witted and finds it difficult to receive or retain the teachings heard; or if one is acting for the sake of protecting many sentient beings.
If it was done intentionally, there is no offense for which one might be exempted from redemption.
If a disciple of the Buddha does not keep swords, staves, bows, or arrows; does not sell light scales or small measures; does not use official authority or influence to seize the property of others;
does not harbor harmful intent to bind or destroy others' success; and does not raise cats, foxes, pigs, or dogs—if [one does these things] intentionally...
If one who maintains [the precepts] commits this, they incur a minor offense.
In the sutra, from "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards, the second section clarifies the keeping of improper vessels; this text is divided into three parts: first, the person [who keeps them];
second, the explanation of what should not be done; and finally, the conclusion regarding the transgression. These may be seen directly in the text and need not be described at length here.
"If a Buddha’s disciple...
This marks the third section, clarifying the precept against fighting and frivolous play. The text is divided into three parts: first, the person;
second, that which one should not practice; and finally, the summary of the transgression. This [opening phrase] designates the person.
With a mind of aversion, one should not observe the fighting of men and women, nor the battles of armies, generals, or bandits;
furthermore, one must not listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, *konghou* lutes, singing, shouting, or musical performances.
One must not play *chubu*, go, *parase*, *tanqi*, *liubo*, ball games, stone-throwing, pitch-pot, or tug-of-war.
One must not use the Eightfold Path, the city, footprints, mirrors, mushrooms, willow branches, alms bowls, or skulls to perform divination;
one must not engage in thievery or act as a messenger for others. If one does so intentionally, one commits a minor offense.

The Sūtra, following the previous section on [avoiding] evil thoughts, now clarifies the second point: those things one should not practice. This further consists of five categories: first, the five things one should not see;
second, the nine things one should not listen to. Regarding the things one should not see: these refer to men and women fighting, as well as soldiers fighting.

Regarding the nine things one should not listen to: first, blowing conch shells; second, drums; third, horns; fourth, *vīṇā* lutes; fifth, *sītara* lutes; sixth, *kinnarī* lutes; seventh, flutes; eighth, *konghōu* lutes; ninth, [the remaining category].
The nine songs of the *pipa* lute, the three non-responding [incantations], the six miscellaneous performances such as *chūbǔ* (backgammon) and others, the five non-responding matters,
and the stalk divination known as the *Chéngxú Jìng* (as recorded in the *Mínglì Suǒbào*).

If a Buddha’s disciple upholds the prohibitive precepts, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they shall recite these precepts during the six periods of day and night as if they were a vajra.
Like one carrying a life-preserving leather bag intending to cross the great ocean, or like the bhikṣu bound by grass, they shall constantly give rise to Mahāyāna faith, knowing for themselves:
"I am a Buddha who is not yet perfected; the Buddhas are Buddhas who have already attained perfection. They shall then resolve upon Bodhicitta.

If, in every thought-moment, the mind does not depart from this [resolve], yet if even a single thought of the two vehicles or of external paths arises, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

According to the Sūtra: "O Sons of the Buddha, from here below is the second section, which contains six precepts clarifying the *śīla* of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

This section has four parts: first, there are three precepts clarifying the obstacles to diligence; next, there is one precept which is the obstacle to the perfection of concentration (*samādhi-pāramitā*); next, one should teach..."

After the "Transformation" section on the Obstruction of the Perfection of Precepts (*śīlapāramitā*), there follows the "Illumination" section on the Obstruction of the Dharma-gift of Precepts. Within the "Essential Continuity" section, three precepts are divided into three parts;
this is the first, the Illumination of the Precept Against Regressing the Mind, which all seven classes of practitioners violate equally, though the gravity differs between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
The eighth precept in the preceding section concerns turning away from the Great toward the Small; here, it is appropriate to explain the practice of the Small Vehicle, and thus it is present.
The analysis of the textual divisions has three parts: first, the person; second, the transgression; and third, the conclusion of the fault, as can be seen in the text.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "To transcend the Bodhisattva-dharma and instead seek skillfulness in the treatises of heterodox paths and various non-Buddhist systems, to treasure them with a deep-seated mind, to delight in them, and to become attached to their flavor—approaching and practicing them not like bitter medicine—is called an offense."
One should understand, according to reason, the number of conditions required for such defiled transgressions.
If a disciple of the Buddha constantly makes all vows to be filial toward their parents and respectful toward their teachers, monks, and nuns;

and vows to obtain excellent teachers, fellow students, virtuous friends, and spiritual mentors who will constantly instruct them in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, the ten stages of departure (*daśa-niryāṇa*), the ten stages of nurturing (*daśa-poṣadha*), and the ten stages of gold (*daśa-suvarṇa*).
"O Gaṅga, the Ten Stages have enabled me to attain understanding and practice according to the Dharma, firmly upholding the Buddha's precepts.
I would rather sacrifice my body and life than let this resolve depart from my mind for even a single thought-moment. If any Bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense."

In the sutra, following the first section, is the second part concerning the precept against failing to generate the great vow; this contains three sections: first, the person; next, the explicit explanation of the ten vows;
and finally, the conclusion regarding the transgression of the constant duty. Following the "person," the second section explains the ten great vows:
1. The vow to generate reverence and obedience toward one's parents; 2. The vow to obtain a good teacher; 3. The vow to obtain good companions who are skilled in knowledge.
The fourth vow explains the Mahāyāna precepts; the fifth vow explains the ten stages of setting forth (*daśa-prasthāna*); the sixth vow explains the ten stages of nurturing (*daśa-anuśamsā*);
the seventh vow explains the ten adamantine stages (*daśa-vajra*); the eighth vow explains the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*); the ninth vow concerns practicing according to the Dharma;
and the tenth vow concerns upholding the Buddha’s Sutra on the Precepts. If all Bodhisattvas [practice thus], the third section concludes as seen in the text.
If a Buddha’s disciple, having made the ten great vows, upholds the prohibitions of the Buddhas and makes this vow, saying:

"I would rather cast this body into a pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of swords than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman."

Furthermore, they make this vow: "I would rather have my body encircled on all sides by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh than, with a body of broken precepts, receive any clothing from a faithful donor."

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and great torrents of fierce fire with this mouth for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever use a mouth that has broken the precepts to eat the food of a hundred flavors offered by faithful donors."

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather lie with this body upon a floor of great, fierce fire and glowing red-hot iron than ever again receive from a faithful donor the hundredfold varieties of beds and seats with a body that has broken the precepts."

Furthermore, he made this vow: "I would rather endure three hundred spear thrusts in this body for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever receive from a faithful donor the four hundred flavors of medicine or medical supplies with a body that has broken the precepts."

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever again receive with a body of broken precepts the various kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, and fields offered out of faith by a donor."

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather have this body smashed from head to foot with an iron hammer until it is reduced to fine dust than ever again receive the respectful prostrations of faithful donors with a body that has broken the precepts."

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by a hundred thousand hot iron knives and spears than ever look upon the beautiful forms of others with a mind that violates the precepts.
Again, he makes this vow: "I would rather have my sense organs pierced all over with a hundred thousand iron awls for one kalpa or two kalpas..."
They shall never, with a mind of broken precepts, listen to pleasant sounds.
Furthermore, they make this vow: "I would rather have my nose cut off by hundreds of thousands of blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily smell various fragrances."
Again, he makes this vow: "I would rather have my tongue severed by hundreds of thousands of blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, consume the hundred-flavored pure foods of others.
Again, he makes this vow: "I would rather have my body split asunder by a sharp axe than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, succumb to craving."
One should wear fine garments and further make this vow: "May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood. If a Bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.
In the sutra, from "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards, the third section on the firm resolve of the non-vow is divided into three parts:
first, the designation of the person; second, the formulation of the ten great vows; and third, the citation of transgressions to conclude the section. This [first part] designates the person.
Following the formulation of the ten great vows, the second part clarifies the formulation of the thirteen vows. The first is: "I vow not to consort with women."
Regarding pure conduct, as stated in the sutra, one should rather cast this body into a pit of blazing, fierce flames and so forth;
that is to say, it is better for this present body to undergo extreme suffering for a brief moment in the present than to undergo long-term suffering for the sake of even a moment’s play.
Second, regarding the vow not to accept clothing: as stated in the sutra, one further makes this vow: "I would rather have a thousand-fold net of hot iron [cast upon me]..."
Because they are equal in weight, there are three [further points]: first, making a vow not to accept food of a hundred flavors;
second, not accepting a hundred kinds of beds and seats; third, not accepting medicine of a hundred flavors; fourth, not accepting houses, rooms, gardens, or groves;
fifth, not accepting honor, respect, or prostrations; sixth, never breaking the resolve against precepts while gazing upon the beautiful forms of others; ninth...
9. One shall never, with a mind that breaks the precepts, listen to pleasant sounds. 10.
One shall not, with a mind that breaks the precepts, greedily smell various fragrances. 11. One shall not, with a mind that breaks the precepts, eat pure food of a hundred flavors.
12. One shall not crave pleasant tactile sensations. 13. One shall vow that all people attain Buddhahood. Question: Regarding the third [vow], the non-acceptance of drink.
What is the difference between eating food and not accepting the hundred flavors? First, four matters are raised to manifest that one does not accept;
subsequently, the sense-gates (*indriya-mukha*) are raised to manifest non-attachment; thus, there is a distinction.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that one does not accept the hundred flavors within the mouth, and subsequently it was stated that one does not crave the hundred flavors within the mind. The intention here is to say that if all bodhisattvas...
When a bodhisattva guards right mindfulness, they do not violate the precepts nor fall into the evil destinies;

however, if they lose right mindfulness, they transgress the pure precepts and undergo immeasurable suffering. Therefore, a bodhisattva makes this vow: "I would rather give up my body and life than ever crave or become attached to odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects.
How does a bodhisattva guard right mindfulness so as not to be attached to the five desires?
This means that Bodhisattvas, observing all the afflictions within saṃsāra, guard their right mindfulness as if holding an oil bowl without spilling a drop.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 22, states:

"For example, suppose there is a great multitude in the world filling a distance of ten li, and a king commands an official to carry a single oil bowl through the midst of them without letting it tip over."
The King said, "If you spill even a single drop, I shall take your life. He then dispatched another man who followed behind with a drawn sword to terrify him.
Having received the King’s command, the minister held his resolve with all his heart as he passed through the midst of that great assembly.
Although he saw various objects of the fivefold sensual desires that were pleasing to the mind, he constantly thought to himself: "If I become negligent and become attached to those desires..."
One would rather discard what one holds than fail to fully save this person; because of such causes and conditions of fear, one would not even discard a single drop of oil.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not lose mindfulness and wisdom within the cycle of birth and death;
because they do not lose them, the mind does not become greedily attached.

"If a Buddha’s disciple..."—the second section below this clarifies the obstacles to the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), also known as the precept against entering difficult places.
This passage is divided into three parts: first, the person; second, what they should practice; and third, the conclusion regarding transgressions. This [opening phrase] marks the person.
One should always practice *dhūta* during the two seasons of winter and summer, sitting in meditation and observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
Regarding the constant practice of these two periods up to the commencement of the summer retreat, this second section clarifies what should be practiced therein;
it has two parts: first the heading, then the explanation. This is the general heading for the *dhūtas*. The "Great Tang" edition reads "Du."
*Duō* (多) is also called *tīduō* (投多), which here means "cultivating and adorning the practice of the precepts," because it cultivates the mind.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 72, states: "The twelve *dhūta* practices are not themselves called 'precepts,' but rather the adornment of the precepts.

Regarding the cultivation of these precept-practices, according to the distinctions of *dhūta* in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are ten; however, since there are thirteen [in another classification], that treatise’s [second]... [fascicle].
25. What is the accomplishment of the dhūta-guṇas?

It refers to always vowing to beg for food, begging in sequence, eating at a single sitting, not eating after having first stopped, wearing only the three robes, wearing only woolen robes (the character *mǎn* [元] means fine hair), wearing robes made of discarded rags, dwelling in an araṇya, constantly residing under trees, constantly residing in the open air, and constantly residing in a charnel ground.
One should always intend to sit upright in a cemetery, remaining as one who sits in the "constant sitting" posture.
Thus relying [on these supports], whether regarding food, clothing, or various bedding, one should practice the dhūta virtues—either twelve or thirteen kinds.
Within the practice of alms-gathering, there are two types: first, gathering alms as they are obtained; second, gathering alms by sequential begging. This is explained in detail, up to...
It should be understood that herein, if one relies on the undifferentiated nature of alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*), there are only twelve items;
however, if one relies on the differentiated nature of alms-gathering, there are thirteen, and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, some sources state that there are twelve dhūta practices, while the practice of receiving food (*bhaikṣya*) has five aspects: (1) not accepting special invitations, and (2) eating only once a day... [and so on].
[The rules are: (4) not drinking warm water after midday; (5) eating in one sitting; (6) moderation in food. Regarding the dwelling places, there are five:
(1) a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*); (2) not lying down [to sleep]; (3) among tombs; (4) at the foot of a tree; (5) in the open air. Regarding clothing, there are two kinds:
(1) properly maintaining the three robes (*tricīvara*); (2) constantly wearing the patched robe (*pāṃsukūla*). Such are the explanations.
There are those who do not employ [these practices], as they differ according to the suitability of their faculties and what they have seen or heard.

When asked for the causes and conditions for teaching these *dhūta* (ascetic) practices, the explanation is as follows: those to be converted (*vineya*) are of three types—first, those greedy for food; second, those greedy for clothing;
and third, those greedy for dwelling. Because they effectively remedy these three types of greed according to their respective order, twelve or ten [practices] are taught.

The three types [of tooth-sticks] are explained extensively in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 25) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Chapter 72); fearing prolixity, I shall provide a brief description here.

One should habitually carry a willow branch (*dantakāṣṭha*), cleansing powder (*snāna-kalka*), the three robes (*tricīvara*), a water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*), an alms bowl (*pātra*), a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), an incense burner (*dhūpa-pātra*), a water filter (*parisrāvaṇa*), and a hand-basin (*karaka*).
A head-cloth, a razor, a fire-starter, tweezers, a cord, a small bed, and the scriptures, the Vinaya, images of the Buddha, and images of Bodhisattvas—
these eighteen kinds of items should always accompany the body when a Bodhisattva practices *dhūta* or travels on pilgrimage for a hundred or a thousand *li*.
As for the practitioner of *dhūta*, from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and [from the fifteenth day of the] eighth month...
From the fifteenth day [of the first month] until the fifteenth day of the tenth month, during these two periods, these eighteen kinds of items must always accompany the person,
like the two wings of a bird. On the days of the *poṣadha*,
when a novice bodhisattva performs the *poṣadha* every half-month and recites the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he should perform it alone.
Whether it be one person reciting, or two, three, or even up to a hundred thousand people, they all recite as one.

The reciters sit on high seats while the listeners sit on low seats; each is clad in the nine-striped, seven-striped, or five-striped *kāṣāya* robe, and they observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in every respect according to the Dharma.
The sutra frequently uses the *śīrṣaka* (twig) as its starting point; the following is a broad explanation in three parts: first, the requisites for *dhūta*;
second, the time for *dhūta*; and third, the *poṣadha*. This is the first part, explaining the eighteen items of the *dhūta* requisites that should always accompany the body:
first, the *śīrṣaka*; second, the *kaṇḍuka* (bean-like tooth-cleaner); and third, the three robes (*tricīvara*).
Regarding the "three robes": the first is traditionally called *saṃghāṭī*, though this is a corruption of the sound; it should be called *saṃghaṭi* or *saṃghāṭi*.

In the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "joined" or "layered," referring to the fact that it is made by cutting pieces together and then sewing them back together, or by making it with double layers.
This robe must be constructed from cut pieces (*khaṇḍika*). As for the remaining two robes, they may or may not be cut, provided they conform to the Dharma.
The Sarvāstivāda school and others divide it into two parts; it is called *uttarāsaṅga*, or alternatively *uttarāsaṅga* or *uttrāsaṅga*.
These variations are due to the shifting of sounds and differences in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation.
In the Tang language, it is called "upper garment" (*shangzhuoyi*), as it is worn on top among those garments most frequently used. Thus it is named.

Some say that the three *antarvāsas*—also called *antavāsa*, *antapapa*, or *antāravastra* (translated into Chinese as "clothing for dwelling" or "inner clothing")—are worn with the left shoulder covered;
these three robes are termed *kāṣāya*. *Kāṣāya* is translated into Chinese as "not of primary colors. All [robes] made of dyed cloth...
If the bark, leaves, flowers, or other parts of a tree do not produce the five flavors and are difficult to eat, they are called *kaṣāya*.
Because this substance dyes cloth a turbid red, the "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*) among the five turbidities is also named after it;
monks in India frequently use this color. Furthermore, as the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra* states: "The word 'universal' (*prapañca*) means 'non-existence'."
Regarding "stain" (*kaṣāya*), another meaning is "to leave behind dust and clothing," or it is called "the robe of intermediate colors.
Tripitaka Master Paramārtha stated that *kāṣāya* means "a robe of crimson blood color. Although there are five different schools in foreign lands, they all use robes of red color;

the terms "black" or "madder-brown" are merely names for specific variations in their dyeing. Sixth is the water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*); seventh is the alms bowl (*pātra*); eighth is the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*); ninth...
1. Iron staff; 2. Incense burner; 3. Water bag; 4. Hand towel; 5. Knife; 6. Fire-starter; 7. Tongs (pronounced *rè*);
8. Ropes; 9. Bed; 10. Sūtras; 11. Vinaya; 12. Images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Some say that if one lacks even one of these eighteen items, one commits a minor offense (*āpatti*). Now, this shall be explained.
In this context, one simply refrains from entering difficult places as a precept. Regarding these eighteen items, whether they are complete or incomplete, there is no transgression.
Following the *dhūta* [practices], the second section clarifies the timing, which may be seen in the text.
Regarding the passage "If, at the time of the *poṣadha*," the third section clarifies the *poṣadha*. *Poṣadha* is translated here as "increase" (*vṛddhi*). Furthermore—
It is named "Nourisher" (*Puṣya*) because it increases and nurtures wholesome qualities; thus it is called "Growth.
When practicing the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), do not enter dangerous places.

These include countries in turmoil, wicked kings, lands with uneven terrain, deep thickets of grass and trees, dangers from lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, wind, and storms, as well as bandits on the road, venomous snakes, and all other such perils.

Since one must not enter any place of difficulty, even those who practice the dhūta austerities, travel on the path, or observe the summer retreat (varṣā) must likewise not enter such places of difficulty;
how much more so for those practicing the dhūtas? If such a person enters a place of difficulty because they have seen it, they commit a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).

Regarding the sūtra’s instruction that one should not enter dangerous places during the dhūta practice: the third point concerns the preliminary declaration of the offense rather than the formal establishment of the offense itself.
This means that first one declares that one ought not to enter dangerous places, and subsequently the formal establishment of the offense is understood.
If a Buddha’s disciple...

From this point downward, the eighth section clarifies the sequential precepts. Because they prohibit the violation of dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*), they are established as offenses common to the seven assemblies, with both major and minor rules being equally enjoined.
The text is divided into four parts: first, the person; second, what should be done; third, what should not be done; and fourth, [the conclusion].
Having finished the formalities, this is the first [section].
One should sit according to the proper sequence: those who have received the precepts earlier sit in front, while those who have received them later sit behind;
one does not inquire whether they are senior or junior bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, persons of noble rank, kings, princes, or even eunuchs and slaves.
The female attendants who have already received the precepts should sit in front, while those who have received them later should sit in successive order behind them.
The sūtra should follow the proper sequence; next, the second section clarifies that there are seven types of assemblies to be conducted:
first, bhikṣus; second, bhikṣuṇīs; third, śikṣamāṇās; fourth, śrāmaṇeras; and fifth, śrāmaṇerīs.
Sixth are the upāsakas (laymen), and seventh are the upāsikās (laywomen). Regarding the explanation of this seating order, there are three interpretations.
The first states: within the assembly of bhikṣus, those who have previously received the bodhisattva precepts are considered the senior seats (*upasthāyaka*).

This refers to a case where, for example, among those with śrāvaka precepts, one person received the precepts later, while among those with bodhisattva precepts, another person received them earlier. Thus, there is one person [who is senior].

Regarding the sequence of receiving precepts: among those who have received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the *śrāvaka* community, they are placed first; among Bodhisattvas, they are placed later.

Within these two groups, those who first received the Bodhisattva precepts are the senior seats (*upādhyāya*), while those who received them later are the junior seats. The remaining six types of assemblies may be understood by analogy with this.
The intent here is that, among these seven classes of practitioners as appropriate, the *bhikṣu* is the superior, followed by the *bhikṣuṇī*.

Regarding the sequence from the intermediate stages down to the final one, it is taught that although there may be a chronological order in which householders receive the bodhisattva precepts, they cannot be said to be superior to those who have left the household life; thus, their sequence should not be considered as being mutually exclusive.

Furthermore, because men and women, as well as the young and the old, each belong to distinct categories, [the sequence] is established accordingly. One view holds that there are cases where one has previously received the śrāvaka precepts but has not yet received the bodhisattva precepts.
Regarding the precepts, there are those of the Śrāvakas received later and those of the Bodhisattvas received earlier.
Among these two groups, whether there are those who possess the Bodhisattva precepts or those who do not, the Bodhisattva precepts serve as the seat of honor because they are the most supreme.
If both individuals have received the Bodhisattva precepts, they further [rank] according to their original Śrāvaka...
The summer retreat (*varṣā*) serves as the sequential basis for the remaining six types [of precepts]; the others should be understood accordingly.
One source states that for a renunciant bodhisattva, the summer retreat alone serves as the sequential basis because they attain renunciation by relying on the *śrāvaka* dharma;
although there are three such explanations, the first is considered superior.
"Do not act like the ignorant followers of external paths, whether old or young, who sit without precedence or sequence according to the law of soldiers and slaves.
In my Buddha-dharma, those who come first sit first, and those who come later sit later.
If a Bodhisattva sits out of this order, they commit a minor offense."
The Sūtra is not like that of the non-Buddhists; this concludes the third section, clarifying that one should not follow the literal text.
As for the fourth section, "The Bodhisattva," it summarizes the faults; the number of requisite conditions should be understood according to reason.
If a Bodhisattva sees an elder approaching and does not yield his superior seat, this constitutes a light offense. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Upon seeing various elders..."
If one encounters a virtuous fellow-practitioner worthy of respect, yet harbors a mind of resentment and fails to rise to welcome them or offer them a superior seat, this is called an offense;
and so forth, as explained at length.
O Disciple of the Buddha!

In this sutra, from the third section below, "If a Buddha’s disciple... and so forth, the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is clarified—namely, the giving of material wealth and the Dharma—as can be understood.

It is established as a precept because it violates the principle of gathering wholesome qualities (kuśalasaṃgraha). All seven assemblies commit this offense, though its gravity differs between the Mahayana and Hinayana. The text is divided into three parts: first, the person;
second, the corresponding application; and third, the conclusion regarding the transgression. This [opening phrase] marks the person.
One should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings by establishing monasteries, mountain forests, gardens, and fields,
as well as constructing Buddha-stūpas and places for winter and summer retreats, for seated meditation, and for all practices of the Way; furthermore,
the Bodhisattva should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings, whether they are afflicted by illness, national calamities, banditry, or the death of a father.
On the day of the passing of one's mother, siblings, preceptors (upādhyāya), or ācāryas, as well as during the third week and up to the seventh week,
one should likewise recite, chant, and expound upon Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, hold assemblies for merit, seek blessings, engage in livelihoods,
and [offer protection] against those burned by great fires, swept away by great floods, blown by black winds, or [threatened] at sea by ships, rivers, great oceans, and rākṣasas.

Those who encounter difficulties, as well as those who recite, chant, or expound this sutra and vinaya— even those with all manner of karmic retributions for sins, the three evil paths, the seven heinous crimes, the eight difficult circumstances,
whose bodies are bound by handcuffs, fetters, pillories, and shackles, and who abound in lust, anger, ignorance, and illness—
all should recite, chant, and expound this sutra and vinaya.
One should frequently instruct and transform others; this second section clarifies what should be done, which is further divided into two parts.
First, it teaches that one should cultivate merit. Second, it clarifies that within the cultivation of merit there are four types:

first, constructing monastic dwellings; second, erecting Buddhist stūpas within gardens and groves; third, establishing places for the summer retreat and seated meditation; and fourth, [the remaining type].

The establishment of the place for practicing the Way can be understood according to the text of the sūtra. Following the section on the Bodhisattva, the second part clarifies the practice of cultivation;
there are seventeen types of what this refers to: first, the difficulty of illness, meaning that many diseases prevail within the country;
second, the difficulty of the state, meaning when an evil king governs the country, or when the country is beset by enemies; third...
Fourth is the danger of bandits; fifth is when one’s honored teacher is present; sixth is when traveling, meaning when coming from or going on a long journey;

seventh is when maintaining life—some versions of the sutra read "maintaining life," which is a synonym for receiving birth, referring to the time of manifesting this life in that [realm]; eighth is the danger of fire; ninth is the danger of water. Nine.
1. The calamity of wind; 2. The calamity of fire; 3. The calamity of water; 4. The calamity of weapons; 5. The calamity of hunger and thirst; 6. The calamity of famine; 7.

The calamity of being born among wild beasts; 8. The calamity of being born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); 9. The calamity of being born among the asuras; 10. The calamity of rākṣasas; 11. All retributions for sins, whether determinate or indeterminate; 12. The three types of retribution—namely, retribution in the present life, in future lives, or subsequent to that—or alternatively, the "three retributions" refers to the retributions of the three miserable realms (*durgati*);

13. The seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*), which shall be explained separately later; 14. The eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). Regarding the eight difficulties, they are as described in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The *Āgama* Sūtras state that there are fifteen [obstacles]: first, hell; second, the animal realm; third, the hungry ghosts; fourth, long-lived devas;
fifth, dwelling in a borderland; sixth, the impairment of the six sense faculties; seventh, perverse views of the mind and consciousness; eighth, the non-appearance of a Buddha.
Fifteenth are the prisons; sixteenth are the three poisons; seventeenth are one's own physical illnesses, as described above.
Among the seventeen supreme leaders, one reads, recites, and lectures upon the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas.
If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not do so, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
[The phrase] "if a newly initiated bodhisattva" concludes the third section on the enumeration of faults, as can be understood from the text; the intended meaning here is as follows:
Thus, when preaching Mahāyāna sūtras according to the true and correct principle during difficult times, one does not incur a minor offense (laghu-pāpaka) by failing to proclaim them;

for the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the pure code of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), sees sentient beings extensively practicing what is unreasonable for the sake of matters pertaining to their present life or future lives, yet harbors a mind of resentment or a mind of malice [and fails to intervene]."
To fail to explain the correct principle as it truly is constitutes an offense and a transgression.
It is an afflicted offense if one fails to explain due to being obscured by indolence or laziness;
it is a non-afflicted offense if there is no transgression when one lacks knowledge, lacks the capacity, or requests another who possesses the capacity to explain.
That person possesses their own intellectual power; or they may be sustained by other virtuous friends; or one may wish to skillfully discipline or subdue them—as explained at length previously.

If one knows that the person will give rise to a mind of resentment when the true principle is taught to them, or will utter evil words, or will misunderstand it erroneously, or lacks affection and respect, or furthermore knows that their nature is corrupt—[in such cases, one should not teach].
If one is ill or traveling, it is not a transgression to fail to explain them;
thus, these nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart, as will be explained in the "Chapter on the Brahma-Assembly.
Following these nine precepts, the second section encourages their observance by pointing forward to subsequent chapters.
The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha.
Following the Buddha’s words, "O Son of the Buddha," from this point downward is the fifth section, which contains nine precepts clarifying the precepts for benefiting sentient beings.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the formal explanation of the nine precepts; second, the concluding summary of the specific explanations, which is further divided into nine sections. This is [the first].

First, it clarifies that restricting the conferral of precepts contradicts the principle of universal benefit; therefore, this rule is established. This section on the obstacles to practice is divided into three parts:

first, the person [to whom the rule applies]; second, the sequential explanation of the conferral of precepts; and third, the citation of the fault and the determination of the offense. This is the first part, which identifies the person.
When conferring the precepts upon others, one must not exercise discrimination; all kings, princes, ministers,
officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, laywomen, male and female libertines, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the six heavens of the desire realm, those without sexual organs,
those with dual organs, eunuchs, slaves, and all ghosts and spirits are fully entitled to receive the precepts.
In the second section following this, which clarifies the method for bestowing the precepts upon others, there are four parts:

first, distinguishing the candidate for ordination; second, explaining the proper deportment; third, distinguishing the seven obstacles (*saptavighna*); and fourth, the rule that one who has left the household life must not prostrate to laypeople.
This is the first part: distinguishing the candidate for ordination. Regarding the "eighteen heavens," these are those mentioned above.

The eighteen Brahmā realms and the various heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are omitted from the brief exposition. Why is this? Because by mentioning the beginning and the end, the middle is naturally revealed;

that is to say, once humans are mentioned first and the various heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are mentioned last, the intermediate categories are established without needing to be stated explicitly.
One should instruct that all the saṃghāṭī robes worn on the body be made of dyed colors corresponding to the Path;
they should all be dyed blue, yellow, red, black, or purple. All dyed garments, even down to bedding, must be of dyed colors.
As for all the clothing worn by the people of various countries, bhikṣus should likewise [adopt] all such dyed colors for the robes they wear on their bodies.
It differs from their secular dress.
The scripture should teach what the body wears; next, from the second section below, its majestic demeanor (*vīrya*) is clarified.
*Kāṣāya* means "foreign garment" (*hu-yi*) or "dust-detaching garment" (*li-chen-yi*).
When one wishes to receive the precepts, the master should ask: "In this present life, have you not committed any of the seven heinous crimes?
A Bodhisattva Dharma Master must not confer the precepts upon one who has committed the seven heinous crimes in this life. The seven heinous crimes are:

shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing one's Upādhyāya (preceptor), killing one's Ācārya (teacher), disrupting the Saṃgha that is performing the *karmavācanā* or turning the Wheel of Dharma, and killing an Arhat.
If one possesses the seven obstructions (*saptāvaraṇa*), one cannot receive the precepts in this very body; all other persons may fully receive the precepts.
As for the passage in the Sūtra concerning the time when one wishes to bestow the precepts, this is the third section below which distinguishes the seven difficulties (*sapta-vighna*).

If one commits the seven difficulties, one cannot receive the precepts in this present life. The meaning here is that if one has committed the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) and has not yet performed repentance, although [the person] is...
If one has performed repentance but has not yet attained an auspicious sign (*lakṣaṇa*), such a person shall not receive the precepts in their present body.
Even if one has previously committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*) and subsequently repents with a sincere mind before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they may still receive the precepts;
however, when this sutra states that one "cannot receive them in the present," it refers to those who have neither yet repented nor attained an auspicious sign.
Because it is stated thus, the *Viniścaya-vibhaṅga-sūtra* (or *Vyākhyā-vinaya-sūtra*) declares: "If there is a bodhisattva who commits one of the five ānantarya crimes—
whether against a woman, or against a man, or intentionally committing an offense against a stūpa, or an offense against the Saṃgha,
or other such offenses— the bodhisattva should, before the thirty-five Buddhas, confess these grave transgressions day and night."
With a sincere heart, one should perform repentance, as explained at length;

furthermore, if a bodhisattva can constantly practice three matters throughout the day and night by invoking the names of all those Buddhas, they will be freed from transgressions and all sorrows and regrets, and will also attain samādhi.
The commentary explains that the "three matters" are: first, prostrating to the Buddha and repenting; second, dedicating merit; and third, making vows.

As stated in detail in that sutra, the meaning here is this: if a person recites the Buddha’s name and contemplates the Buddha’s merits, all their roots of goodness will be immeasurable and boundless;
by means of these, they can extinguish karmic obstacles and attain purity.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 19, says: "Great King, suppose for one month you were to constantly provide offerings of food and clothing with reverence..."
Venerating all sentient beings is not equal to even one-sixteenth part of the merit obtained by someone who recites the Buddha’s name for a single thought-moment.
Suppose one were to forge gold into human figures, chariots, and horses, each carrying a hundred treasures, and use them to practice giving;
this would not be equal to someone who resolves their mind toward the Buddha and takes a single step forward. Or suppose someone says: "If I were to commit [an offense]..."

Regarding the statement that one who commits the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) will certainly not obtain the precepts in their present body, the seven heinous offenses are: first, shedding the blood of a Buddha;
second, killing one’s father; third, killing one’s mother; fourth, killing one’s *upādhyāya* (preceptor); fifth, killing one’s *ācārya* (teacher);
sixth, causing a schism in the *karmavācanā* (ritual) Saṃgha or the Dharma-wheel Saṃgha; and seventh, killing an *ārya* (noble one). Now, to explain these seven heinous offenses:
The fivefold analysis consists of: first, the determination of the essential nature; second, the analysis according to persons; third, the locus; fourth, the time;
and fifth, the analysis according to destinies (*gati*). First, regarding the determination of the essential nature, the various schools differ.

According to the Sarvāstivāda, the sixth [type of unwholesome action], namely mental action, has the nature of *avijñapti* (non-informative action); the remaining six types have the nature of bodily action (*kāyakarman*), as is appropriate for killing and so forth.
Because they are the skillful means for bringing about birth and death, according to the intention of the Sautrāntika school, mental action (*manas-karman*) constitutes their nature.

As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 43: "Furthermore, the statement by the Venerable Upatiṣya that the three types of action constitute the essence [of karma] is difficult to establish logically, since it is not possible for bodily and vocal actions alone to independently induce the fruit of retribution (*vipāka*).
Rather, it is because the matter performed by mental action is weighty that it is admitted to be capable of inducing [retribution]."
Regarding the distinction of the superior maturation (*viśiṣṭavipāka*), based now on the Mahāyāna and its differences from the Sarvāstivāda:
the two types of action—body and speech—have volition (*cetanā*) as their essence. The volition that initiates speech is called "action of speech" (*vākkarman*);

it is not as the Sarvāstivādins maintain, that form and sound constitute its nature, for form and sound are certainly not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of action. Next, regarding the classification by way of persons: [it refers to] those capable of refuting...
Regarding the term "monk" (saṃgha): it refers to a full-fledged bhikṣu, not a layperson or the like; it refers specifically to one who practices [the path], not one who acts out of attachment;

it refers to a practitioner of purity, not one who has broken the precepts, for one who violates the precepts lacks majestic authority. The remaining six types apply to both men and women, whether they possess the precepts or not.
As for the "place": the schism of the Saṃgha that constitutes an immediate retribution (ānantarya) must be effected in a separate location.
It is not directed against the Great Master, for since the Tathāgatas cannot be coerced by words or intimidation, there is nothing else that can prevail over them;
thus, according to the circumstances, the six [offenses] are mentioned. Shedding the blood of a Buddha and causing a schism in the Wheel of Dharma occur when the Buddha is in the world;
after his parinirvāṇa, there is no true Great Master to serve as an adversary.
Regarding the remaining five types of schisms that disrupt the *saṃgha* through formal acts (*karmabheda*), their classification across other times and the five destinies (*gati*) is as follows:
the schism regarding the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-bheda*) and the shedding of blood from the Buddha’s body occur only among humans in Jambudvīpa, because a Buddha appears only in Jambudvīpa.
As for the others, they occur among humans in three continents—excluding Uttarakuru—because killing and so forth do not exist there.
Therefore, these and other such meanings have been explained in detail as they appear in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 9),
the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (fascicles 116 and 119), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (fascicles 17 and 18),
and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (fascicle 43); they are not omitted here for the sake of brevity.

The dharma of those who have left the household life is not to prostrate before kings, nor to prostrate before parents, nor to show reverence to the six kinds of relatives, nor to offer salutations to ghosts or spirits;
rather, they understand the words of the Dharma Master, and there are those who come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Dharma.

From this point on, the fourth section of the *Sūtra on the Dharma for Those Who Have Left the Household Life* clarifies that those who have left the household life do not pay homage to worldly people out of respect for the Dharma.
Nevertheless, if a Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of a malicious mind or a mind of anger, does not immediately bestow the precepts upon all sentient beings, [he commits an offense].
This constitutes the offense of a minor defilement.
Having thus explained the transgression, the Bodhisattva now proceeds from below to the third section, which enumerates the faults and concludes with the determination of the offense:
"If a son of the Buddha..."
In this sutra, from the second section below, "If a disciple of the Buddha... onwards, there is an explanation regarding the administration of precepts for profit.

Since there is the fault of administering them by force when one has no actual understanding, this rule is established. The text is divided into three parts: first, the person; second, the corresponding application;
and third, the citation of the transgression and the determination of the offense. This [first part] identifies the person.

When teaching others to give rise to faith, a bodhisattva acting as a preceptor or instructor for another should instruct the person who wishes to receive the precepts to request two masters: an upādhyāya and an ācārya.
Following the section on "Teaching and Transforming Others," the second part clarifies what should be practiced, which is further divided into two: first, clarifying the person who can teach;

second, clarifying the actual teaching. This is the first [of those two]. Following the passage in the sutra, "When one sees that they wish to receive the Bodhisattva precepts," the second part clarifies the actual teaching that should be given.
Within this, there are four sections: first, the instruction to request two masters; second, the inquiry into the seven [points].
The third [point] is that one should teach the performance of repentance; the fourth is the summary. This constitutes the first instruction: requesting the two masters.
If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, one requests only the *karmavācanā* master and does not request a preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
If one follows the teachings of this sutra, one requests both masters. Why is there such a difference? It is because if a person nearby is capable of acting as a preceptor...
Regarding the term "saṃgha," one should invite two preceptors; this is the primary rule.

However, if there is no one nearby capable of acting as such, and although there are bodhisattvas capable of serving as upādhyāyas who could confer the ordination, the necessary conditions are not met, then it is permissible to receive the precepts by inviting only one preceptor.
Since each case is based on its own specific principle, they do not contradict one another.

The two masters should ask: "Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)? If the candidate currently has the seven obstructing offenses, the masters should not confer the precepts upon them;
if they do not have the seven obstructing offenses, they may receive them.

If there are violations of the ten major precepts, they should be instructed to repent before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, reciting the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts six times throughout the day and night with utmost sincerity.

If one worships the thousand Buddhas of the three periods and attains the vision of auspicious signs—whether for seven days, two weeks, or even up to a year—one must seek to see these auspicious signs.
"Auspicious signs" refers to the Buddha coming to stroke one's head, or seeing radiant light, flowers, and various extraordinary manifestations;

upon seeing these, one immediately attains the extinction of sins. If no auspicious signs appear, then despite performing repentance, there is no benefit; such a person shall not attain the precepts in their present life.
If one receives the *zhòngshòu* (additional) precepts and violates any of the forty-eight minor precepts, one may repent before another person (*duìshǒu chànzuì*) to extinguish the offense;
this differs from the case of the seven prohibitions (*qī zhē*), for the teacher who instructs on these precepts must understand each point thoroughly within this dharma.
Following the two masters’ response, the second section concerning the meaning of the seven difficulties is as previously explained.

Regarding the passage "If there are those who possess the ten ordinary precepts," the third section clarifies the ritual of repentance (*pratideśanā*). However, the sūtras and śāstras differ on this point;
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "If a bodhisattva violates the aforementioned defeats (*pārājika*) due to an intense degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*)."
If one loses the restraint of the Dharma through the transgression of the rules of discipline, it should be conferred again.

If one commits an offense equivalent to a *pārājika* through a transgression involving medium-grade fetters (*madhyama-paryavasthāna*), one should confess and purify the evil deed before three persons, or more than that number.
If one commits an offense equivalent to a *pārājika*, or any other offense, through a transgression involving minor-grade fetters (*mṛdu-paryavasthāna*), [the same procedure applies].
One should understand that the method for confessing and repenting before a single *pudgala* is as previously described.
Herein, the meaning is that the offenses committed consist of two types of accumulations: first, the accumulation of non-restoration; second, the accumulation of restoration.
Within the accumulation of restoration, the method of confession is permitted; having restored it according to the Dharma, one again abides in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Therefore, one who has not yet returned to the assembly of purity does not open the dharma of repentance; if one repents, one cannot yet return to abide in pure precepts.
For this reason, it is only said that one should follow the principle of receiving [the precepts] again. Furthermore, there is also the dharma of repentance.
Moreover, the *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva violates the first precept, they should, before an assembly of ten, with an upright mind and out of compassion..."

The commentary on the "Reiterated Confession" explains that the term "first precepts" refers to the four grave offenses (*caturmahāvaśānīya*). It is called "first" because it points to the beginning of the fifty precepts;
thus, there are two interpretations herein. One interpretation states that there are three types of transgressions regarding these four grave offenses.
What are the three? First, transgression through superior-grade fetters (*paryavasthāna*); second, transgression through middle-grade fetters; and third, transgression through inferior-grade fetters.

If one commits an offense through a superior grade of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*) regarding the first precept, one should confess and repent before ten persons or before the Buddha with a mind of deep compassion.
Through such confession, the sin is extinguished, and one should receive the precepts again. If the sin is not extinguished, although one has received the precepts, one does not actually obtain them.
If one encounters a virtuous friend who understands the nature of the offense, it may be extinguished; this applies to offenses of the middling and inferior grades as well.
One who has violated the first precept attains the extinction of that offense by repenting with a sincere mind before three persons or even before a single person;

yet, this [text] mentions only those cases where one repents before ten persons. It is said that regarding the first offender, the latter case—repentance before a single person—is omitted for brevity.
One interpretation states that among the cases mentioned here of violating the first precept before ten persons, only the middle case is explicitly stated.

Regarding those who commit an offense through a minor degree of entanglement (*mṛdu-paryavasthāna*): why is this so? It is because one who commits an offense through a major degree of entanglement (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*) cannot restore purity;

therefore, that case is not mentioned here. As for the statement regarding "ten persons," since ten is the absolute minimum—whereas two, three, or more would cause no hindrance—there is no contradiction. Question:
If one commits an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) through a major degree of entanglement, one loses the discipline of the vows (*śīla-saṃvara*) and cannot restore it to purity. Why is this?

Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: "Once this single dharma has been practiced, if there are sentient beings who have committed the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and suffer from white leprosy (*śvitra*), it is impossible that it would not be cured.
This applies whether they are Bodhisattvas observing the twenty-four precepts, or śrāmaṇeras observing the ten precepts, or śrāmaṇerīs, bhikṣus, or bhikṣuṇīs observing their respective precepts."
Regarding these various precepts, if one violates any single one, one should repent with a single-minded focus;

it is impossible for the offense not to be restored unless there was a lack of sincerity. [Commentary: This explanation states that according to the capacities of individuals, what is seen and heard differs and cannot be reconciled.
If this is asserted, it is based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states that violating a *pārājika* (defeat) offense occurs through an intense degree of obsession (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*).

If one abandons the vows and cannot restore them to purity, one must necessarily receive them again. However, according to the *Vaipulya* and the *Dhāraṇī* teachings, there is no such thing as a grave offense that causes abandonment;

thus, while the merit of the precepts is abandoned, the essence of the lineage is not. Because the essence of the lineage is not abandoned, one may purify the precepts through repentance according to the Dharma, and they will arise once more.
Alternatively, according to the ultimate meaning as taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is said that they can be restored.

Regarding those who have committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) at a low or medium degree, there is the sense that they can still achieve purification; it is with this underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) that it is said, "It is impossible that they would not be reborn [in the higher realms].
This secret teaching was spoken in order to instill a sense of certainty in those who, having temporarily committed an offense of defeat, remain in a state of hesitation.
Alternatively, according to the Yoga system, this scripture treats the offense of defeat as being equivalent to this [case of purification].
The intent behind the twenty-four precepts differs from this; in this sutra, these are the fundamental *pārājika* rules. Once committed, can one be reborn?
What fault is there in this? Because one has not abandoned the precepts. Thus concludes the fourth section, where the sutra instructs the preceptor to descend [from the seat].

If one does not understand the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas— neither their light nor heavy aspects, nor the characteristics of what is right and wrong— and does not understand the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the nature of the lineage of practice (śikṣāgotra),
the nature of cultivation (bhāvanāgotra), the indestructible nature, the nature of the lineage of the path (mārgagotra), and the nature of the true dharma;

and if one cannot comprehend, in each and every instance, the various degrees of contemplative practice, the entry into and emergence from the ten factors of dhyāna, and all dharmas of conduct within these teachings— then one has not grasped the essential meaning of this dharma.
Regarding the phrase "if one does not understand the sūtra" and so forth: this is the third section, which raises the fault and concludes with the offense.

First, the fault is raised; subsequently, the offense is concluded. This "fault" refers to a lack of understanding. Regarding the failure to understand the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth), there are two types:

first, understanding through faith (*adhimukti*), and second, understanding through realization (*adhigama*). Because these two types of understanding have not been attained, it is said that one "does not understand."
Regarding the nature of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*), the sūtras and śāstras differ;

according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, that which precedes the arousal of the mind of enlightenment is called the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛtisthagotra*), while that which follows the arousal of the mind is called the "lineage of practice" (*samudānītagotra*). Thus, the thirty-fifth fascicle of that treatise asks: "What is the lineage?
Briefly, there are two kinds: first, the abiding lineage of original nature (*mūlaprakṛtisthagotra*), which has been transmitted successively from beginningless time..."
That which is obtained through the natural law (*dharmatā*) of coming [into being] is called the "lineage abiding in its original nature" (*prakṛtistha-gotra*).

As for the lineage accomplished through cultivation (*samudānīta-gotra*), this refers to that which is obtained by having previously practiced roots of virtue; this is called the lineage accomplished through cultivation.

Here, the intended meaning is that the lineage accomplished through the impression of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) is called the "cultivated lineage" (*paripuṣṭa-gotra*); according to the *Mūlakarma-sūtra*, the stage of the cultivated lineage is situated at the tenth level.
To explain this, that sutra states that within the stage of the nature of cultivation (*śikṣāgotra*) there are ten types of persons:

the Bodhisattva abiding in the stage of generating the mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), the Bodhisattva abiding in the stage of purifying the ground (*bhūmi-pariśodhana-vihāra*), and so on, up to the tenth, the Bodhisattva abiding in the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Alternatively, some say that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that those of the lineage of cultivation also exist within the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*), whereas the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) exists only above the ten stages of understanding. Thus it is said.
The *Benye jing* (Sutra on Fundamental Karma) states that the six lineages (*gotra*) are also called the six wisdoms:

the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*), the wisdom of illumination-and-quiescence (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-prajñā*), and the wisdom of quiescence-and-illumination (*vipaśyanā-śamatha-prajñā*).

Since "wisdom of hearing when appropriate" and "wisdom of reflection when appropriate" are subsumed within the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*), we know that the lineage exists at a level above the ten understandings. Although there are two interpretations, the former is superior according to the *Benye jing*.
