It is only said that the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-vyākhyāna*) consist of the wisdoms of hearing and reflection; it does not say that the impression of hearing exists solely in the ten stages of understanding, as it does not apply to the higher or lower stages.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with this sūtra’s statement regarding the "nature of the cultivated seeds" (*śikṣita-bīja-gotra*), which takes only the ten stages of understanding. Why is this?
Because within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), whether one regresses or progresses is determined; for this reason, it is not mentioned here, as in the original text.
The *Yejing* (Sutra on Karma) states: "O Son of the Buddha, regarding those who either regress or progress:

prior to the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), among all the dharmas of ordinary beings, one who generates the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi* and practices the Buddha-dharma within a state of faith and conceptualization is of the category of regressive roots of goodness.
However, if one practices the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to ten kalpas, one shall attain entry into the Ten Abodes."

It is said that those prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) are termed "stages of decline" (*hānabhāgīya*). This is a provisional designation for the "stage of decline" applied to a portion of indolent sentient beings;
in reality, however, they do not decline. Question: If those prior to the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*) are stages of decline, why does the verse in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state:
"Through the power of purification and supremacy, with a firm mind, ascending is called Bodhi"?
Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva first cultivates [the path] for three incalculable great eons," the commentary explains:

from the beginningless past, as one has flowed through the cycle of birth and death, at what point can it be said that the cultivation of practice begins for the first time during these three incalculable eons? To answer this question, the verse says:
"One whose firm mind ascends forward will never abandon the Great [Vehicle], even when encountering evil friends who employ means to destroy it."
The Bodhicitta is explained extensively, up to the stage of the Great Bodhicitta. The roots of goodness cultivated therein increase and become firm from moment to moment;

they advance without regression and do not give rise to complacency. This is termed the initial practice during the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). The commentary explains that there are two kinds of regression:
first, the regression of active manifestation (*samudācāra*), and second, the regression of seeds (*bīja*). [This applies to] the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the Bodhi...
If it refers to the manifest activity (*samudācāra*), there may indeed be the sense of regression; based on this principle, the Sūtra speaks of regression.

However, regarding the seeds of the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla-bīja*), there is absolutely no sense of regression. For this reason, the Śāstra states that they do not regress, and thus there is no contradiction.
As for the term "nature of nurturing" (*paripuṣṭa-svabhāva*), it refers to the lineage (*gotra*) within the six types of natures among these ten practices.

Furthermore, "non-destruction of nature" refers to the nature of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), while "nature of the path-species" (*mārgākāra-gotra*) refers to the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*).
These ten dedications and four roots of goodness are termed the "nature of the path-species. As for "right nature" (*samyaktva*), it refers precisely to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);

because one abandons the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) and enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*), it is called "right nature," or alternatively, it is the severing of the evil destinies, the categories of wrong karma, and the afflictions.
Therefore, it is said that "right nature" (*samyaktva*) has some who explain it as "universal nature. This reveals the nature of the noble path of the ten stages;

thus, it is called "path-nature. Regarding "right nature," both equal enlightenment (*samatā-bodhi*) and wondrous enlightenment (*vicitra-bodhi*) are termed right nature, because the causal practice is perfectly fulfilled and the fruit is fully manifested.
As for "right nature," the rest is as previously explained. The intention here is to reveal the six types of lineage (*gotra*).

Regarding the six lineages (*gotra*), as stated in the *Mūlakarma-sūtra*: the lineage of the stage of cultivation (*śikṣā-gotra*), the lineage of the stage of nature (*prakṛti-gotra*), the lineage of the stage of the path (*mārga-gotra*), the lineage of the noble ones (*ārya-gotra*), the lineage of wondrous awakening (*samyak-bodhi-gotra*), and the lineage of sublime awakening (*vimala-bodhi-gotra*). These are also called the six patiences (*kṣānti*):

the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), the patience of dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*), the conforming patience (*anuloma-kṣānti*), the correct patience (*samyak-kṣānti*), the stainless patience (*vimala-kṣānti*), and the patience of omniscience (*sarvajña-kṣānti*). For a detailed discussion on the variations in the number of these categories, refer to the *Yogācārabhūmi-ṭīkā*.
The practitioner of meditation is said to practice the eighteen bases of mastery (*aṣṭādaśa-abhibhvāyatana*) by contemplating various forms to a greater or lesser extent;
or, to a greater or lesser extent, they may practice within other meditative applications as appropriate. Regarding the phrase "entering and emerging from the ten factors of dhyāna":
the concentration of the ten factors of dhyāna is either entered into or emerged from; the "ten factors of dhyāna" refers to these ten [factors].
The eight factors of dhyāna are cultivated as ten factors. In the first dhyāna, five factors are present: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā).
To the second dhyāna, internal clarity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) is added; its remaining three factors have already been explained. To the third dhyāna, three factors are added:
equanimity (upekṣā), mindfulness (smṛti), and clear comprehension (saṃprajanya); its remaining factor has already been explained.
The fourth dhyāna adds two factors, namely neither-pain-nor-pleasure; since the other three types have already been explained previously, it is said that there are ten dhyāna-factors.
Within such modes of practice, one also attains this factor; the intention regarding this factor is termed "non-understanding."
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and fame, maliciously seeks out disciples who are greedy for profit,
and falsely pretends to understand all the sutras and vinayas— thereby deceiving both themselves and others— then when they confer the precepts upon others,
they commit a secondary offense (light defilement).
In the sutra, following the section on Bodhisattvas, the second part correctly raises the fault and concludes with the offense.

If one asks what distinguishes this from the eighteenth precept, the explanation is as follows: the eighteenth precept directly states the fault without explaining it as acting as a teacher for others;

this precept, however, differs because it concerns receiving a fee for bestowing the precepts upon others. To seek gain and profit while gathering and managing a retinue of disciples constitutes a defiled transgression.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If, due to the predominant power of attachment to offerings and service, one manages a circle of disciples with a mind of craving and defilement, this is called an offense;
it is a defiled transgression. There is no transgression if one manages a circle of disciples without craving for offerings and service and without a mind of craving and defilement.
According to this teaching, even if one has not yet investigated the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),..."
Seeking no profit, but with a mind conjoined with compassion, one should bestow [the precepts] according to one's capacity and strength;
there is no transgression in doing so, provided that the number and conditions [of the recipient] are understood as they truly are.
If a Buddha’s disciple,
for the third time, speaks the text of the precepts for others to hear, there are three parts: first, clarifying the designation of the person, as indicated by the words "If a Buddha’s disciple."

One must not, for the sake of gain or offerings, preach these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before those who have not received the Bodhisattva precepts, before non-Buddhists or evil persons, nor before those with wrong views.
With the exception of kings, one must not preach them to anyone else.
These evil people, who do not receive the Buddha’s precepts, are called animals; they shall not see the Triple Gem from lifetime to lifetime.
Those who are like wood or stone, devoid of mind, are called people of externalist heterodox views; they are no different from wooden stumps.
The Sūtra does not benefit them. This second section clarifies that one must not preach the precepts before those who have not yet received the precepts;
this means that before one has resolved to attain the Mahāyāna, one must not preach the ten Buddha-precepts, even if they have not yet formally received the precepts.

For those who have already made the great vow, it is faultless to explain [the precepts]; however, this statement that one may not recite the precepts before receiving them is spoken from a general perspective.
It is because most people who come to receive the bodhisattva precepts might give rise to fear or slander;
therefore, this restriction was established. The exception for kings and princes means that one should not fail to explain [the precepts] to them.
Because it destroys the Dharma, it is said that the "precepts of the thousand Buddhas" refer to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa;
if a Bodhisattva preaches the precepts taught by these seven Buddhas before such evil persons, they commit a secondary offense (light defilement).
Furthermore, the third section on the self-inflicted confession of offenses in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that the *Śīlaparivarta* (Holding the Ground) Sūtra, in its fourth fascicle, says:

"One who wishes to receive the precepts should first be told the characteristics of what constitutes an offense and what does not within the Bodhisattva precepts, so that the recipient may observe for themselves whether they are capable of receiving the precepts.
Moreover, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "Those who do not believe in or accept the teachings, and those who..."

One who has accomplished the Upāsaka precepts but has not accomplished the Śrāmaṇera precepts, nor the Prātimokṣa precepts, is not permitted to hear the Bodhisattva precepts; to hear them constitutes an offense.
If a Bhikṣu violates the Prātimokṣa precepts and, being neither ashamed nor remorseful, hears the Bodhisattva precepts, he incurs a Thullaccaya offense. If he commits a Thullaccaya offense...
Without shame and without regret, one hears the Bodhisattva precepts and incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. (Examination).
If a Buddha’s disciple...
[From here on] the fourth section below clarifies the precept on receiving offerings from those who have broken the precepts; this textual division has three parts: first, ...
Regarding the phrase "the person should not be the last to incur the offense," this refers to the person themselves.

Because they have left the household life with faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, one who conceives the thought of violating these holy precepts shall not receive the offerings of any donors, nor may they walk upon the ground of the king, nor drink the water of the king. Fifth.
A thousand great ghosts constantly obstruct his path, saying, "Great thief! When he enters houses, cities, or dwellings, these ghosts further sweep away his footprints.
All people of the world revile him, saying, "Thief within the Buddha-dharma!
No sentient being wishes to see such a person who violates the precepts; he is no different from a beast, no different from a block of wood."

Following the section on "arising from faith," this second part clarifies what should not be practiced: namely, that those who have broken the precepts should not receive offerings of faith and the like.
Regarding the term "great thieves": just as worldly thieves can plunder wealth and treasures and even take one's life, so too are these great thieves;
they can plunder the wisdom-life of others' *dharmakāya* and their constant [virtue].
Because it is a great jewel of merit such as [the sands of] the Ganges, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 15, states:
"A person who violates the precepts cannot be lived with, just as a wicked thief is difficult to approach;
a person who violates the precepts is difficult to dwell with, just like a venomous snake. Although a person who violates the precepts resembles a bhikṣu, he is like a corpse before one's eyes."
Among human beings, one who breaks the precepts is like a counterfeit pearl among genuine pearls, or like an *eranda* tree within a sandalwood grove.
If such a person who breaks the precepts wears the Dharma robes, they are merely wrapping their body in sheets of molten copper and iron.
If they hold an alms bowl, it is a vessel for boiling bronze. And whatever food they consume, they are merely swallowing [molten metal].
To swallow glowing iron balls or drink molten copper is to become a hell-guardian who watches over those receiving offerings and provisions;
to enter a vihāra is to enter a great hell; and to sit upon the seats and mats of the Saṃgha is to sit upon a bed of hot iron.
If one violates the true precepts, one commits a minor offense.
This concludes the third section on the determination of offenses from the sutra:
"O Sons of the Buddha."
In this sutra, from the fifth section onward, the text on the precept against failing to make offerings is divided into three parts, as can be understood from the previous [explanation].

One should always, with a single mind, receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahayana sutras and vinayas; even if one must flay one's own skin to serve as paper and draw blood to serve as ink, one should do so.
One should use marrow as ink, break bones to serve as pens, and write down the Buddha’s precepts upon tree bark, grain paper, silk, or bamboo slips;

these should all be transcribed and maintained. Furthermore, one should always use chests and bags made of the seven treasures, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels to store the volumes of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
One should frequently perform the second vidyā, which consists of six parts: first, receiving (*udgrahaṇa*), meaning to receive from before the teacher what was previously not understood;
second, maintaining (*dhāraṇa*), meaning not to forget after having received it; third, reading (*vācana*); fourth, reciting (*svādhyāya*);

fifth, transcribing (*lekhana*); and sixth, making offerings (*pūjana*). Regarding the fifth, transcribing, the text states "peeling off skin to serve as paper," etc., which serves as an illustration.
His mind was filled with such profound compassion for the Dharma that he did not spare even his own body or life, as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 18.
Furthermore, there was once a Brahmin who loved the Dharma; for twelve years, he traveled throughout Jambudvīpa seeking to know the noble Dharma but could not find it.
At that time, neither a Buddha existed in the world nor did the Buddha-Dharma remain; yet a certain Brāhmaṇa said to him, "I possess it."
"If you truly love the sublime Dharma, I shall give it to you. He replied, "I truly love the sublime Dharma.
The Brahmin said, "If you truly love the sublime Dharma, you must take your own skin as paper, your bones as a pen, and write with your blood;
then I shall give it to you. He did exactly as he was told, breaking his bones, flaying his skin, and writing the verse with his blood.
One should practice in accordance with the Dharma and should not accept what is contrary to the Dharma; the Buddha-Dharma brings peace and security both in this life and in future lives.
If one makes offerings that are not in accordance with the Dharma, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the sutras, if they are not in accordance with the Dharma, the third section on the determination of offenses states in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:

"If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), on any day [fails to perform offerings] to the Tathāgata or to a shrine (*caitya*) built for the Tathāgata;
or to the True Dharma (*saddharma*) or to a scripture (*pustaka*) made for the True Dharma; or to the Saṅgha..."

That is to say, if the assembly of Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions who have already entered the great stages were not to make offerings—whether small or great—with various articles of worship;
or were not to pay homage with at least one prostration of the body;
or were not to praise the true merits of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha with at least one four-line verse of speech; or were not to [offer] with at least one thought of the mind...
If one passes days and nights in vain without recollecting the Three Jewels with pure faith and according to their true qualities, it is called an offense.
If one commits this violation out of a lack of respect, indolence, or laziness, it is an afflicted offense;
if one commits it through a lapse of mindfulness, it is a non-afflicted offense. There is no offense if the mind is deranged or [if...]
Having entered the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśaya-bhūmi*), one is forever free from transgressions.
If a disciple of the Buddha constantly gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*) and enters any city, town, or house, upon seeing any sentient beings, they should proclaim:
"All you sentient beings, you should all receive the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts. If they see oxen, horses, pigs, or...
Regarding all sheep and other animals, one should mentally reflect and verbally declare: "You are animals; arouse the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva enters any place—be it mountains, rivers, forests, or fields—they must cause all sentient beings therein to arouse the bodhicitta.
If a Bodhisattva does not arouse the mind to teach and transform sentient beings in this way, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
In this sutra, from "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards, the sixth precept concerning the failure to teach and transform sentient beings is divided into three sections.
This first section identifies the person [who commits the offense]. From "One should always give rise to great compassion" onwards, the second section clarifies what should be practiced.
Regarding the "Three Refuges," as stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*: "Good son, in order to destroy all sufferings and sever all..."
Because of the afflictions and the sensation of sorrow regarding the unsurpassed bliss of quiescent extinction, one takes the three refuges for this reason.
As to what you asked regarding what constitutes the three refuges: Good son, they are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
The Buddha is the one who can teach the Dharma that abandons the causes of affliction and attains right liberation; the Dharma is precisely that which abandons the causes of affliction.
The Sangha of true liberation refers to those who have destroyed the causes of affliction and attained right liberation. Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast" states:
"Good son, if a person can receive the three refuges, you should know that the karmic fruit obtained by this person is inexhaustible," and so forth, as extensively explained.
It further says that for one who receives and maintains the precept of speech without forgetting, the fruit is manifested in the present body.
Because one who attains the rank of king and observes the eight precepts for a single day and night can be reborn in the heavens, the fifteenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a butcher named Viśālakṣa who slaughtered countless sheep at midday.
Śāriputra then received the eight precepts from him for one day and one night. By this cause and condition, when his life ended, he attained [rebirth in heaven]."
Regarding the *Sūtra on Being the Son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North*, if one does not transform [others], it constitutes an offense as explained below in the third section.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "To gather disciples while harboring a mind of resentment and failing to provide timely and unerring instruction is called an offense; it is a defiled transgression."

If a Buddha’s disciple constantly practices teaching and transformation, giving rise to a heart of great compassion, they must not stand when entering the homes of wealthy patrons (*dānapati*) or among all the assemblies to preach the Dharma to laypeople.
Before an assembly of laypeople, a *dharmabhāṇaka* bhikṣu must sit upon a high seat;
he must not stand on the ground to preach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly. When preaching the Dharma, the *dharmabhāṇaka* shall occupy a high seat [adorned with] incense...

One should offer flowers as an act of worship to the fourfold assembly of listeners, rising from one's seat; one should be as filial and obedient toward parents and respectful and compliant toward the teacher’s instructions as a fire-worshipping Brahmin.
If the one who preaches the Dharma does not preach in accordance with the Dharma, they commit a minor offense.
In this sutra, from the seventh section below, "The Precept on Teaching the Dharma Unlawfully," the text is divided into four parts:
first, the identification of the person and the constant practice; second, from "If one does not teach the Dharma," the explanation of what should not be practiced;
third, from "One who teaches the Dharma," the explanation of what should be done; and fourth, the conclusion regarding the offense.
The text is intelligible.
If there are sons of the Buddha who have received the Buddha’s precepts with faith— whether they be kings, crown princes, officials, or disciples of the fourfold assembly— if they,
relying on their own high status and nobility, destroy the Buddha-dharma and its precepts by openly establishing restrictive laws to constrain the fourfold assembly;
If a Bodhisattva intentionally prevents his disciples from leaving the household life to practice the Way, or likewise prevents them from creating images of the Buddha or constructing stupas,
sutras, and vinaya— thereby destroying the Three Jewels— he commits a secondary offense of defilement.
In this sutra, from the eighth section below, "The Precept Against Destroying the Dharma through Arrogance," the text is divided into two parts:

first, the identification of the person; second, the citation of the transgression and the determination of the offense. This [first part] identifies the person. As for the phrase "All those who, with faith... and so forth, the second part cites the transgression and determines the offense.
It first clarifies the fault and then determines the offense; thus, one should understand the manifestation of the fault according to the text. Sutra.
Furthermore, the second offense is established as a deliberate act.
If a disciple of the Buddha, having left the household life with a sincere heart, yet for the sake of fame and profit, preaches the precepts of the Seven Buddhas before kings and officials,
and arbitrarily binds bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or disciples of the bodhisattva precepts [with worldly constraints], it is an offense.
The worms within a lion’s body eat the lion’s own flesh; it cannot be destroyed by external paths or celestial Māras.
One who has received the Buddha’s precepts should protect them as one would cherish an only child or serve one's parents.

Yet, when hearing externalists or evil persons slander the Buddha’s precepts with wicked words, it is as if three hundred spears pierce one’s heart, or as if struck by a thousand swords and ten thousand staves.
Since their bodies are equal and without distinction, one would rather enter hell for a hundred kalpas than hear the sound of a single evil word regarding the breaking of the Buddha’s precepts,
let alone break the Buddha’s precepts oneself or teach others to do so. Because such actions destroy the causes and conditions of the Dharma and lack the heart of filial piety,
to act intentionally constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).

In this sutra, from the ninth precept downward—concerning the breaking of the Dharma and its personal conditions—the internal meaning is the destruction of harmony, while the external benefit is the severance of faith and joy;
therefore, it is thus prescribed. The text is divided into three parts, as should be understood according to the text.
As for the above nine precepts, they should be understood as obstacles to the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) as appropriate.
These nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind.
Following these nine precepts, the second section explains the exhortation to uphold them; above this, the individual explanations of the forty-eight minor precepts have been set forth.
"O sons of the Buddha, you must receive and uphold these forty-eight minor precepts. All Bodhisattvas of the past have already studied them;
all Bodhisattvas of the future shall study them; and all Bodhisattvas of the present are now studying them."
"O Sons of the Buddha, these are the forty-eight minor precepts. This concludes the third section, the general exhortation to receive and uphold them.

Above this was the second section, the explanation of the forty-eight minor precepts. Within that, there were two parts: first, the explanation of the ten major precepts, and second, the explanation of the minor precepts.
Now, the second part, the formal explanation of the characteristics of the precepts, is complete.

"Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! These ten grave and forty-eight light precepts have been recited by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—those of the past, those of the future, and those of the present—and I now likewise recite them.
All of you in this great assembly—whether kings, princes, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, or laywomen who have received and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts—should receive and uphold them."

Those who read, recite, explain, copy, and circulate this scroll on the eternally abiding Buddha-nature and precepts throughout the three periods of time will cause the transformations of all sentient beings to continue without end;
they shall behold a thousand Buddhas, with each Buddha extending a hand to them, never falling into the evil realms or the eight difficulties, and always being reborn among humans or in the heavens.
Now, beneath this tree, I briefly expound the Dharma-precepts of the Seven Buddhas for you all.
One should single-mindedly study the Prātimokṣa and joyfully practice it,
as is extensively explained in detail for each of the three thousand scholars within the "Exhortation to Study" section of the *Animitta-devaputra-parivarta*.

In the third section, following the disciples’ hearing of the sutra, there is a general exhortation for its circulation, which contains two parts: first, the Buddha’s exhortation to uphold and circulate it;

second, the bodhisattvas’ practice thereof. Within the former, there are five points: first, the Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—have already recited and will recite this, serving as proof that it is not false;
second, "You all" and so forth, which is the actual exhortation for circulation; third, attaining [the vision of] a thousand Buddhas...
The following clarifies the four benefits of the propagation [of this teaching]. First, "I now" and below encourages the present upholding.

Fifth, as in the "Chapter on Signlessness," the locations where it will be expounded are indicated in advance. Regarding the three thousand learners, although there are five textual sections such as the "Threefold Vinaya of Dignified Conduct," the first section concludes with the Tathāgata’s exhortation for the propagation and upholding [of the teaching].
At that time, those in the assembly who heard the Buddha recite it themselves received and upheld it with joy, honoring it in their hearts.
After some time, the second bodhisattva among those sitting and listening descended to practice what he had been taught. Above, the correct exposition has been completed in two parts;
this concludes the first.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha completed the teaching on the Chapter of the Ten Inexhaustible Precepts within the Chapter on the Mind-Ground Dharma-Door of Vairocana Buddha in the World of the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury; the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis likewise taught this,
from the palace of King Māheśvara up to this site beneath the Bodhi tree, in the Chapter on the Teaching at the Ten Abodes.
For the sake of the unspeakably vast assembly of all bodhisattvas, he likewise upholds, recites, and explains its meaning:
the treasury of the mind of all Buddhas, the treasury of the earth, the treasury of the precepts,
the treasury of immeasurable practices and vows, and the treasury of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature of cause and effect.
At that time, Śākyamuni himself set forth the second major section, which provides a summary of what was previously explained regarding the "Heart-Treasury.
The ten world-oceans are called the Heart-Treasury. The "Earth-Treasury" refers to the forty stages of mind (*citta-bhūmi*). The "Precept-Treasury" concludes the inexhaustible precepts.
The "Infinite Practices and Vows" refers to the ten patiences (*kṣānti*) and so forth as the infinite practices, and the ten great vows.

The phrase "the causes and fruits of immeasurable vows" summarizes what was previously stated: that the precepts are the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the seed of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Furthermore, the statement "because there is a cause for each successive stage, there is the eternally abiding Dharma-body Buddha-nature in each successive stage" summarizes what was previously stated: that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Thus, as all Buddhas have expounded the entire, immeasurable treasury of all dharmas, all sentient beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of worlds receive,
uphold, rejoice in, and practice them. If one were to extensively open the characteristics of the mind-ground,
these characteristics are as explained in the "Seven Practices Chapter" of the *Buddhāvatamsaka-rāja-sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "The Sūtra as it truly is, spoken by all Buddhas," etc., within this there are three major sections: first, the Introduction;
second, the Main Exposition; and third, the Distribution. From here below begins the third section, which clarifies the Distribution.
I prostrate to the Unsurpassed Great Teacher, Who possesses unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena,
The Greatly Compassionate One who rescues and protects all;
To the Bodhisattvas who have realized the two kinds of emptiness Within the ocean of profound and subtle sūtras, And to all others who have made great vows.
Now, relying on the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*, I shall briefly explain the pure precepts of the bodhisattva and determine the distinctions between their observance and violation.
Having received these subtle roots of goodness from the Buddha, the noble Maitreya, and others,
may those with discernment bestow them as gifts and realize the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
The wise person, strong in patience and wisdom, Is able to uphold such a Dharma.
Before attaining the path of Buddhahood, they securely obtain five kinds of benefits: First, the Buddhas of the ten directions Pity them and constantly protect them;
Second, at the time of death, They possess right view and their mind is joyful; Third, in every place where they are born...
A pure friend to bodhisattvas, possessing a fourfold mass of merit;

having fully accomplished the perfection of ethical discipline, he is endowed with the nature of morality and the fullness of merit and wisdom in both this life and future lives. This is the sphere of activity of the Buddhas;
the wise should contemplate it well. Those who calculate in terms of a self and cling to signs cannot believe in this Dharma.
The one who has realized the cessation of grasping Is likewise not a place for planting seeds.
Desiring to grow the sprout of Bodhi And to illuminate the world with light, One should contemplate in stillness The true nature of all phenomena:
Neither arising nor ceasing, Neither eternal nor annihilated, Neither identical nor different.

Neither coming nor going—within such a single mind, The Bodhisattva should perform their duties through skillful means and diligent adornment, And should train in them according to the proper sequence.
Regarding those in training and those beyond training, one should not give rise to discriminatory thoughts; This is called the foremost path, And it is also called the Mahāyāna.
All bases of conceptual proliferation are entirely extinguished from this source;
all the *sarvajñā* (omniscience) of the Buddhas emerges from this source.
Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, you should rouse great valor regarding the pure precepts of the Buddhas, guarding and upholding them like a bright jewel, as did the Bodhisattvas of the past.
Those who have already trained in this, those yet to come shall train, and those of the present are training now—
this is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity, praised by the Holy Lord. Having followed [the teaching] and spoken thus,
may this immeasurable mass of merit be dedicated to sentient beings, so that we may together proceed toward omniscience.
May those who hear this Dharma swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.
*Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra*, Scroll Lower End (Great Tail).
